chapters.title: Book 1
paragraphs: Every state is a kind of community, and every community is established with a view to some good — for human beings always act in order to obtain what they take to be good. But if all communities aim at some good, then the state, or political community, which is the highest of all and embraces all the rest, aims at the highest good, and to a greater degree than any other.

There is a mistaken view that the statesman, the king, the head of a household, and the master of slaves are all the same, differing not in kind but only in the number of those they govern. On this view, the ruler over a few is called a master; over more, the manager of a household; over a still larger number, a statesman or king — as though there were no real difference between a great household and a small state. The supposed difference between king and statesman is this: when the rule is personal, the ruler is a king; when, on the principles of political science, citizens rule and are ruled in turn, he is called a statesman.

But all this is a mistake, for governments differ in kind. This will be evident to anyone who follows the method we have used so far. As in other branches of inquiry, so in politics, the compound should always be resolved into its simplest elements or smallest parts. We must therefore look at the elements that make up the state, in order to see how they differ from one another, and whether any scientific distinction can be drawn between the different forms of rule.

Whoever considers things in their first growth and origin — whether a state or anything else — will obtain the clearest view of them. In the first place, there must be a union of those who cannot exist without each other. There is the union of male and female, that the race may continue. This union is not formed from deliberate purpose, but because, like other animals and plants, human beings have a natural desire to leave behind an image of themselves. There must also be a union of natural ruler and subject, so that both may be preserved. For the one who can foresee with his mind is by nature intended to be lord and master, while the one who can work with his body is a subject, and by nature a slave; hence master and slave have the same interest. Nature, however, has distinguished between the female and the slave. She is not stingy, like the smith who fashions the Delphian knife for many uses; she makes each thing for a single purpose, and every instrument is best made when intended for one use and not for many. Among the barbarians, however, no distinction is made between women and slaves, because there is no natural ruler among them: they are a community of slaves, male and female. Hence the poets say —
‘It is fitting that Hellenes should rule over barbarians’ — as though they thought the barbarian and the slave were by nature one and the same.
Out of these two relationships — between man and woman, master and slave — the family first arises. Hesiod is right when he says,

‘First a house, and a wife, and an ox for the plough’ — for the ox is the poor man’s slave. The family is the association established by nature for the supply of men’s daily needs. Its members are called by Charondas ‘companions of the cupboard’ [omosipuous], and by Epimenides the Cretan ‘companions of the manger’ [omokapous]. But when several families are united, and the association aims at something more than the supply of daily needs, the village comes into being. The most natural form of village appears to be a colony from the family, made up of the children and grandchildren, who are said to be ‘suckled with the same milk.’ This is why Hellenic states were originally governed by kings: the Hellenes were under royal rule before they came together, as the barbarians still are. Every family is ruled by the eldest, and so in the colonies of the family the kingly form of government prevailed, since they were of the same blood. As Homer says of the Cyclopes:
‘Each one gives law to his children and to his wives.’

For they lived dispersedly, as was the manner in ancient times. This is why men say the gods have a king — because they themselves are, or in ancient times were, under the rule of a king. They imagine not only the forms of the gods, but also their ways of life, to be like their own.

When several villages are united in a single community, complete and large enough to be nearly or wholly self-sufficient, the state comes into being. It originates in the bare needs of life, but it continues to exist for the sake of a good life. And so, if the earlier forms of society are natural, so too is the state, for it is their end, and the completed nature is the end. What each thing is when fully developed we call its nature, whether we are speaking of a man, a horse, or a family. Besides, the final cause and end of a thing is the best, and self-sufficiency is the end and the best.

Hence it is evident that the state is a creation of nature, and that man is by nature a political animal. He who is by nature, and not by mere accident, without a state, is either above humanity or below it. He is the
‘Tribeless, lawless, hearthless one’ whom Homer denounces — the outcast who is a lover of war, who may be compared to an unprotected piece in the game of draughts.

Why man is more of a political animal than bees or any other gregarious animal is evident. Nature, as we often say, makes nothing in vain, and man is the only animal she has endowed with the gift of speech. Mere sound is only an indication of pleasure or pain, and is therefore found in other animals — their nature reaches as far as the perception of pleasure and pain and the intimation of these to one another, and no further. The power of speech, however, is meant to set forth what is expedient and inexpedient, and likewise the just and the unjust. It is the special characteristic of man that he alone has any sense of good and evil, of just and unjust; and the association of living beings who share this sense makes a family and a state.

Thus the state is by nature clearly prior to the family and to the individual, since the whole is necessarily prior to the part. If the whole body be destroyed, there will be no foot or hand except in an equivocal sense — as we might speak of a stone hand; for once destroyed the hand will be no better than that. Things are defined by their function and capacity, and we should not say they are the same when they are no longer the same, but only that they share the same name. The proof that the state is a creation of nature and prior to the individual is that the individual, when isolated, is not self-sufficient, and is therefore like a part in relation to the whole. He who is unable to live in society, or who has no need to because he is sufficient for himself, must be either a beast or a god — he is no part of a state. A social instinct is implanted in all men by nature, and yet whoever first founded the state was the greatest of benefactors. For man, when perfected, is the best of animals, but when separated from law and justice he is the worst of all. Armed injustice is the more dangerous, and he is equipped at birth with the weapons of intelligence and with moral qualities which he may use for the worst ends. So if he lacks virtue, he is the most unholy and the most savage of animals, the most full of lust and gluttony. Justice is the bond of men in states, and the administration of justice — the determination of what is just — is the principle of order in political society.

Since the state is made up of households, before speaking of the state we must speak of the management of the household. The parts of the household are the persons who compose it, and a complete household consists of slaves and freemen. We should begin by examining everything in its smallest elements, and the first and smallest parts of a family are master and slave, husband and wife, father and children. We have therefore to consider what each of these three relations is and ought to be — the relation of master and servant, of husband and wife, and thirdly of parent and child. (I say gamike and teknopoietike, there being no adequate words for the latter two relations.) There is another element of a household as well: the so-called art of money-making, which according to some is identical with household management, and according to others, a principal part of it. The nature of this art will also have to be considered.

Let us first speak of master and slave, with an eye both to the needs of practical life and to attaining a better theory of their relation than now exists. Some hold that the rule of a master is a science, and that the management of a household, the mastership of slaves, and political and royal rule are all the same — as I said at the outset. Others affirm that the rule of a master over slaves is contrary to nature, that the distinction between slave and freeman exists by law only and not by nature, and that, since it is an interference with nature, it is therefore unjust.

Property is part of the household, and therefore the art of acquiring property is part of the art of managing the household — for no man can live well, or indeed live at all, unless he is provided with the necessaries of life. And as in the arts which have a definite sphere the workers must have the proper instruments for accomplishing their work, so it is in the management of a household. Instruments are of various kinds: some are living, others lifeless. The pilot of a ship has a lifeless instrument in the rudder, and a living one in the look-out man — for in the arts the servant is a kind of instrument. A possession, too, is an instrument for maintaining life. And so, in the arrangement of the family, a slave is a living possession, and property is a number of such instruments. The servant is himself an instrument that takes precedence of all others. For if every instrument could accomplish its own work, obeying or anticipating the will of others — like the statues of Daedalus, or the tripods of Hephaestus, which, the poet says,

‘of their own accord entered the assembly of the Gods’; or if, in the same way, the shuttle would weave and the plectrum touch the lyre without a hand to guide them — then master craftsmen would not need servants, nor masters slaves. Another distinction, however, must be drawn here: the instruments commonly so called are instruments of production, whereas a possession is an instrument of action. The shuttle, for example, is not only of use; something else is made by it. With a garment or a bed, on the other hand, there is only the use. Further, since production and action differ in kind, and both require instruments, the instruments they employ must likewise differ in kind. But life is action, not production, and therefore the slave is the minister of action — for he ministers to his master’s life. Again, a possession is spoken of in the way a part is spoken of: for a part is not only a part of something else, but wholly belongs to it; and this is also true of a possession. The master is only the master of the slave; he does not belong to him. The slave, however, is not only the slave of his master, but wholly belongs to him. Hence we see the nature and office of a slave: he who is by nature not his own but another’s, and yet is a man, is by nature a slave. He may be said to belong to another who, being a human being, is also a possession. A possession may be defined as an instrument of action, separable from the possessor.
But is there anyone marked out by nature to be a slave, for whom such a condition is expedient and right? Or is all slavery a violation of nature?

There is no difficulty in answering this question, on grounds both of reason and of fact. For that some should rule and others be ruled is a thing not only necessary but expedient. From the hour of their birth, some are marked out for subjection, others for rule.

There are many kinds of rulers and subjects, and the rule which is exercised over better subjects is itself the better — to rule over men, for example, is better than to rule over wild beasts. The work that is done by better workmen is the better work, and where one rules and another is ruled, they may be said to share in a common task. In all things which form a composite whole made up of parts — whether continuous or discrete — a distinction between the ruling and the subject element comes to light. Such a duality exists in living creatures, but not in them only; it originates in the constitution of the universe. Even in things that have no life there is a ruling principle, as in musical harmony. But we are wandering from the subject. Let us therefore restrict ourselves to the living creature, which in the first place consists of soul and body. Of these two, the one is by nature ruler and the other subject. We must, however, look for the intentions of nature in things that retain their nature, not in things that are corrupted. We must therefore study the man who is in the most perfect state both of body and soul, for in him we shall see the true relation of the two — though in bad or corrupted natures the body will often appear to rule over the soul, because they are in an evil and unnatural condition. First, then, we may observe in living creatures both a despotic and a constitutional rule. The soul rules the body with a despotic rule, while the intellect rules the appetites with a constitutional and royal rule. It is clear that the rule of the soul over the body, and of the mind and the rational element over the passionate, is natural and expedient — whereas the equality of the two, or the rule of the inferior, is always harmful. The same holds of animals as well as men. Tame animals have a better nature than wild ones, and all tame animals are better off when they are ruled by man, for they are then preserved. Again, the male is by nature superior, the female inferior; the one rules and the other is ruled. This principle, of necessity, extends to all mankind. Where there is such a difference as that between soul and body, or between men and animals — as in the case of those whose business is to use their body and who can do nothing better — the lower sort are by nature slaves, and it is better for them, as for all inferiors, that they should be under the rule of a master. For he who can be, and therefore is, another’s, and who participates in reason just enough to apprehend it but not to possess it, is a slave by nature. The lower animals cannot even apprehend reason; they obey their instincts. Indeed the use made of slaves and of tame animals is not very different, for both with their bodies minister to the needs of life. Nature would like to distinguish between the bodies of freemen and slaves, making the one strong for servile labour, the other upright — and although useless for such service, useful for political life in the arts both of war and peace. But this does not hold universally: for some slaves have the souls, and others the bodies, of freemen. And surely if men differed from one another in the mere forms of their bodies as much as the statues of the gods do from men, all would acknowledge that the inferior class should be slaves of the superior. If there is a difference in the body, how much more must there be in the soul? But the beauty of the body is seen, whereas the beauty of the soul is not seen. It is clear, then, that some men are by nature free and others slaves, and that for these latter slavery is both expedient and right.

Yet that those who take the opposite view have a certain right on their side may also be easily seen. The words ‘slavery’ and ‘slave’ are used in two senses. There is a slave or slavery by law, as well as by nature. The law I speak of is a kind of convention, according to which whatever is taken in war belongs to the victors. Many jurists impeach this right, as they would an orator who proposed an unconstitutional measure: they detest the notion that, because one man has the power to do violence and is superior in brute strength, another should be his slave and subject. Even among philosophers there is disagreement. The origin of the dispute, and the reason the arguments cross, is this. Virtue, when furnished with means, may be deemed to have the greatest power of doing violence; and since superior power is only found where there is superior excellence of some kind, power is thought to imply virtue. But does it likewise imply justice? That is the question. To draw a distinction between them, some assert that justice is benevolence, while others reply that justice is nothing more than the rule of a superior. If the two views are taken as antagonistic and exclusive — that is, if the notion that justice is benevolence excludes the idea of a just rule by a superior — then the alternative, namely that no one should rule over others, has no force or plausibility, since it implies that not even the one superior in virtue ought to rule or be master. Some, clinging as they think to a principle of justice (for law and custom are a kind of justice), assume that slavery in war is justified by law — but they are not consistent. For what if the cause of the war is unjust? No one would ever say that someone unworthy to be a slave is rightly a slave. If that were so, men of the highest rank would be slaves, and the children of slaves, if they or their parents happened to have been taken captive and sold. This is why Hellenes do not like to call themselves slaves, but confine the term to barbarians. Yet in using this language they really mean the natural slave we spoke of at first; for it must be admitted that some are slaves everywhere, others nowhere. The same principle applies to nobility. Hellenes regard themselves as noble everywhere, not only in their own country, but they consider barbarians noble only at home — implying that there are two sorts of nobility and freedom: the one absolute, the other relative. The Helen of Theodectes says,
‘Who would presume to call me servant, when on both sides I am sprung from the stem of the gods?’

What else can this mean, except that they use goodness and badness to distinguish freedom from slavery and noble birth from low birth? They suppose that, just as human beings produce human beings and animals produce animals, good men must produce a good man. Nature may aim at this result, but she often fails to achieve it.

We see, then, that there is some foundation for this difference of opinion, and that some actual slaves and freemen are not so by nature, while in some cases there is a marked distinction between the two classes — making it expedient and right for the one to be slaves and the others masters: the one practising obedience, the other exercising the authority nature intended them to have. The abuse of this authority is harmful to both, for the interests of part and whole, of body and soul, are the same; the slave is a part of the master, a living but separated part of his bodily frame. Where the relation between them is natural, they are friends and have a common interest; where it rests merely on law and force, the reverse is true.

The previous remarks are quite enough to show that the rule of a master is not a constitutional rule, and therefore that all the different kinds of rule are not, as some affirm, the same. There is one rule exercised over subjects who are by nature free, and another over subjects who are by nature slaves. The rule of a household is a monarchy, for every house is under one head; whereas constitutional rule is government of freemen and equals. The master is not called a master because he has science, but because he is of a certain character — and the same applies to the slave and the freeman. Still, there may be a science for the master and a science for the slave. The science of the slave would be like that taught by the man of Syracuse, who made money by instructing slaves in their ordinary duties. Such knowledge may be carried further, to include cookery and similar menial arts. Some duties are of the more necessary, others of the more honourable sort — as the proverb says, ‘slave before slave, master before master.’ But all such branches of knowledge are servile. There is likewise a science of the master, which teaches the use of slaves; for the master as such is concerned not with the acquisition of slaves but with their use. Yet this so-called science is nothing great or wonderful, since the master need only know how to order what the slave must know how to execute. Hence those whose position places them above toil have stewards to attend to their households, while they occupy themselves with philosophy or with politics. The art of acquiring slaves — the art, that is, of justly acquiring them — differs both from the art of the master and the art of the slave, being a species of hunting or war. Enough, then, of the distinction between master and slave.

Let us now inquire into property generally, and into the art of money-making, in accordance with our usual method of resolving a whole into its parts — for the slave has been shown to be a part of property. The first question is whether the art of money-making is the same as the art of managing a household, or a part of it, or merely instrumental to it; and if instrumental, whether in the way that the art of making shuttles is instrumental to weaving, or in the way that the casting of bronze is instrumental to the art of the statuary. For these are not instrumental in the same way: the one provides tools, the other material — and by material I mean the substratum out of which any work is made. Wool is the material of the weaver, bronze of the statuary. It is easy to see that household management is not identical with the art of money-making, for the one uses the material the other provides. The art that uses household stores can be no other than the art of household management. There is, however, some doubt whether the art of money-making is a part of household management or a distinct art. They appear to be connected, since the money-maker has to consider where money and property can be procured. But there are many sorts of property and wealth. There is husbandry, and the care and provision of food in general — are these parts of the money-making art, or distinct arts? Again, there are many sorts of food, and therefore many kinds of lives, both of animals and men. They must all have food, and the differences in their food have produced differences in their ways of life. Of beasts, some are gregarious, others solitary; they live in the way best adapted to sustain them, according to whether they are carnivorous, herbivorous, or omnivorous. Their habits are determined by nature in such a way that they may obtain the food of their choice with greater ease. But since different individuals have different tastes, the same things are not naturally pleasant to all of them; and so even the lives of carnivorous and of herbivorous animals differ further among themselves. In the lives of men, too, there is great variety. The laziest are shepherds, who lead an idle life and get their subsistence without trouble from tame animals; their flocks must wander from place to place in search of pasture, and the shepherds are compelled to follow them, cultivating a kind of living farm. Others support themselves by hunting, which is of various kinds. Some are pirates; others, who dwell near lakes, marshes, rivers, or a sea where there are fish, are fishermen; others live by pursuing birds or wild beasts. The greater number obtain a living from the fruits of the soil. These are the modes of subsistence which prevail among those whose industry is employed directly upon the products of nature, whose food is not acquired by exchange or retail trade — there is the shepherd, the husbandman, the pirate, the fisherman, the hunter. Some gain a comfortable living from two employments combined, eking out the deficiencies of one with another: the life of a shepherd may be combined with that of a brigand, the life of a farmer with that of a hunter. Other modes of life are similarly combined, in any way the needs of men may require. Property, in the sense of a bare livelihood, seems to be given by nature herself to all, both at birth and when they are grown. Some animals bring forth, along with their offspring, enough food to last until the young can supply themselves — the vermiparous and oviparous animals are an instance — and the viviparous animals carry within themselves, up to a certain point, a supply of food for their young, which is called milk. In the same way we may infer that, after the birth of animals, plants exist for the sake of animals, and the other animals exist for the sake of man — the tame for use and food, the wild, if not all, at least the greater part of them, for food and for the provision of clothing and various instruments. Now if nature makes nothing incomplete and nothing in vain, the inference must be that she has made all animals and plants for the sake of man. And so, in one point of view, the art of war is a natural art of acquisition, for it includes hunting — an art we ought to practise against wild beasts and against those men who, though intended by nature to be governed, will not submit. War of this kind is naturally just.

Of the art of acquisition, then, there is one kind which is natural and is part of the management of a household. Either we must suppose the necessaries of life to exist beforehand, or the art of household management must provide a store of them for the common use of the family or state. They are the elements of true wealth, for the amount of property needed for a good life is not unlimited — although Solon in one of his poems says that
‘No bound to riches has been fixed for man.’

But there is a boundary fixed, just as there is in the arts: for the instruments of any art are never unlimited in number or in size, and wealth may be defined as a number of instruments to be used in a household or in a state. So we see that there is a natural art of acquisition, practised by managers of households and by statesmen, and we have seen the reason for it.

There is another variety of the art of acquisition which is commonly and rightly called the art of making money, and which has in fact suggested the notion that wealth and property have no limit. Being closely connected with the preceding, it is often identified with it. Yet though they are not very different, neither are they the same. The kind already described is given by nature; the other is gained by experience and art.
Let us begin our discussion of the matter with the following considerations.

Of everything we possess there are two uses, both belonging to the thing as such, but not in the same way: one is the proper, the other the improper or secondary use. A shoe, for example, is used for wear and is used for exchange — both are uses of the shoe. He who gives a shoe in exchange for money or food to someone who needs one does indeed use the shoe as a shoe, but this is not its proper or primary purpose, for a shoe is not made to be an object of barter. The same may be said of all possessions, for the art of exchange extends to all of them. It arises at first in a natural manner from the fact that some have too little and others too much. Hence we may infer that retail trade is not a natural part of the art of money-making; had it been so, men would have ceased to exchange when they had enough. In the first community, which is the family, this art is obviously of no use, but only begins to be useful when the society increases. The members of the family originally had all things in common; in a more divided state of society they still shared in many things, but had different things to give in exchange for what they wanted — a kind of barter that is still practised among barbarous nations who exchange with one another the necessaries of life and nothing more, giving and receiving wine, for example, in exchange for corn and the like. This sort of barter is not part of the money-making art and is not contrary to nature, but is needed for the satisfaction of men’s natural wants. The other and more complex form of exchange grew out of the simpler. When the inhabitants of one country became more dependent on those of another, importing what they needed and exporting their surplus, money necessarily came into use. The various necessaries of life are not easily carried about, and so men agreed to employ in their dealings with one another something which was intrinsically useful and easily applicable to the purposes of life — for example, iron, silver, and the like. Its value was at first measured by size and weight, but in time they put a stamp upon it, to save the trouble of weighing and to mark the value.

Once the use of coin had been discovered, out of the barter of necessary articles arose the other art of money-making — namely, retail trade. This was at first probably a simple matter, but became more complicated as soon as men learned by experience from where, and by what exchanges, the greatest profit might be made. Originating in the use of coin, the art of money-making is generally thought to be chiefly concerned with it, and to be the art that produces wealth and money — having to consider how they may be accumulated. Indeed, wealth is assumed by many to be only a quantity of coin, because the art of money-making and retail trade are concerned with coin. Others maintain that coined money is a mere sham, a thing not natural but only conventional, which would have no value or use for any of the purposes of daily life if another commodity were substituted by the users. And indeed, the man who is rich in coin may often be in want of necessary food. How can that be wealth which a man may have in great abundance and yet perish of hunger — like Midas in the fable, whose insatiable prayer turned everything set before him into gold?

Men seek a better notion of wealth and of the art of making money than the mere acquisition of coin, and they are right to do so. Natural wealth and the natural art of money-making are a different thing; in their true form they are part of the management of a household. Retail trade, by contrast, is the art of producing wealth — not in every way, but by exchange. It seems to be concerned with coin, for coin is the starting-point and the goal of exchange. There is no bound to the wealth that springs from this art of money-making. As in the art of medicine there is no limit to the pursuit of health, and as in the other arts there is no limit to the pursuit of their several ends — for they aim at accomplishing their ends to the uttermost (though of the means there is a limit, since the end is always the limit) — so too in this art of money-making there is no limit to the end, which is wealth of the spurious kind, namely the acquisition of money. But the art of household management has a limit: the unlimited acquisition of money is not its business. And so, from one point of view, all wealth must have a limit. Yet in fact we find the opposite to be the case, for all money-makers increase their hoard of coin without limit. The source of the confusion is the close connection between the two kinds of money-making. In either, the instrument — that is, wealth — is the same, although the use is different, and so they pass into one another. Each is a use of the same property, but with a difference: accumulation is the end in the one case, while there is a further end in the other. Hence some are led to believe that making money is the object of household management, and the whole idea of their lives is that they ought either to increase their money without limit, or at least not to lose it. The origin of this disposition is that they are intent only on living, not on living well; and since their desires are unlimited, they also desire that the means of gratifying them should be without limit. Even those who aim at a good life seek the means of obtaining bodily pleasures, and since the enjoyment of these appears to depend on property, they are absorbed in making money. So arises the second species of money-making. As their enjoyment is in excess, they seek an art that produces excess of enjoyment; and if they are unable to supply their pleasures by the art of money-making, they try other arts, using in turn every faculty in a manner contrary to nature. The quality of courage, for example, is not intended to make money, but to inspire confidence; nor is this the aim of the general’s art or the physician’s — the one aims at victory, the other at health. Yet some men turn every quality and every art into a means of making money. This they conceive to be the end, and to its promotion all things must contribute.

Thus we have considered the unnecessary art of money-making, and why men want it; we have also considered the necessary art of money-making, which we have seen to be different from the other, and to be a natural part of the art of managing a household, concerned with the provision of food — not, however, like the former kind, unlimited, but having a limit.

And we have found the answer to our original question, whether the art of money-making is the business of the manager of a household and of the statesman or not — namely, that it is an art presupposed by them. Political science does not make men, but takes them from nature and uses them; and nature provides them with food from the element of earth, air, or sea. At this stage begins the duty of the manager of a household, who has to order the things nature supplies. He may be compared to the weaver, who has not to make but to use wool, and to know what sort of wool is good and serviceable, what sort bad and unserviceable. Were this otherwise, it would be hard to see why the art of money-making is part of household management, while the art of medicine is not — for surely the members of a household must have health just as they must have life or any other necessity. From one point of view the master of the house and the ruler of the state have to consider health; from another, not they but the physician. So in one way the art of household management, in another the subordinate art, has to consider money. Strictly speaking, however, as I have already said, the means of life must be provided beforehand by nature; for the business of nature is to furnish food to that which is born, and the food of the offspring always remains over in the parent. Hence the art of making money out of fruits and animals is always natural.

Of the two sorts of money-making, one, as I have just said, is part of household management, the other is retail trade. The former is necessary and honourable; the latter is a kind of exchange that is justly censured, for it is unnatural, and a mode by which men gain at one another’s expense. The most hated sort, and with the greatest reason, is usury, which makes a gain out of money itself, not from the natural use of it. Money was intended to be used in exchange, not to increase at interest. The very term ‘usury’ — tokos, meaning the birth of money from money — is applied to the breeding of money because the offspring resembles the parent. Of all modes of making money, this is the most unnatural.

Enough has been said about the theory of money-making; we will now turn to the practical part. The discussion of such matters is not unworthy of philosophy, but to be engaged in them practically is illiberal and irksome. The useful parts of money-making are, first, knowledge of livestock — which kinds are most profitable, and where, and how. For example, what sort of horses, sheep, oxen, or other animals are most likely to give a return. A man ought to know which of these pay better than others, and which pay best in particular places, for some do better in one place and some in another. Secondly, husbandry, which may be either tillage or planting; and the keeping of bees, of fish, of fowl, or of any animals useful to man. These are the divisions of the true or proper art of money-making, and they come first. Of the other kind, which consists in exchange, the first and most important division is commerce — of which there are three kinds: commerce by sea, commerce by land, and selling in shops, these again differing as they are safer or more profitable. The second is usury; the third, service for hire — of this, one kind is employed in the mechanical arts, the other in unskilled and bodily labour. There is still a third sort of money-making, intermediate between this and the first or natural mode, which is partly natural but is also concerned with exchange of the fruits and other products of the earth. Some of these latter, although they bear no fruit, are still profitable — for example, wood and minerals. The art of mining, by which minerals are obtained, has many branches, since there are various kinds of things dug out of the earth. Of the several divisions of money-making I now speak generally; a detailed consideration would be useful in practice, but it would be tiresome to dwell on at greater length now.

Those occupations are most truly arts in which there is the least element of chance. They are the meanest in which the body is most worn down; the most servile in which there is the greatest use of the body; and the most illiberal in which there is the least need of excellence.

Works on these subjects have been written by various persons — for example, by Chares of Paros and Apollodorus of Lemnos, who treated of tillage and planting, while others have treated of other branches; anyone who cares for such matters may consult their writings. It would also be well to collect the scattered stories of the ways in which individuals have succeeded in amassing a fortune, since all this is useful to those who value the art of making money. There is the anecdote of Thales the Milesian and his financial device, which involves a principle of universal application, but is attributed to him on account of his reputation for wisdom. He was reproached for his poverty, which was supposed to show that philosophy was of no use. According to the story, he knew by his skill in the stars while it was still winter that there would be a great harvest of olives the coming year. So, having a little capital, he gave earnest-money for the use of all the olive-presses in Chios and Miletus, which he hired at a low price because no one bid against him. When the harvest-time came and many wanted them all at once and on a sudden, he let them out at any rate he pleased and made a great deal of money. Thus he showed the world that philosophers can easily be rich if they like, but their ambition is of another sort. He is supposed to have given a striking proof of his wisdom; but, as I was saying, his device for getting money is of universal application, and is nothing but the creation of a monopoly. It is an art often practised by cities when they are in want of money: they make a monopoly of provisions.

There was a man of Sicily who, having money deposited with him, bought up all the iron from the iron mines. Afterwards, when the merchants from their various markets came to buy, he was the only seller, and without much increasing the price he gained 200 per cent. When Dionysius heard of it, he told the man he might take away his money, but that he must not remain at Syracuse — for he thought the man had discovered a way of making money injurious to his own interests. He had the same idea as Thales: both contrived to create a monopoly for themselves. Statesmen ought to know these things, for a state is often as much in need of money, and of such devices for obtaining it, as a household — or even more so. Hence some public men devote themselves entirely to finance.

Of household management we have seen that there are three parts: the rule of a master over slaves, which has already been discussed; the rule of a father; and the rule of a husband. A husband and father rules over wife and children, both of whom are free, but the rule differs — the rule over his children is a royal rule, the rule over his wife a constitutional one. For although there may be exceptions to the order of nature, the male is by nature fitter for command than the female, just as the elder and full-grown is superior to the younger and more immature. In most constitutional states, however, the citizens rule and are ruled by turns; for the idea of a constitutional state implies that the natures of the citizens are equal and do not differ at all. Nevertheless, when one rules and another is ruled, we try to create a difference of outward forms, modes of address, and titles of respect — which may be illustrated by the saying of Amasis about his foot-pan. The relation of the male to the female is of this kind, but with a permanent inequality. The rule of a father over his children is royal, for he receives both love and the respect due to age, exercising a kind of royal power. Hence Homer has appropriately called Zeus ‘father of gods and men,’ because he is king of them all. A king is the natural superior of his subjects, but he should be of the same kin or kind with them — and such is the relation of elder and younger, of father and son.

It is clear, then, that household management attends more to men than to the acquisition of inanimate things, and to human excellence more than to the excellence of property which we call wealth, and to the virtue of freemen more than to the virtue of slaves. A question may indeed be raised: whether there is any excellence at all in a slave beyond merely instrumental and ministerial qualities — whether he can have the virtues of temperance, courage, justice, and the like; or whether slaves possess only bodily and ministerial qualities. Whichever way we answer, a difficulty arises. If they have virtue, in what will they differ from freemen? On the other hand, since they are men and share in reason, it seems absurd to say they have no virtue. A similar question may be raised about women and children: do they too have virtues? Ought a woman to be temperate and brave and just, and is a child to be called temperate or intemperate, or not? In general, we may ask of the natural ruler and the natural subject whether they have the same or different virtues. A noble nature is equally required in both — but if so, why should one of them always rule and the other always be ruled? Nor can we say this is a question of degree, for the difference between ruler and subject is a difference of kind, and therefore not of degree. Yet how strange is the supposition that the one ought, and the other ought not, to have virtue. If the ruler is intemperate and unjust, how can he rule well? If the subject is, how can he obey well? If he is licentious and cowardly, he will certainly not do his duty. It is evident, therefore, that both must have a share of virtue, but varying according to their various natures. This is at once indicated by the soul, in which one part naturally rules and the other is subject. We maintain that the virtue of the ruler is different from that of the subject — the one being the virtue of the rational, the other of the irrational part. The same principle obviously applies generally, and so almost all things rule and are ruled according to nature. But the kind of rule differs: the freeman rules over the slave in another manner from that in which the male rules over the female, or the man over the child. The parts of the soul are present in all of them, but in different degrees. The slave has no deliberative faculty at all; the woman has, but it is without authority; the child has, but it is immature. So it must be with the moral virtues also: all may be supposed to share in them, but only in the manner and degree required by each for the fulfilment of his duty. Hence the ruler ought to have moral virtue in perfection, for his function is entirely that of a master craftsman, and the master craftsman is reason. The subjects, on the other hand, require only that measure of virtue which is proper to each of them. Clearly, then, moral virtue belongs to all of them; but the temperance of a man and of a woman, or the courage and justice of a man and of a woman, are not, as Socrates maintained, the same. The courage of a man is shown in commanding, of a woman in obeying. This holds of all the other virtues, as will be more clearly seen if we look at them in detail; for those who say generally that virtue consists in a good disposition of the soul, or in doing rightly, or the like, only deceive themselves. Far better than such definitions is the way of speaking of those who, like Gorgias, enumerate the virtues. All classes must be deemed to have their special attributes, as the poet says of women — though this is not equally the glory of man. The child is imperfect, and so his virtue is obviously not relative to himself alone, but to the perfect man and to his teacher. In the same way, the virtue of the slave is relative to a master. We determined that a slave is useful for the wants of life, and so he will obviously require only so much virtue as will prevent him from failing in his duty through cowardice or intemperance. Someone may ask whether, if what we are saying is true, virtue will not also be required in the artisans, since they often fail in their work through misconduct. But is there not a great difference in the two cases? The slave shares in his master’s life; the artisan is less closely connected with him, and only attains excellence in proportion as he becomes a slave — that is, is under the direction of a master. The meaner sort of mechanic has a special and separate slavery; and whereas the slave exists by nature, this is not so of the shoemaker or other artisan. It is plain, then, that the master ought to be the source of excellence in the slave — but not merely because he possesses the art that trains him in his duties. Hence those are mistaken who forbid us to converse with slaves and say we should employ command only, for slaves stand even more in need of admonition than children.

The relations of husband and wife, of parent and child, their several virtues, what in their dealings with one another is good and what is evil, and how we may pursue the good and escape the evil — all this will have to be discussed when we speak of the different forms of government. For since every family is part of a state, and these relationships are the parts of a family, the virtue of the part must have regard to the virtue of the whole. And so women and children must be trained by education with an eye to the state — if the virtues of either of them are supposed to make any difference in the virtues of the state. They must make a difference, since the children grow up to be citizens, and half the free persons in a state are women.

Of these matters enough has been said. Of what remains, let us speak at another time. Regarding our present inquiry as complete, we will make a new beginning. And first, let us examine the various theories of a perfect state.

chapters.title: Book 2
paragraphs: We intend to ask which kind of political community is best for people who have the fullest opportunity to achieve the life they consider ideal. To do so, we must examine not only this ideal constitution but other constitutions as well: those found in states that are actually well governed, and theoretical arrangements that enjoy a good reputation. In this way we can bring their useful and valuable features to light. No one should think that, because we look beyond these arrangements, we want to pursue philosophical ingenuity at the expense of truth. We undertake the inquiry only because every constitution known to us has defects.

Let us start at the natural starting point of the inquiry. There are three possible arrangements: the members of a state may share everything, share nothing, or share some things while keeping others separate. Sharing nothing is plainly impossible. A state is a community, and its members must at least share a place: a single city occupies a single place, and its citizens are the people who participate in that city. But in a well-organized state, should they share everything that can be shared, or only certain things? We can imagine citizens sharing wives, children, and property, as Socrates proposes in Plato's Republic. Which arrangement is better: the one under which we now live, or this proposed new organization of society?

Sharing women in common raises many difficulties. Socrates does not seem to establish, through his arguments, the principle on which he bases the necessity of this institution. Furthermore, if we take it literally as a means to the end he assigns to the state, it is impossible; yet he never defines precisely the restrictions or qualifications it requires. I mean the assumption from which Socrates argues: that a state becomes better the more completely it becomes one. Is it not plain that a state can become so completely one that it ceases to be a state? A state is by nature a plurality. As it becomes increasingly unified, it changes from a state into a household, and from a household into a single person; for a household is more completely one than a state, and an individual more completely one than a household. We should therefore avoid this utmost unity even if we could achieve it, since it would destroy the state. Besides, a state consists not merely of a number of men, but of men of different kinds. People who are all alike do not constitute a state. A state differs in this respect from a military alliance, whose usefulness depends on the number of its members even if they are alike in kind. An alliance aims at mutual protection, and the question is like that of the two pans of a balance: which has the greater weight?

Similarly, a state differs from a nation where the people do not live scattered in villages but are organized as the Arcadians are. In a state, the elements that must be brought into unity differ in kind. This is why reciprocity, as I have already observed in the Ethics, preserves states; the principle may also be described as reciprocal proportion (Nicomachean Ethics, section 6). Free men who are equals must maintain this principle. They cannot all govern at once, but must take turns after a year, or after some other interval, or according to an established order of succession. Under this arrangement everyone governs. The arrangement resembles one in which shoemakers and carpenters exchange their trades, instead of the same people remaining shoemakers and carpenters throughout their lives.

Clearly, in politics as in the trades, it is better for the same people to continue in their positions whenever that is possible. But the natural equality of citizens may make it impossible. If excluding anyone from government would be unjust, whether governing is a benefit or a burden, rotation is then preferable to everyone exercising power at once. Equals make way for equals, just as those who governed before made way for them. One group thus governs and another is governed, each taking its turn, as though the people themselves had changed. In the same way, they hold a variety of offices. It follows that a city is not naturally one in the sense that some people claim. What they describe as the greatest good for cities would actually destroy them; yet the good of anything must surely be what keeps it in existence.

There is another reason why this extreme unification of the state is plainly undesirable. A household is more self-sufficient than a single person, and a city more self-sufficient than a household. Indeed, a city comes into existence only when the community has grown large enough to support itself. If self-sufficiency is something we should seek, then the lesser degree of unity is preferable to the greater.

Even if we grant that the greatest possible unity is best for a community, it is certainly not established by everyone saying 'mine' and 'not mine' at the same moment. Socrates treats this as the sign of a perfectly united state. But 'everyone' is ambiguous. If it means that each individual uses 'mine' and 'not mine' at the same time as every other individual, Socrates' purpose might perhaps be achieved to some extent: each man would call the same person his own son or his own wife, and would speak in the same way about property and everything belonging to him. Yet people who shared their wives and children would not speak in this sense. They would speak of 'all of us', not of 'each of us'. Their property, too, would belong to them collectively, rather than separately to each person. There is an evident fallacy here in the word 'all'. Like 'both', 'odd', and 'even', it has more than one sense and can produce logical puzzles in an argument. Having everyone call the same thing his own, in the sense that each individual claims it, might be admirable, but it cannot be put into practice. If the other sense is intended, the sense that distinguishes 'all' from 'each', this unity does nothing to promote agreement. A further objection follows. What belongs to the largest number of people receives the least attention. Each person mainly considers his own concerns and scarcely considers the common interest, except where it affects him individually. Among the other reasons for this is that people more readily neglect a duty when they expect someone else to perform it. Thus a household with many attendants often receives less useful service than one with few. Every citizen would have a thousand sons, none of whom would be his son individually. Each child would be as much anyone else's son as his, and all would neglect him equally; this is the arrangement in Plato's Republic. Furthermore, on this principle everyone would call another person 'mine' or 'not mine' according to that person's success or misfortune. However small his own share in the whole, he would say of each member of the thousand, or whatever the city's population might be, 'this one is mine', or 'this one is his'. Even then he could not be sure. No one could know who had happened to have a child, or whether a child once born was still alive.

But which is preferable: to call every one of two thousand or ten thousand citizens 'mine', or to use 'mine' in its usual, narrower sense? Under the usual arrangement, a person whom one man calls his son is another man's brother, cousin, kinsman, blood relation, or relative by marriage, either directly or through another of his relations. People distinguish these relationships from their membership in a tribe or ward. How much better it is to be someone's actual cousin than a son in Plato's sense! Nor could anyone prevent brothers, children, fathers, and mothers from occasionally recognizing each other. Children resemble their parents, and they would inevitably discover signs of their relationship. Geographers say that this does in fact happen. According to them, in Upper Libya, where women are shared, children are nevertheless assigned to particular fathers because they look like them. Some women, like the females of other animals, including mares and cows, have a pronounced tendency to bear offspring resembling the parents. An example was the Pharsalian mare named Dicaea, 'the Just'.

The founders of such a community would find it difficult to prevent other evils: assaults, intentional and unintentional killings, quarrels, and slander. These are especially impious when directed against fathers, mothers, or close relatives, and less so when the people involved are unrelated. Moreover, they are much likelier to occur when people do not know their relationship; once they have occurred, the customary acts of atonement cannot be performed. Again, how strange that Socrates, after making children common to all, should prohibit lovers only from sexual intercourse, while allowing familiarities between father and son or between brothers! Nothing could be more indecent, since such love is improper even without those familiarities. It is equally strange to forbid intercourse solely because its pleasure is so intense, as though it made no difference whether the people concerned were father and son or brothers.

Sharing wives and children would seem more appropriate for the farmers than for the guardians. It would weaken the ties between the farmers, as is desirable in a subject class, and would make them obedient and unlikely to rebel. In short, this law would produce precisely the opposite of what good laws ought to produce. Socrates' purpose in regulating women and children in this way would defeat itself. We consider friendship the greatest good a state can possess, and its protection against revolution. Socrates himself praises nothing more highly than the unity of the state, which he, like everyone else, says friendship creates. But the unity he praises resembles that desired by the lovers in the Symposium. As Aristophanes says there, their affection is so excessive that they want to grow together and become one instead of two; in that event, one or both would certainly cease to exist. In reality, the opposite of the intended result would occur. In a state where women and children were common to all, affection would become diluted: a father certainly would not say 'my son', nor a son 'my father'. Just as a small amount of sweet wine disappears when mixed into a great quantity of water, so the sense of relationship expressed by these names would disappear in such a community. The supposed father would have no particular reason to care for the son, the son for the father, or brothers for one another.

The two things that chiefly arouse care and affection are the feeling that something belongs to you and the feeling that you love it. Neither could exist in a state organized in this way. Moreover, transferring newborn children from farmers or artisans to the guardians, or from guardians to a lower class, would be extremely difficult to arrange. Those who give up or transfer children inevitably know which children they are transferring, and to whom. The evils already mentioned, including assaults, forbidden loves, and killings, would occur more frequently among people transferred into the lower classes or assigned a place among the guardians. They would no longer address members of another class as brothers, children, fathers, or mothers. Consequently, blood relationship would give them no reason to fear committing these crimes. Let this conclude our discussion of sharing wives and children.

We should next examine the arrangements for property. Should citizens in the best state hold their possessions in common? We can discuss this independently of the rules about women and children. Even if women and children belong to individual families, as is now the universal practice, might there still be an advantage in owning and using possessions together? Three arrangements are possible. First, people might own the land separately but put its produce into a common supply for everyone to consume; some nations follow this practice. Second, the land might belong to everyone and be cultivated jointly, while its produce is divided among individuals for their private use. This kind of common ownership is said to exist among certain barbarians. Third, both the land itself and what it produces might be held in common.

The situation is different, and easier to manage, when the farmers are not themselves citizens. When citizens cultivate the land, however, the ownership question creates endless difficulties. Unless work and enjoyment are shared equally, those who work hard and receive little will inevitably resent those who do little work but receive or consume a great deal. Living together and sharing things is always difficult, especially when what is shared is property. We can see this in groups of travelling companions: they generally fall out on the journey and quarrel over whatever small incident arises. The same holds for servants. We are most likely to become irritated with those whom we encounter most often in everyday life.

These are only a few of the difficulties associated with common ownership. Our present arrangement, if improved by good habits and laws as it could be, would be much better and would combine the advantages of both systems. Property ought to be common in one respect, but normally held privately. Where each person has his own distinct interest, people will not make complaints against each other, and their work will advance because each attends to his own affairs. Yet among good people, when it comes to using property, the proverb will hold: 'Friends share everything.' We can already find traces of this principle. It is therefore practicable; in well-governed states it already operates to some degree, and it could be extended. Each man owns his own property, but puts some of it at his friends' disposal and shares the use of other things with them. The Lacedaemonians, for instance, use each other's slaves, horses, and dogs as though they owned them themselves. When they are out in the country, they also take from the fields whatever provisions they need. Clearly, then, private ownership combined with common use is better. The legislator's particular task is to cultivate this generous disposition. Moreover, the pleasure of feeling that something is one's own is immeasurably greater. Nature has implanted self-love in us for a purpose. Selfishness is rightly condemned, but selfishness is excessive self-love, not simply loving oneself. It resembles a miser's excessive love of money, for everyone, or nearly everyone, has some affection for money and similar possessions. There is also immense pleasure in showing kindness or doing a service to friends, guests, or companions, and this is possible only when one has property of one's own. Excessive unification of the state destroys this advantage. Such a state abolishes two virtues. One is temperance in relations with women: refraining from another man's wife out of temperance is an honourable act. The other is generosity in the use of property. If everyone shares everything, no one can demonstrate generosity or perform a generous action, because generosity consists in the way a person uses his property.

Legislation of this kind can appear benevolent without actually being so. People listen eagerly and readily persuade themselves that, somehow, everyone will become everyone else's friend. This is especially true when they hear someone denouncing the evils now found in states: lawsuits over contracts, convictions for perjury, flattery of the rich, and similar things, all attributed to private ownership. Yet these evils arise from a quite different source, the wickedness of human beings. In fact, we observe far more quarrelling among those who share everything than among private owners, even though the former are few in comparison with the enormous number of people who possess property individually.

We must also calculate not only the evils citizens would escape, but the advantages they would forfeit. The life proposed for them seems altogether impossible to put into practice. Compare Nicomachean Ethics IV.1, section 1, and Republic 465. Socrates' mistake comes from the false conception of unity with which he begins. Both household and state should have unity, but only in certain respects. A state can reach a degree of unity at which it stops being a state. Or, while still existing, it can become a worse state, just as harmony becomes mere unison, or a rhythm is reduced to a single foot. As I said, the state is a plurality. Education should unite its members and form them into a community. It is strange that someone who devises an educational system that he thinks will make the state virtuous should expect these regulations to improve its citizens, instead of relying on philosophy, habits, and laws. Consider the laws about common meals in Sparta and Crete: through these the legislator has already made property common to a certain extent. We should not dismiss the experience of the ages. If these proposals were good, they would surely have become known over the course of so many years. Nearly everything has been discovered, although discoveries are sometimes left unconnected, and in other cases people fail to use the knowledge they possess. Watching such a constitution actually being established would clarify much. The legislator could not create any state without dividing its citizens into groups for common meals, and into phratries and tribes. Yet all this legislation finally amounts only to prohibiting the guardians from farming, a prohibition the Lacedaemonians already attempt to enforce. Again, Socrates has not explained, and it is not easy to determine, what the general constitution of such a community would be. The citizens outside the guardian class form the majority, but nothing has been settled about them. Must the farmers also own their property collectively? Or will each have private land in addition to the common land he cultivates? Will their wives and children belong to individual families or to everyone? If they share everything, like the guardians, how do they differ from the guardians, and what benefit do they gain from submitting to their rule? On what basis would they submit at all? Perhaps the rulers would adopt the Cretans' ingenious practice: the Cretans give their slaves institutions like their own, but forbid them physical training and the possession of weapons. If, instead, the lower classes have marriage and property arrangements like those of other cities, what kind of community will result? Will there not be two states within one, each hostile to the other? One class will consist of guardians, acting as watchmen; another will contain the farmers, alongside artisans and the remaining citizens. In that case, lawsuits, quarrels, and all the evils that Socrates identifies in other states will exist among them too. He does indeed say that such excellent education will spare citizens the need for many laws, including regulations for the city and the markets. But his education is confined to the guardians. Again, he lets farmers own the land on condition that they pay tribute. On those terms they will probably be far more difficult to control and more self-important than Helots, Penestae, or slaves generally. Socrates nowhere decides whether the lower class must share wives and property just as the upper class does. Nor does he settle the related questions of its education, government, and laws. It is difficult, though extremely important, to discover what character the lower classes must have if the guardians' common way of life is to be sustained.

Again, if Socrates shares women among everyone but retains private property, the men will attend to the fields, but who will attend to the home? What will happen if the farming class shares both property and wives? Nor is it reasonable to argue from the example of animals that men and women should pursue the same occupations: animals do not have households to manage. Socrates' organization of government also contains dangers, because he gives permanent rule to the same people. If this often causes unrest among people of low standing, how much greater will the danger be among spirited warriors? It is clear that his rulers must always be the same people. The gold that God mixes into human souls is not given first to one person and then to another, but always to the same people. As he says, from birth God mixes gold into some people and silver into others, but bronze and iron into those intended to become artisans and farmers. Furthermore, he denies the guardians happiness, saying that the legislator should make the entire state happy. But the whole cannot

be happy unless most, all, or at least some of its parts possess happiness. [Compare section 2. Bekker brackets these words.] Happiness differs in this respect from the property of being even in numbers. A whole number can be even although none of its component parts is even; happiness cannot exist in that fashion. If the guardians are not happy, who is? Certainly not the artisans or the ordinary people. These are the difficulties in the Republic discussed by Socrates, and there are other difficulties just as serious.

The same objections, or almost the same ones, apply to Plato's later work, the Laws. We should therefore briefly examine the constitution described there. In the Republic, Socrates definitively settles only a few matters altogether: the sharing of women and children, common ownership of property, and the state's organization. He divides the population into two classes, farmers and warriors. From the warriors he selects a third class, the state's counsellors and rulers. But he does not decide whether farmers and artisans will take part in government, or whether they too will bear arms and perform military service. He certainly believes that women should receive the guardians' education and fight beside them. The rest of the work consists of discussions of the guardians' education and digressions away from the principal subject. The Laws contains almost nothing except laws, with relatively little discussion of the constitution. Although Plato intended this constitution to resemble the ordinary kind more closely, he gradually brings it back towards the other, ideal form. Apart from sharing women and property, he assumes that everything will be alike in the two

states. Their education will be identical; in both, citizens will be free from servile work, and both will have common meals. The sole difference is that the Laws includes women in the common meals and provides for about five thousand warriors, whereas the Republic provides for only one thousand.

Socrates' discussions are never commonplace. They invariably show elegance, originality, and thought, although we can hardly expect perfection in every respect. Still, we must remember that the five thousand citizens just mentioned would need territory as extensive as Babylonia, or some other enormous country. Such a territory would be necessary to support so many people without work, along with their women and attendants, whose numbers would be many times greater. In constructing an ideal, we may make the assumptions we wish, but we should not assume what is impossible.

The Laws says that a legislator must keep two things in view: the population and the territory. Yet he must also remember neighbouring countries if the state for which he makes laws is to enjoy a real political life. A state's military force must be effective against its neighbours as well as useful within its own borders. Even if we do not accept that an active life is the best life, either for individuals or for states, a city should still inspire fear in its enemies, whether it is advancing against them or withdrawing from them.

Another question concerns the amount of property: should this not be specified more clearly? Socrates says that a man should own enough to live temperately; [Republic IV, 423 A; see the note on that passage.] This is only another way of saying that he should live well, although living well is the higher or more general idea. Yet someone may live temperately and still live miserably. A better definition would require enough property to live both temperately and generously. If the two are separated, generosity will go together with luxury, while temperance will go together with hardship. Generosity and temperance are the only virtues directly concerned with using property. One cannot use property mildly or courageously, but one can use it temperately and generously. Exercising these virtues therefore necessarily involves property. There is also an inconsistency in equalizing property without regulating the number of citizens. He leaves population unrestricted, believing that, however many children some couples produce, the childlessness of a certain number of other marriages will provide a sufficient balance. He believes this because it happens in existing states. But Plato's imagined state would require greater care than ours do. Among us, whatever the number of citizens, property continues to be divided among them, so no one is left without a share. If property could not be divided, as in the Laws, the additional people, whether few or many, would receive nothing. One might have expected a limit on population to be even more necessary than a limit on property. That limit should take account of the likelihood of children dying and married couples being unable to have children. The neglect of this matter, so common in existing states, constantly produces poverty among citizens; and poverty gives rise to revolution and crime. Pheidon the Corinthian, one of the earliest legislators, believed that the number of households and citizens should stay constant, even though the original allotments might all have been unequal in size. The Laws adopts the opposite principle. We shall have to explain later what arrangement we ourselves consider right.

The Laws leaves another question unanswered. Socrates does not explain what distinguishes rulers from their subjects. He says only that their relationship should resemble that of warp and weft, made from different kinds of wool. He permits a man's total property to grow to five times its original value; why, then, should his land not also increase to some degree? Again, will his arrangement of residences make household management easier? He gives every individual two homesteads in different places, yet living in two houses is difficult.

The government as a whole tends towards neither democracy nor oligarchy, but towards an intermediate arrangement, generally called a polity, whose members are the heavily armed soldiers. If Plato wanted a constitution suitable for the greatest number of states, he was probably right. But if he meant that this constitution came closest to his first, ideal state, he was not; many people would prefer the Lacedaemonian constitution, or perhaps some other, more aristocratic government. Some maintain that the best constitution combines every existing form. They praise the Lacedaemonian constitution because it contains oligarchy, monarchy, and democracy: the king supplies monarchy, the council of elders oligarchy, and the Ephors the democratic element, since the Ephors are chosen from the people. Others, however, call the Ephoralty a tyranny and locate democracy in the common meals and the customs of daily life. The Laws maintains that the best state combines democracy and tyranny, which are either not constitutions at all or the worst constitutions of all. Those who combine several forms come closer to the truth, because a state is better when it consists of a greater variety of elements. The constitution proposed in the Laws contains no monarchy whatsoever. It is simply a combination of oligarchy and democracy, with the greater weight on oligarchy. Its method of appointing magistrates shows this. Choosing magistrates by lot from a previously selected group does combine the two principles. But other provisions are oligarchical: the law compels wealthy people to attend the assembly, vote for magistrates, and carry out other political duties, while leaving the rest free to participate or not. Likewise oligarchical are the efforts to draw most magistrates from the richest classes and the highest officeholders from those with the greatest incomes. The oligarchical principle also governs the council's selection. All must vote, but the obligation applies to choosing members from the first class, an equal number from the second, and another equal number from the third. In the last case, however, the obligation does not extend to every voter in the third and fourth classes. Only voters in the first and second classes must take part in selecting candidates from the fourth. He then requires an equal number of candidates to be selected from each class. This gives the advantage to people of higher standing and greater income, because many members of the lower classes, being under no obligation, will not vote. These considerations, and others we shall bring forward when discussing similar polities, suggest that states like Plato's should not be built from democracy and monarchy. There is a further danger in choosing magistrates from a group that has itself already been elected. If even a few people agree to act together, they can always secure the electoral result they want. Such, then, is the constitution set out in the Laws.

Other constitutions have been proposed by private individuals, philosophers, and statesmen. All resemble established or existing constitutions more closely than either of Plato's proposals. No one else has introduced such innovations as sharing women and children or providing public dining tables for women. Other legislators start with necessities. Some regard the regulation of property as the most important question of all, since it is the issue around which every revolution turns. Phaleas of Chalcedon recognized this danger and was the first to say that citizens ought to possess equal amounts of property. He believed that equalization would be easy in a newly founded colony, but less easy in a state already established. In the latter case, the quickest route to the desired result would be for wealthy families to give dowries without receiving them, while poor families received dowries without giving them.
