But medicine has three kinds of judge: the apothecary, the physician of the higher class, and the intelligent person who has studied the art. Every art has people of this last kind, and we grant them the capacity to judge quite as much as we grant it to professional practitioners. Surely the same principle should govern elections? A correct choice can be made only by someone with knowledge. A geometer chooses correctly in matters of geometry, and a pilot in matters of navigation. Private individuals may be familiar with certain occupations or arts, but they cannot judge better than those who know them professionally. This argument would deny the multitude both the election of magistrates and the examination of their conduct. Yet our earlier answer may meet these objections to a considerable extent. If the people are not entirely degraded, their collective judgment can equal or surpass that of experts, even though each individual judges less well than a specialist. Furthermore, in certain arts the practitioner is not the only or the best judge of what he produces. Understanding a house is not confined to the builder: its user, the householder, will even judge it better. Likewise, a pilot judges a rudder better than the carpenter, and a guest judges a feast better than the cook.

This difficulty seems adequately answered, but a related one remains. It appears strange that inferior people should exercise authority over matters more important than those entrusted to good people. Yet electing magistrates and holding them accountable are the most important matters of all. As I said, some states assign these functions to the people, giving the assembly supreme authority over them.

People of any age and with only a small property qualification can sit in the assembly, deliberate, and judge. Yet major officials, such as controllers and generals, must meet a high qualification. We can solve this difficulty as we solved the previous one, and the existing democratic practice may in fact be defensible.

Authority belongs not to the individual dicast, councillor, or assembly member, but to the court, council, and assembly. Individual officials and participants are merely parts of these bodies. This gives the many a claim to greater authority than the few. The people, council, and courts contain numerous members whose combined property exceeds that of one or a few holders of high office. Let this suffice on that question.

Our discussion of the initial question shows most clearly that good laws should be supreme. Magistrates, whether one or several, should decide only matters the law cannot specify precisely, because a general rule cannot easily cover every particular case. What makes a law good, however, has not yet been clearly established; the original difficulty remains. Laws are necessarily good or bad, just or unjust, in relation to a state's constitution. Correct constitutions must therefore have just laws, while distorted constitutions must have unjust ones.

In every science and art, the end pursued is some good. This is especially and pre-eminently true of the highest of them all, the political science with which we are concerned. Its good is justice, meaning the common interest. Everyone regards justice as a kind of equality, and to some extent accepts the philosophical distinctions we established in the Ethics. People acknowledge that justice concerns persons and that equals should receive equal treatment. But equality or inequality in what? This is the difficulty the political philosopher must resolve. Some will probably argue that public offices should be distributed unequally according to any respect in which a citizen excels, even if he otherwise differs in no way from the community. They suppose that a difference in any one respect establishes different rights and claims. If that is true, a man's complexion, height, or any other advantage would entitle him to more political power. The error is obvious and can be illustrated by other arts and sciences. Among equally skilled flute-players, better birth supplies no reason for receiving better flutes. It does not improve their playing; the best instrument belongs to the best musician. If the meaning of this argument is not yet sufficiently clear, it will become clearer as we carry the discussion further. Suppose an outstanding flute-player is greatly inferior in birth and beauty. Either quality may be a greater good than flute-playing, and others may surpass him in those qualities by a larger proportion than he surpasses them musically. Nevertheless, he should receive the finest flutes, unless wealth and birth improve flute-playing, which they do not. Moreover, the opposing principle would make every good comparable with every other. If a particular height can be compared in this way, height generally could be measured against either height or freedom. Suppose A surpasses B in height more than B surpasses A in virtue, and height generally is superior to virtue. Then every quality becomes commensurable, which is absurd. If some amount of one quality exceeds an amount of another, some other amount must equal it.

Since such comparison is impossible, political claims to office rightly do not rest on every kind of inequality, any more than claims in the arts do. For example, the fact that some people run slowly and others quickly gives no reason to assign the former little political authority and the latter a great deal. Speed receives its reward in athletic contests. Rival claims to office must instead depend on qualities that help constitute a state, such as wealth and virtue. The noble, freeborn, and wealthy therefore have reasonable claims. Officeholders must be free people and taxpayers: a state can no more consist entirely of poor people than entirely of slaves. But if wealth and freedom are necessary, justice and courage are equally necessary. Without the former the state cannot exist; without the latter it cannot exist well.

If we consider only the state's existence, all or at least some of these claims seem just. But if we consider living well, education and virtue have the stronger claim, as I said earlier. Equality in one respect should not mean equality in everything, nor inequality in one respect inequality in everything. Constitutions founded on either assumption are therefore distortions. As we have acknowledged, each group has a claim in a particular sense, but none has an absolute claim. The wealthy ground their claim to political authority on owning a greater share of the land, which is the common element of the state, and because they are generally more reliable in contractual dealings. Free people claim on grounds closely related to those of the nobly born. Nobles are citizens in a fuller sense than those of humble birth, since good birth is always esteemed in one's own country. Moreover, descendants of better ancestors are likely to be better themselves: nobility is excellence of lineage. Virtue also has a genuine claim, since we have recognized justice as a social virtue that embraces the others. The many, in turn, may advance their

claim against the few, since collectively they are stronger, wealthier, and better than the few. But suppose all the groups composing a state live together in one city: the good, the rich, the noble, and the rest. Is there then any doubt about who should govern? Within each constitution already mentioned, the answer is clear. Constitutions are distinguished by their governing bodies: in one the wealthy govern, in another the virtuous, and so forth. But where all these different elements coexist within the same political community, a genuine difficulty arises. By what principle are we to settle their competing claims to govern? Suppose the virtuous are very few. Should we judge their numbers by the tasks they must perform, asking whether they can administer the state, or must they be numerous enough to form a state themselves? Objections can be raised against each of these groups that aspires to the possession of political power. Claims based on wealth or ancestry have no secure basis in justice. On the wealth principle, a single person richer than everyone else together would plainly deserve to govern them all. Similarly, someone whose ancestry was outstanding would deserve superiority over everyone claiming authority as freeborn. Aristocracy, government by the best, faces the same problem concerning virtue. If one citizen is better than all the other rulers, however good they are, the same principle of justice gives him authority over them. And if the people's claim rests on their superior strength, one person or a minority stronger than the multitude should govern instead of the multitude.

Taken together, these considerations suggest that none of the principles by which people claim the right to rule and subject everyone else to their authority is unconditionally correct. Those claiming to master the state because of their virtue or their wealth could fairly be answered by the multitude: the many are often better and richer than the few, not, as I emphasize, as individuals, but as a collective body. We can meet another ingenious objection, sometimes advanced, in much the same way. Suppose all the elements just discussed coexist in one state. Some then ask whether a legislator seeking to enact the most just laws should legislate for the advantage of the higher classes or for that of the multitude. Justice and right must here be understood in the sense of equality. What is right as equality must in turn be considered in relation to the state's advantage and the common good of its citizens. A citizen is someone who participates in both governing and being governed. His character differs with the constitution under which he lives. In the best state, however, he is willing and able both to submit to government and to govern, with the life of virtue as his purpose.

Suppose, however, that one person, or several too few to constitute a whole state, possesses such extraordinary virtue that everyone else's virtue and political capacity cannot be compared with his or theirs. Such people can no longer be regarded as ordinary parts of the state. Treating the superior person as equal to those so far beneath him in virtue and political ability would be unjust. He may truly be called a god among human beings. We can therefore see that legislation necessarily concerns those equal in birth and power. People of outstanding virtue have no law above them: they themselves are law. [Compare section 4.] Trying to legislate for them would be ridiculous. They would probably reply as the lions did in Antisthenes' fable, when the hares addressed the animals' council and demanded equality for everyone: 'Where are your claws?' This is also the reason democratic states introduced the institution of ostracism. Equality is the aim they pursue above everything else. They therefore ostracize and expel from the city for a period those who appear to possess too much preponderance, whether through their wealth, the number of their friends, or some other source of political influence. Myth gives the same reason for the Argonauts leaving Heracles behind: the Argo refused to carry him because she feared he would outweigh the rest of her crew. Those who denounce tyranny and condemn Periander's advice to Thrasybulus are therefore not wholly just in their criticism. The story says that a herald came to Periander seeking advice. Periander said nothing, but cut down the tallest ears of corn until the field was level. The herald did not understand, but reported what he had seen. Thrasybulus understood: he should eliminate the foremost men in the state. This policy is useful not only to tyrants, nor confined to them in practice; oligarchies and democracies need it equally. Ostracism has the same purpose, disabling and banishing the most prominent citizens. Great powers treat entire cities and peoples similarly. The Athenians did so to the Samians, Chians, and Lesbians: once secure in their empire, they humbled their allies in violation of their treaties. The Persian king has repeatedly crushed the Medes, Babylonians, and others whenever memories of former greatness revived their spirit.

This problem affects every constitution, correct as well as distorted. Distorted governments may adopt this policy for their own benefit, but governments pursuing the common good adopt it too. The arts and sciences offer parallels. A painter will not give a figure a disproportionately large foot, however beautiful the foot itself may be. A shipbuilder will not make the stern or any other part excessively large. A chorus-master will not admit a singer whose voice is louder or better than everyone else's. Monarchs can likewise use compulsory measures and still remain in harmony with the cities they govern, provided that their government serves the interest of the state itself. When superiority is acknowledged, therefore, the case for ostracism rests on a certain kind of political justice. It would be better for the legislator to organize the state from the beginning so that no such remedy was needed. If the need arises, the next best course is to correct the problem through ostracism or a similar measure. In practice, states have misapplied the principle, using ostracism for factional purposes rather than the public good. Within distorted constitutions, and from their particular standpoint, it is just and useful; it is not just without qualification. In the best state, serious doubts arise not over applying it to excessive strength, wealth, popularity, or similar advantages, but over applying it to extraordinary virtue. What should be done with such a person? No one would propose expelling and exiling him. Yet he should not be a subject either: that would resemble claiming the right to govern Zeus through rotation of office. The only alternative is for everyone gladly to obey him, in accordance with what appears to be nature's order, and for such people to reign for life. This discussion leads naturally to kingship, which we recognize as a correct constitution. Let us examine whether a state or a country ought to be placed under a king if it is to enjoy good government, or ought instead to receive some other form of government. We must also ask whether monarchy, although advantageous to certain peoples, might prove harmful to others. First, however, is kingship a single kind or does it have several forms? There are several, and their manner of governing is not identical. Of lawful kingships, the Lacedaemonian is regarded as closest to the true pattern. Yet its kings lack absolute authority except on military expeditions, when they command the army. Religious matters also belong to them. In truth the kingly office amounts to a particular kind of military command: a generalship held permanently and without the ordinary obligation to give an account. They cannot impose death except on campaign and in the field, following the ancient practice described in Homer. Agamemnon tolerates attacks in the assembly, but when the army marches into battle he possesses authority over life and death. Does he not say:

'If I discover a man skulking away from battle, nothing will save him from the dogs and vultures, because death lies in my hands.' This is one type of kingship: lifelong military command. Such kingships may be either hereditary or elective.

Another kind of monarchy, common among barbarians, closely resembles tyranny. Nevertheless, it is hereditary and lawful. Barbarians are more servile in character than Hellenes, and Asiatics more so than Europeans, and therefore do not rebel against despotic government. These kingships resemble tyrannies because their peoples are naturally slaves, yet their hereditary and lawful character protects them from overthrow. Consequently, the guards surrounding these rulers are of the kind appropriate to a king, rather than the kind a tyrant would employ: they consist of citizens, while tyrants employ mercenaries. Kings govern willing subjects under law, whereas tyrants govern unwilling subjects. Citizens protect their kings; tyrants require protection against their citizens.

These are two kinds of monarchy. A third existed in ancient Hellas under the name Aesymnetia, or dictatorship. Broadly, it was an elected tyranny. Like barbarian monarchy it was lawful, but unlike it, it was not hereditary. The office might last for life, for a fixed number of years, or until a specified task was completed. For example, the

Mitylenaeans elected Pittacus to lead them against the exiles commanded by Antimenides and the poet Alcaeus. In one of his irregular songs Alcaeus himself says, 'They chose Pittacus as tyrant', reproaching his fellow citizens for 'making low-born Pittacus tyrant of their cowardly, ill-fated city, while unanimously crying out his praises'.

These governments were despotic in possessing tyrannical power, but kingly in being elected and accepted by their subjects. A fourth type is the kingship of heroic times: hereditary, lawful rule over a willing people. The first chiefs benefited their people through practical arts or warfare. They brought them together into a community or obtained land for them, becoming kings with their subjects' consent. Their descendants inherited this authority. They took command of their people whenever they went to war, and presided over religious sacrifices, with the exception of those rites that required the services of a priest. They were also responsible for deciding lawsuits, doing so either after swearing an oath or without taking an oath. When swearing, they extended their sceptre as the form of the oath. Originally, their authority covered everything in city and countryside and in foreign territories. Later they surrendered some privileges, and the people removed others. In some states only their sacrificial duties remained. Where their office retained more substance, their additional power was limited to commanding warfare beyond the frontier.

These, then, are the four different forms of royal government that we have distinguished. First is the heroic form, governing willing subjects but confined to particular tasks: the king commanded armies, judged disputes, and supervised religion. Second is barbarian kingship, a hereditary despotism exercised according to law. Third is the authority of the Aesymnete or Dictator, an elected tyranny. Fourth is the Lacedaemonian form, essentially a hereditary, lifelong generalship. These four kinds differ from one another in the ways I have described.

There is a fifth kind of royal government, in which one person has the disposal and direction of everything, just as a tribe or state collectively controls its common property. It corresponds to household management. As management of a household is kingly rule within a home, so this kingship manages a city, a nation, or several nations as a household.

Only two of these forms require examination: Lacedaemonian kingship and absolute kingship. For the most part, the other kinds occupy an intermediate position between these two. Their rulers possess less power than the absolute king, but more than the Lacedaemonian king. Our inquiry thus reduces to two questions. First, does a permanent military commander benefit the state, and should this office belong to one family or pass among citizens in rotation? Second, is it advantageous for one person to possess supreme authority in everything? The first question concerns laws rather than constitutions. Any constitution could include a lifelong generalship, so this

question can be left aside for the present. The other sort of kingship does constitute a distinct form of government. We must now examine that constitution and briefly go through the difficulties it presents. Our starting question will be whether a state benefits more from being governed by the best individual or from being governed by the best laws.

Supporters of kingship argue that laws state general rules and cannot accommodate particular circumstances. They regard strict adherence to written instructions as absurd in any science. Even in Egypt a doctor may change a treatment after the fourth day; earlier changes are made at his own risk. They infer that government confined to written laws plainly cannot be best. Yet a ruler surely cannot dispense with the general principle embodied in law. A ruler free from passion is better than one moved by it. Law has no passions, while a human heart can never escape their influence.

Someone may reply that an individual nevertheless gives better advice in particular cases. Our answer is that a king must legislate and laws must be enacted. Those laws should lose authority when they fail to fit the case, but retain it otherwise. A further question remains: when law cannot decide a matter at all, or cannot decide it adequately, should the single best man decide, or should everyone? Under present practice, assemblies convene to judge, deliberate, and decide individual cases. Any assembly member considered alone is certainly inferior to the wise man. But the state consists of many individuals. A meal to which all guests contribute is better than a banquet supplied by one person; likewise, a multitude judges many matters better than any individual.

Furthermore, the many are harder to corrupt than the few, just as a large volume of water resists contamination better than a small one. An individual may be overwhelmed by anger or another passion, inevitably distorting his judgment. It is unlikely that a great number would all become angry and mistaken simultaneously. Suppose they are free people who never violate the law but fill the gaps it necessarily leaves. If expecting such virtue from the whole multitude is unrealistic, suppose only that most are good men and good citizens. We can then ask which is less open to corruption: a single good person who governs, or a number of rulers every one of whom is good? Surely the many. You may object that factions can divide them, while one man cannot be divided against himself. We may answer that their characters are as good as his. If we call the government of many good men aristocracy, and that of one man kingship, aristocracy will benefit states more than kingship, whether or not government rests on force, provided several men equal in virtue can be found.

Kingships were probably the earliest governments because ancient cities were small and people of exceptional virtue were few. Such people became kings as benefactors, and only good men can confer benefits. When many people of equal merit emerged, they ceased to tolerate one man's pre-eminence, wanted shared government, and established a constitution. [Compare below, section 15, and section 12.] The governing class soon deteriorated and enriched itself from public funds. Wealth became the route to honour, and oligarchies naturally arose. These became tyrannies, which in turn became democracies. The governing classes' greed continually reduced their numbers and strengthened the multitude, until it attacked its masters and established democracy. Now that cities have grown larger, it seems that no other form of government remains possible.

Even if we accept that kingship is best for states, what should happen to the king's family? Should his children inherit his authority? If they are no better than ordinary people, that would be harmful. A defender of kingship may say that the king, though able to do so, will not pass power to his children. But expecting that is hardly realistic; it asks too much of human nature. His means of force present another difficulty. Should he have guards strong enough to compel those who resist him? If not, how can he govern his kingdom? Even a lawful ruler who never acts arbitrarily or against the law still requires force to uphold it.

Where the monarchy is limited, answering this question presents no great difficulty. The king's force should exceed that of one individual or several individuals, but remain smaller than the people's combined strength. The ancients followed this rule when granting guards to someone appointed dictator or tyrant. Thus when Dionysius asked the Syracusans for permission to keep guards, someone advised granting him only a fixed number.
Rule by one person is considered contrary to nature.

Our argument now leads to the king who governs entirely according to his own will. As I have already said, limited monarchy, or lawful kingship, is not a separate constitution. Any government, whether democracy or aristocracy, may appoint a lifelong general, and often a single person is given supreme control of internal administration. Epidamnus has such an office, and Opus has one with narrower powers. Some consider absolute monarchy, in which a sovereign arbitrarily rules all citizens in a community of equals, wholly unnatural. They argue that natural equals have the same natural rights and worth. Giving equal offices to unequal people, or unequal offices to equals, is as wrong as prescribing identical food and clothing for different bodily constitutions, or different provisions for identical ones. Justice therefore seems to require equals to govern and be governed in turn. This brings us to law, because an established order of succession is a law. The rule of law is preferable to any individual's rule. By the same reasoning, even when particular people should govern, they ought merely to guard and administer the law. Everyone agrees that magistrates are necessary; the objection is that giving one man authority over people who are all equal is unjust. There may indeed be particular cases in which the law seems incapable of arriving at a decision. Yet if the law cannot determine them, can an individual person do so? The answer is that law trains officials for precisely this purpose, assigning them matters it leaves unsettled and requiring their best judgment. [Compare section 2; V.1, sections 10-11; and V.4, section 7.] Law also permits amendments suggested by experience, but the officials remain its servants. To ask law to rule is to ask God and reason alone to rule. To ask a human being to rule introduces something animal as well: desire is a wild beast, and passion distorts rulers' minds even when they are the best men. Law is reason free from desire. We are told that a sick person needs a doctor and will not recover by being treated from a book. But this comparison with the arts misses the point. A doctor does not act irrationally out of friendship: he treats his patient and receives a fee. Magistrates often act from hostility or favouritism. Indeed, a patient who suspected his doctor of accepting a bribe from enemies to kill him would prefer the book. Even doctors consult other doctors when ill, and trainers employ other trainers for their own exercise, recognizing that feelings may prevent them from judging their own cases correctly. It is evident, therefore, that when people search for justice, they search for what stands in the middle, impartial between the parties. The law itself occupies that neutral position. Moreover, customary laws carry greater weight and concern more important matters than written laws. A person may govern more safely than written law, but not more safely than customary law.

Nor is it easy for one person to oversee many affairs. He must appoint numerous assistants. What difference does it make whether they already occupied their positions or were appointed by him because he needed them? [Compare Nicomachean Ethics, section 7.] If, as I said, a good man's superiority entitles him to govern, two good men are better than one. This is expressed in the ancient saying and in Agamemnon's prayer:

Even today, certain officials, including judges, are empowered to decide matters the law cannot settle. No one doubts that, wherever law can prescribe and decide, it does so best. There are, however, some matters that a general law can encompass and other matters that it cannot encompass in the same way. This gives rise to the disputed question whether the best law or the best man should govern. Legislation cannot cover the particular circumstances over which people deliberate. Everyone accepts that people must decide such cases; the argument is that many judges should do so, rather than only one. Every ruler trained by law judges well. It would be strange to suppose one person could see better with two eyes, hear better with two ears, or act better with two hands or feet than many people with many. Kings themselves already acquire numerous eyes, ears, hands, and feet by making colleagues of people friendly to them and their governments. These colleagues must support both monarch and government, since otherwise they will not do what he wishes. Yet friendship implies similarity and equality. If he therefore thinks his friends should

govern, he must also think that those who resemble him and are his equals ought to take part in government. These are the principal disputed points concerning monarchy. But might the arguments be true in some circumstances and not in others? A master's relationship to his servants can have a natural justice and usefulness, as can a king's relationship to his subjects and the relations of free citizens with one another. Tyranny has no such natural justice or advantage, nor does any other distorted constitution, since these governments come into existence contrary to nature. From our discussion it is clear that, where people are alike and equal, it is neither useful nor just for one person to be master of all the others. This is so whether there are laws, or no laws and the ruler himself takes the place of law. A good man should not be master over other good men, nor a bad man over other bad men. Even if he surpasses them in virtue, that superiority gives no right to rule except in the particular case already mentioned, to which I shall return once more. Before doing so, I must establish what kinds of people are fitted for kingship, what kinds for aristocracy, and what kinds for constitutional government.

A people naturally capable of producing a lineage outstanding in virtue and political ability is suited to kingship. A people willing to be governed as free persons by those whose virtue equips them for political command is suited to aristocracy. Constitutional freedom suits a people containing a naturally warlike multitude capable of governing and obeying in turn, under laws assigning office to the prosperous according to merit. If, however, a family or individual so excels in virtue as to surpass everyone else, it is just for that family to hold royal supremacy or for that citizen to become king of the entire people. As I said, granting them authority agrees with the ground of right commonly invoked by founders of aristocracies, oligarchies, and democracies. All acknowledge the claim of excellence, although they identify different kinds of excellence. It also agrees with our earlier principle. Killing, ostracizing, or exiling such a person would be wrong, as would requiring him to take a turn under others' government. A whole is naturally superior to a part, and someone with this pre-eminence stands to the others as a whole to its part. The only remaining course is therefore to grant him supreme power and obey him continually, rather than in rotation. These are our conclusions about kingship and its several forms, and our answer to whether it benefits states, which states it benefits, and in what way.

We maintain that there are three correct constitutions. The best must be governed by the best, with one man, a family, or several people outstanding in virtue, and with rulers and subjects fitted respectively to govern and be governed so as to attain the most desirable life. At the beginning of our inquiry we showed that a good man's virtue necessarily coincides with a citizen's virtue in the best state. Clearly, then, the same means that make a man truly good will enable him to form a truly good state, whether aristocratic or ruled by a king. The same education and habits produce a good man, a good statesman, and a good king. Having reached these conclusions, we must discuss the best state and explain how it arises and becomes established. Anyone who would pursue this inquiry in the proper manner . . .

chapters.title: Book 4
paragraphs: In all arts and sciences which embrace the whole of any subject, and are not restricted to a part only, it is the province of a single art or science to consider all that pertains to a single subject. The art of gymnastic, for example, considers not only the suitableness of different modes of training to different bodies, but what sort is absolutely the best — for the absolutely best must suit that which is by nature best and best furnished with the means of life — and also what common form of training is adapted to the great majority of men. And if a man does not desire the best habit of body, or the greatest skill in gymnastics, that might be attainable, the trainer or the teacher of gymnastic should still be able to impart any lower degree of either. The same principle equally holds in medicine, ship-building, the making of clothes, and the arts in general.

Hence it is obvious that government too is the subject of a single science, which has to consider what kind of government would be best and most in accordance with our aspirations, if there were no external impediment, and also what kind of government is adapted to particular states. The best is often unattainable, and so the true legislator and statesman ought to be acquainted not only with what is best in the abstract, but also with what is best relatively to circumstances. We should be able further to say how a state may be constituted under any given conditions — both how it is originally formed, and, when formed, how it may be longest preserved — the supposed state being so far from the very best that it is unprovided even with the conditions necessary for the very best, and not even the best under the circumstances, but of an inferior type.

He ought, moreover, to know the form of government best suited to states in general; for political writers, although they have excellent ideas, are often unpractical. We should consider not only what form of government is best, but also what is possible and what is easily attainable by all. There are some who would have nothing but the most perfect — for which many natural advantages are required. Others speak of a more attainable form, and although they reject the constitution under which they are living, they extol some one in particular, for example the Lacedaemonian. Any change of government to be introduced should be one which men will be both willing and able to adopt, since there is quite as much trouble in the reformation of an old constitution as in the establishment of a new one — just as to unlearn is as hard as to learn. Therefore, in addition to the qualifications of the statesman already mentioned, he should be able to find remedies for the defects of existing constitutions. This he cannot do unless he knows how many forms of government there are. It is often supposed that there is only one kind of democracy and one of oligarchy; but this is a mistake. To avoid such mistakes, we must ascertain what differences there are in the constitutions of states, and in how many ways they are combined. The same political insight will enable a man to know which laws are the best, and which are suited to different constitutions. The laws are, and ought to be, relative to the constitution, and not the constitution to the laws. A constitution is the organization of offices in a state; it determines what is to be the governing body, and what is the end of each community. But laws are not to be confounded with the principles of the constitution: they are the rules according to which the magistrates should administer the state, and proceed against offenders. So we must know the number and varieties of the several forms of government, if only with a view to making laws — since the same laws cannot be equally suited to all oligarchies and to all democracies, and there is certainly more than one form both of democracy and of oligarchy.

In our original discussion about governments, we divided them into three true forms — kingly rule, aristocracy, and constitutional government — and three corresponding perversions: tyranny, oligarchy, and democracy. Of kingly rule and of aristocracy we have already spoken, since the inquiry into the perfect state is the same thing as the discussion of the two forms thus named: both imply a principle of virtue provided with external means. We have already determined how aristocracy and kingly rule differ from one another, and when the latter should be established. In what follows we have to describe the so-called constitutional government, which bears the common name of all constitutions, and the other forms — tyranny, oligarchy, and democracy.

It is obvious which of the three perversions is the worst, and which is next in badness. The perversion of the first and most divine is necessarily the worst. Just as a royal rule, if it is to be more than a mere name, must exist by virtue of some great personal superiority in the king, so tyranny, the worst of governments, is necessarily the farthest removed from a well-constituted form. Oligarchy is a little better, but a long way from aristocracy; and democracy is the most tolerable of the three.

A writer who preceded me has already made these distinctions, but his point of view is not the same as mine. He lays down the principle that of all good constitutions — under which he would include a virtuous oligarchy and the like — democracy is the worst, but the best of the bad ones. We maintain, on the contrary, that they are all defective, and that one oligarchy is not to be accounted better than another, but only less bad.

Not to pursue this question further at present, let us begin by determining (1) how many varieties of states there are, since of democracy and oligarchy there are several; (2) what constitution is the most generally acceptable, and what is eligible in the next degree after the perfect, or any other aristocratical and well-constituted form of government — if any other there be — which is at the same time adapted to states in general; (3) of the other forms of government, to whom each is suited; for democracy may meet the needs of some better than oligarchy, and conversely. In the next place, (4) we have to consider in what manner a man ought to proceed who desires to establish some one among these various forms, whether of democracy or of oligarchy. Lastly, (5) having briefly discussed these subjects to the best of our power, we will endeavour to ascertain whence arise the ruin and preservation of states, both generally and in individual cases, and to what causes they are to be attributed.

The reason why there are many forms of government is that every state contains many elements. In the first place, we see that all states are made up of families; and in the multitude of citizens there must be some rich and some poor, and some in a middle condition. The rich are heavy-armed, and the poor not. Of the common people, some are husbandmen, some traders, some artisans. Among the notables, too, there are differences of wealth and property — for example, in the number of horses they keep, since they cannot afford to keep them unless they are rich. Hence in old times the cities whose strength lay in cavalry were oligarchies, and they used cavalry in wars against their neighbours — as was the practice of the Eretrians and Chalcidians, and of the Magnesians on the river Maeander, and of other peoples in Asia. Besides differences of wealth, there are differences of rank and merit,

and there are some other elements which were mentioned earlier, when in treating of aristocracy we enumerated the essentials of a state. Of these elements, sometimes all, sometimes the lesser and sometimes the greater number, have a share in the government. It is evident, then, that there must be many forms of government, differing in kind, since the parts of which they are composed differ from each other in kind. A constitution is an organization of offices which all the citizens distribute among themselves, according to the power that different classes possess — for example the rich or the poor — or according to some common equality subsisting among them, or some power common to both. There must, therefore, be as many forms of government as there are modes of arranging the offices, according to the superiorities and other inequalities of the different parts of the state.

There are generally thought to be two principal forms. As men say of the winds that there are but two — north and south — and that the rest are only variations of these, so of governments there are said to be only two forms: democracy and oligarchy. Aristocracy is considered to be a kind of oligarchy, as being the rule of a few; and the so-called constitutional government to be really a democracy — just as among the winds we make the west a variation of the north, and the east of the south. Similarly, of harmonies there are said to be two kinds, the Dorian and the Phrygian, and the other arrangements of the scale are comprehended under one of these two.

About forms of government this is a very favourite notion. But in either case the better and more exact way is to distinguish, as I have done, the one or two which are true forms, and to regard the others as perversions — whether of the most perfectly attempered harmony or of the best form of government. We may compare the oligarchical forms to the severer and more overpowering modes, and the democratic to the more relaxed and gentler ones.

It must not be assumed, as some are fond of saying, that democracy is simply that form of government in which the greater number are sovereign — for in oligarchies, and indeed in every government, the majority rules. Nor again is oligarchy that form of government in which a few are sovereign. Suppose the whole population of a city to be 1300, and that of these 1000 are rich and do not allow the remaining 300, who are poor but free, and in all other respects their equals, a share of the government — no one will say that this is a democracy. In the same way, if the poor were few and the masters of the rich, who outnumber them, no one would ever call such a government, in which the rich majority have no share of office, an oligarchy. We should rather say that democracy is the form of government in which the free are rulers, and oligarchy that in which the rich rule; it is only an accident that the free are the many and the rich are the few. Otherwise, a government in which offices were given according to stature, as is said to be the case in Ethiopia, or according to beauty, would be an oligarchy — since the number of tall or good-looking men is small. Yet oligarchy and democracy are not sufficiently distinguished merely by these two characteristics of wealth and freedom. Both contain many other elements, and so we must carry our analysis further. The government is not a democracy in which the freemen, being few in number, rule over the many who are not free, as at Apollonia on the Ionian Gulf, and at Thera — for in each of these states the nobles, who were also the earliest settlers, were held in chief honour, although they were but a few out of many. Neither is it a democracy when the rich have the government because they exceed in number, as was formerly the case at Colophon, where the bulk of the inhabitants possessed large property before the Lydian War. The form of government is a democracy when the free, who are also poor, and the majority, govern; and oligarchy when the rich and the noble govern, they being at the same time few in number.

I have said that there are many forms of government, and have explained to what causes the variety is due. Why there are more than those already mentioned, what they are, and whence they arise, I will now proceed to consider, starting from the principle already admitted: that every state consists not of one, but of many parts. If we were going to speak of the different species of animals, we should first determine the organs indispensable to every animal — for example, organs of sense, instruments of receiving and digesting food, such as the mouth and the stomach, and organs of locomotion. Assuming that there are only so many kinds of organs, but that there may be differences in them — different kinds of mouths, stomachs, perceptive and locomotive organs — the possible combinations of these differences will necessarily furnish many varieties of animals. (Animals cannot be the same which have different kinds of mouths or of ears.) When all the combinations are exhausted, there will be as many sorts of animals as there are combinations of the necessary organs. In the same way, the forms of government already described are composed, as I have repeatedly said, not of one but of many elements. One element is the food-producing class, called husbandmen. A second is the class of mechanics, who practise the arts without which a city cannot exist; some of these arts are absolutely necessary, others contribute to luxury or the grace of life. The third class is that of traders — by which I mean those engaged in buying and selling, whether in commerce or in retail trade. A fourth is the class of serfs or labourers. The warriors make up the fifth class, and they are as necessary as any of the others, if the country is not to be the slave of every invader. How can a state with any title to the name be of a slavish nature? The state is independent and self-sufficing, but a slave is the reverse of independent. Hence we see that this subject, though ingeniously, has not been satisfactorily treated in the Republic. Socrates says that a state is made up of four sorts of people who are absolutely necessary: a weaver, a husbandman, a shoemaker, and a builder. Afterwards, finding that they are not enough, he adds a smith, and again a herdsman, to look after the necessary animals; then a merchant, and then a retail trader. All these together form the complement of the first state — as if a state were established merely to supply the necessaries of life, rather than for the sake of the good, or stood equally in need of shoemakers and of husbandmen. He does not admit a military class into the state until the country has increased in size and is beginning to encroach on its neighbour’s land, whereupon they go to war. Yet even among his four original citizens, or whatever the number of those he associates in the state, there must be someone to dispense justice and determine what is just.

And as the soul may be said to be more truly part of an animal than the body, so the higher parts of states — the warrior class, the class engaged in the administration of justice, and in deliberation, which is the special business of political common sense — these are more essential to the state than the parts that minister to the necessaries of life.

Whether their several functions are the functions of different citizens, or of the same — for it may often happen that the same persons are both warriors and husbandmen — is immaterial to the argument. The higher as well as the lower elements are equally to be considered parts of the state; if so, the military element must be included. There are also the wealthy who minister to the state with their property; these form the seventh class. The eighth class is that of magistrates and officers, since the state cannot exist without rulers. So some must be able to take office and to serve the state, either always or in turn. There only remains the class of those who deliberate and who judge between disputants; we were just now distinguishing them. If the fair and equitable organization of all these elements is necessary to states, then there must also be persons who have the ability of statesmen. Many are of opinion that different functions can be combined in the same individual: the warrior may be a husbandman, or an artisan; the counsellor may be a judge. And all claim to possess political ability, and

think they are quite competent to fill most offices. But the same persons cannot be rich and poor at the same time. For this reason the rich and the poor are regarded in an especial sense as parts of a state. Again, because the rich are generally few in number while the poor are many, they appear to be antagonistic; and as the one or the other prevails, they form the government. Hence arises the common opinion that there are two kinds of government — democracy and oligarchy.

I have already explained that there are many differences of constitutions, and to what causes the variety is due. Let me now show that there are different forms both of democracy and of oligarchy, as will indeed be evident from what has preceded. In both the common people and the notables, various classes are included. Of the common people, one class are husbandmen, another artisans, another traders who are employed in buying and selling, another the seafaring class — whether engaged in war or in trade, as ferrymen or as fishermen. (In many places any one of these classes forms quite a large population: fishermen at Tarentum and Byzantium, crews of triremes at Athens, merchant seamen at Aegina and Chios, ferrymen at Tenedos.) To the classes already mentioned may be added day-labourers, those who, owing to their needy circumstances, have no leisure, and those who are not free of birth on both sides; and there may be other classes as well. The notables again may be divided according to their wealth, birth, virtue, education, and similar differences.

Of forms of democracy, first comes that which is said to be based strictly on equality. In such a democracy the law says that it is just for nobody to be poor, and for nobody to be rich, and that neither should be masters, but both equal.

If liberty and equality, as some think, are chiefly to be found in democracy, they will be best attained when all persons alike share in the government to the utmost. And since the people are the majority, and the opinion of the majority is decisive, such a government must necessarily be a democracy. Here, then, is one sort of democracy. There is another in which the magistrates are elected according to a certain property qualification, but a low one: he who has the required amount of property has a share in the government, but he who loses his property loses his rights. Another kind is that in which all the citizens who are under no disqualification share in the government, but the law is supreme. In another, everybody, if he is a citizen, is admitted to the government, but the law is supreme as before. A fifth form of democracy, in other respects the same, is that in which not the law, but the multitude, has the supreme power, and supersedes the law by their decrees. This state of affairs is brought about by the demagogues. In democracies subject to the law, the best citizens hold the first place, and there are no demagogues; but where the laws are not supreme, demagogues spring up. The people becomes a monarch — many in one — and the many have the power in their hands not as individuals, but collectively. Homer says that ‘it is not good to have a rule

of many,’ but whether he means this corporate rule, or the rule of many individuals, is uncertain. The people, who are now a monarch and no longer under the control of law, seek to exercise monarchical sway and grow into a despot. The flatterer is held in honour, and this sort of democracy stands to other democracies as tyranny stands to other forms of monarchy. The spirit of both is the same, and they alike exercise a despotic rule over the better citizens. The decrees of the demos correspond to the edicts of the tyrant, and the demagogue is to the one what the flatterer is to the other. Both have great power: the flatterer with the tyrant, the demagogue with democracies of the kind we are describing. The demagogues make the decrees of the people override the laws, and refer all things to the popular assembly. So they grow great, because the people have all things in their hands, and they hold in their hands the votes of the people, who are too ready to listen to them. Further, those who have any complaint to bring against the magistrates say, ‘Let the people be judges’ — and the people are too happy to accept the invitation. So the authority of every office is undermined. Such a democracy is fairly open to the objection that it is not a constitution at all, since where the laws have no authority, there is no constitution. The law ought to be supreme over all, and the magistracies and the government should judge only of particulars. So that if democracy is a real form of government, the sort of constitution in which all things are regulated by decrees is clearly not a democracy in the true sense of the word — since decrees relate only to particulars.

These, then, are the different kinds of democracies. Of oligarchies, too, there are different kinds. One is where the property qualification for office is so high that the poor, although they form the majority, have no share in the government — yet anyone who acquires the qualification may obtain a share. Another sort is when there is a qualification for office, but a high one, and vacancies in the governing body are filled by co-optation. If the election is made out of all the qualified persons, a constitution of this kind inclines to an aristocracy; if out of a privileged class, to an oligarchy. Another sort of oligarchy is when the son succeeds the father. There is a fourth form, likewise hereditary, in which the magistrates are supreme and not the law. Among oligarchies, this is what tyranny is among monarchies, and what the last-mentioned form of democracy is among democracies; in fact this sort of oligarchy receives the name of a dynasty (or rule of powerful families).

These are the different sorts of oligarchies and democracies. It should, however, be remembered that in many states the constitution established by law, although not democratic, may, owing to the character and habits of the people, be administered democratically; and conversely, in other states the established constitution may incline to democracy but be administered in an oligarchical spirit. This most often happens after a revolution, since governments do not change at once. At first the dominant party is content with encroaching a little upon their opponents. The laws which existed previously continue in force, but the authors of the revolution have the power in their hands.

From what has been said we may safely infer that there are so many different kinds of democracies and of oligarchies. It is evident that either all the classes we mentioned must share in the government, or some only and not others. When the class of husbandmen and those who possess moderate fortunes have the supreme power, the government is administered according to law. The citizens, being compelled to live by their labour, have no leisure, and so they set up the authority of the law and attend assemblies only when necessary. Since they all obtain a share in the government when they have acquired the qualification fixed by the law, nobody is excluded — the absolute exclusion of any class would be a step towards oligarchy. But leisure cannot be provided for them unless there are revenues to support them. This is one sort of democracy, and these are the causes which give birth to it. Another kind is based on the mode of election, which naturally comes next in order. In this, everyone to whose birth there is no objection is eligible, and may share in the government if he can find leisure. In such a democracy the supreme power is vested in the laws, since the state has no means of paying the citizens. A third kind is when all freemen have a right to share in the government, but do not actually share, for the reason already given; so in this form too the law must rule. A fourth kind of democracy is that which comes latest in the history of states. In our own day, when cities have far outgrown their original size, and their revenues have increased, all the citizens have a place in the government through the great preponderance of their numbers. They all, including the poor — who receive pay and therefore have leisure to exercise their

rights — share in the administration. Indeed, when they are paid, the common people have the most leisure, since they are not hindered by the care of their property, which often fetters the rich, who are thereby prevented from taking part in the assembly or in the courts. So the state is governed by the poor, who are a majority, and not by the laws. So many kinds of democracies there are, and they grow out of these necessary causes.

Of oligarchies, one form is that in which the majority of the citizens have some property, but not very much. This is the first form, which allows anyone who obtains the required amount the right of sharing in the government. Since the sharers in the government are a numerous body, it follows that the law must govern, and not individuals. In proportion as they are further removed from a monarchical form of government, and in respect of property have neither so much as to be able to live without attending to business, nor so little as to need state support, they must admit the rule of law and not claim to rule themselves. But if the men of property in the state are fewer than in the former case, and own more property, there arises a second form of oligarchy. The stronger they are, the more power they claim, and with this object in view, they themselves select those of the other classes who are to be admitted to the government — but, not being yet strong enough to rule without the law, they make the law represent their wishes. When this power is intensified by a further diminution of their numbers and increase of their property, there arises a third and further stage of oligarchy, in which the governing class keeps the offices in their own hands, and the law ordains that the son shall succeed the father. When, again, the rulers have great wealth and numerous friends, this sort of dynastia, or family despotism, approaches a monarchy: individuals rule, and not the law. This is the fourth sort of oligarchy, and is analogous to the last sort of democracy.

There are still two forms besides democracy and oligarchy. One of them is universally recognized and included among the four principal forms of government, which are said to be (1) monarchy, (2) oligarchy, (3) democracy, and (4) the so-called aristocracy or government of the best. But there is also a fifth, which retains the generic name of polity, or constitutional government. This is not common, and so has not been noticed by writers who attempt to enumerate the different kinds of government — like Plato in his books about the state, who recognizes four only. The term ‘aristocracy’ is rightly applied to the form of government described in the first part of our treatise, since only that can rightly be called aristocracy (the government of the best) which is a government formed of the best men absolutely, and not merely of men who are good when tried by any given standard. In the perfect state, the good man is absolutely the same as the good citizen; whereas in other states the good citizen is only good relatively to his own form of government. But there are some states differing from oligarchies, and also differing from the so-called polity or constitutional government. These are termed aristocracies, and in them magistrates are chosen both according to their wealth and according to their merit. Such a form of government is not the same as the two just now mentioned, and is termed an aristocracy. For indeed, in states which do not make virtue the aim of the community, men of merit and of reputation for virtue may be found. So where a government has regard to wealth, virtue, and numbers, as at Carthage, that is aristocracy; and so also where it has regard only to two out of the three, as at Lacedaemon — to virtue and numbers — and the two principles of democracy and virtue temper each other. There are these two forms of aristocracy in addition to the first and perfect state, and there is a third form, namely the polities which incline towards oligarchy.

I have yet to speak of the so-called polity, and of tyranny. I put them in this order, not because a polity or constitutional government is to be regarded as a perversion any more than the above-mentioned aristocracies. The truth is that they all fall short of the most perfect form of government, and so they are reckoned among perversions; and other forms — the really perverted forms — are perversions of these, as I said before. Last of all I will speak of tyranny, which I place last in the series because I am inquiring into the constitutions of states, and tyranny is the very reverse of a constitution.

Having explained why I have adopted this order, I will proceed to consider constitutional government — whose nature will now be clearer, since oligarchy and democracy have been defined. Polity, or constitutional government, may be described generally as a fusion of oligarchy and democracy. But the term is usually applied to those forms of government which incline towards democracy, and the term aristocracy to those which incline towards oligarchy — since birth and education are commonly the accompaniments of wealth. Moreover, the rich already possess the external advantages, the lack of which is a temptation to crime, and so they are called noblemen and gentlemen.

Inasmuch as aristocracy seeks to give predominance to the best of the citizens, people say also of oligarchies that they are composed of noblemen and gentlemen. It seems impossible that the state governed by the best citizens should be ill-governed, and equally impossible that the state which is ill-governed should be governed by the best. But we must remember that good laws, if they are not obeyed, do not constitute good government. There are two parts of good government: one is the actual obedience of the citizens to the laws; the other is the goodness of the laws which they obey — since they may obey bad laws as well as good. There is a further subdivision: they may obey either the best laws attainable to them, or the best absolutely.

The distribution of offices according to merit is a special characteristic of aristocracy, since the principle of an aristocracy is virtue, as wealth is of an oligarchy, and freedom of a democracy. In all of them there of course exists the right of the majority, and whatever seems good to the majority of those who share in the government has authority. Generally, however, a state of this kind is called a constitutional government, and not an aristocracy, since the fusion goes no further than the attempt to unite the freedom of the poor and the wealth of the rich, who commonly take the place of the noble. There are three grounds on which men claim an equal share in the government — freedom, wealth, and virtue (the fourth, good birth, is the result of the two last, being only ancient wealth and virtue). It is clear, then, that the admixture of two elements — that is, of the rich and the poor — is to be called a polity or constitutional government, and the union of the three is to be called aristocracy, or the government of the best. More than any other form of government, except the true and ideal, this last has a right to that name. Thus far I have described the different forms of states which exist besides monarchy, democracy, and oligarchy, and what they are; how aristocracies differ from one another, and polities from aristocracies — and that the two latter are not very unlike is obvious. Next we have to consider how, beside oligarchy and democracy, the so-called polity or constitutional government springs up, and how it should be organized. The nature of it will be at once understood from a comparison of oligarchy and democracy. We must ascertain their different characteristics, and, taking a portion from each, put the two together, like the parts of an indenture. There are three modes in which fusions of government may be effected. The nature of the fusion will be made intelligible by an example of the manner in which different governments legislate, say concerning the administration of justice. In oligarchies they impose a fine on the rich if they do not serve as judges, and to the poor they give no pay; but in democracies they give pay to the poor and do not fine the rich. (1) The union of these two modes is a common or middle term between them, and is therefore characteristic of a constitutional government, since it is a combination of both. This is one mode of uniting the two elements. (2) A mean may be taken between the enactments of the two: democracies require no property qualification, or only a small one, from members of the assembly; oligarchies a high one. Here neither of these is the common term, but a mean between them. (3) There is a third mode, in which something is borrowed from the oligarchical and something from the democratical principle. The appointment of magistrates by lot, for example, is democratical, and election of them oligarchical; democratical again when there is no property qualification, oligarchical when there is. In the aristocratical or constitutional state, one element will be taken from each — from oligarchy, the mode of electing to offices; from democracy, the disregard of qualification. Such are the various modes of combination.

There is a true union of oligarchy and democracy when the same state may be termed either a democracy or an oligarchy; those who use both names evidently feel that the fusion is complete. Such a fusion there is also in the mean, since both extremes appear in it. The Lacedaemonian constitution, for example, is often described as a democracy, since it has many democratical features. In the first place, the youth receive a democratical education. The sons of the poor are brought up with the sons of the rich, who are educated in such a manner as to make it possible for the sons of the poor to be educated like them. A similar equality prevails in the following period of life, and when the citizens are grown to manhood the same rule is observed: there is no distinction between the rich and poor. They all have the same food at their public tables, and the rich wear only such clothing as any poor man can afford. Again, the people elect to one of the two greatest offices of state, and in the other they share — they elect the Senators and share in the Ephoralty. By others the

Spartan constitution is said to be an oligarchy, because it has many oligarchical elements. That all offices are filled by election and none by lot is one of these oligarchical characteristics; that the power of inflicting death or banishment rests with a few persons is another; and there are others. In a well-tempered polity, both elements should appear, and yet neither; the government should rely on itself, not on foreign aid, nor on the goodwill of a majority of foreign states (they might be equally well-disposed when there is a vicious form of government), but on the general willingness of all classes in the state to maintain the constitution.

Enough of the manner in which a constitutional government, and the so-called aristocracies, ought to be framed. Of the nature of tyranny I have still to speak, in order that it may have its place in our inquiry, since even tyranny is reckoned by us a form of government, although there is not much to be said about it. I have already, in the former part of this treatise, discussed royalty or kingship according to the most usual meaning of the term, and considered whether it is or is not advantageous to states, and what kind of royalty should be established, and from where, and how it

should be established. When speaking of royalty, we also spoke of two forms of tyranny, both of which are according to law and so easily pass into royalty. Among barbarians there are elected monarchs who exercise a despotic power, and despotic rulers were also elected in ancient Hellas, called Aesymnetes or dictators. These monarchies, when compared with one another, exhibit certain differences. They are, as I said before, royal in so far as the monarch rules according to law and over willing subjects, but tyrannical in so far as he is despotic and rules according to his own fancy. There is also a third kind of tyranny, which is the most typical form, and is the counterpart of the perfect monarchy. This tyranny is just that arbitrary power of an individual which is responsible to no one, and governs all alike, whether equals or betters, with a view to its own advantage, not that of its subjects, and therefore against their will. No freeman, if he can escape from it, will endure such a government.
The kinds of tyranny are such, and so many, and for the reasons I have given.

We have now to inquire what is the best constitution for most states, and the best life for most men — neither assuming a standard of virtue above ordinary persons, nor an education exceptionally favoured by nature and circumstances, nor yet an ideal state which is an aspiration only — but having regard to the life in which the majority are able to share, and to the form of government which states in general can attain. As to those aristocracies, as they are called, of which we were just speaking, they either lie beyond the possibilities of the greater number of states, or they approximate to the so-called constitutional government, and so need no separate discussion. The conclusion at which we arrive respecting all these forms rests upon the same grounds. If it has been truly said in the Ethics that the happy life is the life according to unimpeded virtue, and that virtue is a mean, then the life which is in a mean — and in a mean attainable by every

one — must be the best. The same criteria of virtue and vice apply both to cities and to constitutions, since the constitution is, in a figure, the life of the city. In all states there are three elements: one class is very rich, another very poor, and a third in a mean. It is admitted that moderation and the mean are best, and so it will clearly be best to possess the gifts of fortune in moderation, since in that condition of life men are most ready to listen to reason. But he who greatly excels in beauty, strength, birth, or wealth, or, on the other hand, who is very poor, very weak, or very much disgraced, finds it difficult to follow reason. Of these two, the one sort grow into violent and great criminals, the others into rogues and petty rascals. And two sorts of offences correspond to them: the one committed from violence, the other from roguery. The petty rogues are disinclined to hold office, whether military or civil, and their aversion to these two duties is as great an injury to the state as their tendency to crime.

Again, those who have too much of the goods of fortune — strength, wealth, friends, and the like — are neither willing nor able to submit to authority. The evil begins at home: when they are boys, by reason of the luxury in which they are brought up, they never learn, even at school, the habit of obedience. The very poor, on the other hand, who are at the opposite extreme, are too degraded. So the one class cannot obey, and can only rule despotically; the other knows not how to command, and must be ruled like slaves. Thus arises a city, not of freemen, but of masters and slaves — the one despising, the other envying. Nothing can be more fatal to friendship and good fellowship in states than this, since good fellowship tends to friendship, and when men are at enmity with one another, they would rather not even share the same path. A city ought to be composed, as far as possible, of equals and similars, and these are generally the middle classes. Hence the city composed of middle-class citizens is necessarily best governed; they are, as we say, the natural elements of a state. This is the class of citizens most secure in a state, since they do not, like the poor, covet their neighbours’ goods, nor do others covet theirs, as the poor covet the goods of the rich. Neither plotting against others nor plotted against themselves, they pass through life safely. Wisely, then, did Phocylides pray:

‘Many things are best in the mean; I desire to be of a middle condition in my city.’ It is manifest, then, that the best political community is formed by citizens of the middle class, and that those states are likely to be well-administered in which the middle class is large, and larger if possible than both the other classes — or at any rate than either singly. The addition of the middle class turns the scale, and prevents either of the extremes from being dominant. Great, then, is the good fortune of a state in which the citizens have a moderate and sufficient property; for where some possess much and others nothing, there may arise an extreme democracy or a pure oligarchy, and a tyranny may grow out of either extreme — either out of the most rampant democracy, or out of an oligarchy. But it is not so likely to arise out of a middle and nearly equal condition. I will explain the reason of this hereafter, when I speak of the revolutions of states. The mean condition of states is clearly best, since no other is free from faction; and where the middle class is large, there are least likely to be factions and dissensions. For a similar reason, large states are less liable to faction than small ones, since in them the middle class is large; whereas in small states it is easy to divide all the citizens into two classes — rich or poor — and to leave nothing in the middle.

Democracies are safer and more permanent than oligarchies, because they have a middle class which is more numerous and has a greater share in the government. When there is no middle class, and the poor greatly exceed in number, troubles arise, and the state soon comes to an end. A proof of the superiority of the middle class is that the best legislators have been of a middle condition: Solon, for example, as his own verses testify; and Lycurgus, since he was not a king; and Charondas, and almost all legislators. These considerations will help us to understand why most governments are either democratical or oligarchical. The reason is that the middle class is seldom numerous in them; and whichever party — the rich or the common people — transgresses the mean and predominates, draws the government to itself, and so arises either oligarchy or democracy.

There is another reason: the poor and the rich quarrel with one another, and whichever side gets the better, instead of establishing a just or popular government, regards political supremacy as the prize of victory. The one party sets up a democracy, the other an oligarchy. Both parties which had supremacy in Hellas looked only to the interest of their own form of government, and established in states either democracies or oligarchies — they thought of their own advantage, and not at all of the public. For these reasons, the middle form of government has rarely, if ever, existed, and only among a very few. One man alone of all who ever ruled in Hellas was induced to give this middle constitution to states. But it has now become a habit among the citizens of states not even to care about equality; all men are seeking for dominion, or, if conquered, are willing to submit.

What, then, the best form of government is, and what makes it the best, is now evident. Of other states, since we say there are many kinds of democracy and many of oligarchy, it is not difficult to see which has the first place, and which the second or any other in the order of excellence — now that we have determined which is the best. That which is nearest to the best must necessarily be better, and that which is furthest from it worse, if we are judging absolutely and not relatively to given conditions. I say ‘relatively to given conditions,’ since a particular government may be preferable for some, while another form may be better for others.

We have now to consider what kind of government is suitable to what kind of men. I may begin by assuming, as a general principle common to all governments, that the portion of the state which desires permanence ought to be stronger than that which desires the reverse. Every city is composed of quality and quantity. By quality I mean freedom, wealth, education, good birth; by quantity, superiority of numbers. Quality may exist in one of the classes that make up the state, and quantity in the

other. The meanly-born, for example, may be more in number than the well-born, or the poor than the rich, yet they may not exceed in quantity as much as they fall short in quality. There must, then, be a comparison of quantity and quality. Where the number of the poor is more than proportioned to the wealth of the rich, there will naturally be a democracy, varying in form with the sort of people who compose it in each case. If the husbandmen exceed in number, the first form of democracy will arise; if the artisans and labouring class, the last; and so with the intermediate forms. But where the rich and the notables exceed in quality more than they fall short in quantity, oligarchy arises, similarly assuming various forms according to the kind of superiority possessed by the oligarchs.

The legislator should always include the middle class in his government. If he makes his laws oligarchical, to the middle class let him look; if he makes them democratical, he should equally try by his laws to attach this class to the state. Only there can the government ever be stable, where the middle class exceeds one or both of the others; and in that case there will be no fear that the rich will unite with the poor against the rulers. Neither of them will ever be willing to serve the other, and if they look for some form of government more suitable to both, they will find none better than this — since the rich and the poor will never consent to rule in turn, because they mistrust one another. The arbiter is always the one trusted, and he who is in the middle is an arbiter. The more perfect the admixture of the political elements, the more lasting will be the state. Many even of

those who desire to form aristocratical governments make a mistake — not only in giving too much power to the rich, but in attempting to overreach the people. There comes a time when out of a false good there arises a true evil, since the encroachments of the rich are more destructive to the state than those of the people.

The devices by which oligarchies deceive the people are five in number. They relate to (1) the assembly; (2) the magistracies; (3) the courts of law; (4) the use of arms; (5) gymnastic exercises. (1) The assemblies are thrown open to all, but either the rich only are fined for non-attendance, or a much larger fine is inflicted on them.

(2) As to the magistracies, those qualified by property cannot decline office on oath, but the poor may. (3) In the law-courts the rich, and the rich only, are fined if they do not serve; the poor are let off with impunity. Or, as in the laws of Charondas, a large fine is inflicted on the rich, and a smaller one on the poor.
