Many other examples might be cited of murders and conspiracies which have arisen from similar causes.

Fear is another motive which has caused conspiracies, as well in monarchies as in more popular forms of government. Thus Artapanes conspired against Xerxes and slew him, fearing that he would be accused of hanging Darius against his orders — he being under the impression that Xerxes would

forget what he had said in the middle of a meal, and that the offence would be forgiven. Contempt, too, is a cause of conspiracies. Sardanapalus was slain by one who saw him carding wool with his women, if the story-tellers say truly — and the tale may be true, if not of him, of someone else. Dion attacked the younger Dionysius because he despised him, and saw that he was equally despised by his own subjects, and that he was always drunk. Even the friends of a tyrant will sometimes attack him out of contempt: the confidence he reposes in them breeds contempt, and they think they will not be found out. The expectation of success is likewise a sort of contempt: the assailants are ready to strike, and think nothing of the danger, because they seem to have the power in their hands. Thus generals of armies attack monarchs — as, for example, Cyrus attacked Astyages, despising the effeminacy of his life and believing that his power was worn out. So, again, Seuthes the Thracian conspired against Amadocus, whose general he was.

Sometimes men are actuated by more than one motive — like Mithridates, who conspired against Ariobarzanes partly out of contempt and partly from love of gain. Bold natures, placed by their sovereigns in a high military position, are most likely to make the attempt in the expectation of success: courage is emboldened by power, and the union of the two inspires them with the hope of an easy victory.

Attempts whose motive is ambition arise from other causes. There are men who will not risk their lives in the hope of gains and rewards, however great, but who nevertheless regard the killing of a tyrant simply as an extraordinary action which will make them famous and honourable in the world; they wish to acquire not a kingdom, but a name. It is rare, however, to find such men. He who would kill a tyrant must be prepared to lose his life if he fails. He must have the resolution of Dion, who, when he made war upon Dionysius, took with him very few troops, saying that ‘whatever measure of success he might attain would be enough for him, even if he were to die the moment he landed; such a death would be welcome to him.’ But this is a temper to which few can attain.

Once more, tyrannies, like all other governments, are destroyed from without by some opposite and more powerful form of government. That such a government will have the will to attack them is clear, since the two are opposed in principle, and all men, if they can, do what they will. Democracy is also antagonistic to tyranny, on the principle of Hesiod, ‘Potter hates Potter,’ since they are nearly akin — for the extreme form of democracy is tyranny. Royalty and aristocracy are both alike opposed to tyranny, since they are constitutions of a different type. Hence the Lacedaemonians put down most of the tyrannies, and so did the Syracusans during the time when they were well governed.

Again, tyrannies are destroyed from within when the reigning family is divided among itself, as that of Gelo was, and more recently that of Dionysius. In the case of Gelo, Thrasybulus, the brother of Hiero, flattered the son of Gelo and led him into excesses, in order that he might rule in his name. The family then conspired to get rid of Thrasybulus and save the tyranny; but the party who conspired with them seized the opportunity and drove them all out. In the case of Dionysius, Dion, his own relative, attacked and expelled him with the assistance of the people; he afterwards perished himself.

There are two chief motives which induce men to attack tyrannies: hatred and contempt. Hatred of tyrants is inevitable, and contempt is also a frequent cause of their destruction. We see that most of those who have acquired their power have retained it, but those who have inherited it have lost it almost at once — since, living in luxurious ease, they have become contemptible and offer many opportunities to their assailants. Anger, too, must be included under hatred, and produces the same effects. It is oftentimes even more ready to strike: the angry are more impetuous in making an attack, since they do not listen to reason. Men are very apt to give way to their passions when they are insulted. To this cause is to be attributed the fall of the Peisistratidae and of many others. Hatred is more reasonable, but anger is accompanied by pain, which is an impediment to reason; whereas hatred is painless.

In a word, all the causes I have mentioned as destroying the last and most unmixed form of oligarchy, and the extreme form of democracy, may be assumed to affect tyranny — indeed, the extreme forms of both are only tyrannies distributed among several persons. Kingly rule is little affected by external causes, and so is lasting; it is generally destroyed from within. The destruction may come about in two ways: (1) when the members of the royal family quarrel among themselves, and (2) when the kings attempt to administer the state too much after the fashion of a tyranny, and to extend their authority contrary to the law. There are now no royalties; monarchies, where they exist, are tyrannies. The rule of a king is over voluntary subjects, and he is supreme in all important matters; but in our own day men are more upon an equality, and no one is so immeasurably superior to others as to represent adequately the greatness and dignity of the office. Hence mankind will not, if they can help it, endure such a rule, and anyone who obtains power by force or fraud is at once thought to be a tyrant. In hereditary monarchies, a further cause of destruction is the fact that kings often fall into contempt, and, although possessing not tyrannical but only royal power, are apt to outrage others. Their overthrow is then readily effected — there is an end to the king when his subjects do not want to have him; but the tyrant lasts, whether they like him or not.

The destruction of monarchies is to be attributed to these and the like causes. They are preserved, generally speaking, by the opposite causes. Considered separately: (1) royalty is preserved by the limitation of its powers. The more restricted the functions of kings, the longer their power will last unimpaired; for then they are more moderate and not so despotic in their ways, and are less envied by their subjects. This is the reason why the kingly office has lasted so long among the Molossians. And for a similar reason it has continued among the Lacedaemonians, since there it was always divided between two, and afterwards further limited by Theopompus in various respects, and most particularly by the establishment of the Ephoralty. He diminished the power of the kings, but established on a more lasting basis the kingly office, which was thus made in a certain sense not less, but greater. There is a story that when his wife once asked him whether he was not ashamed to leave to his sons a royal power which was less than he had inherited from his father, he replied: ‘No indeed, for the power which I leave to them will be more lasting.’

(2) As to tyrannies, they are preserved in two most opposite ways. One is the old traditional method, in which most tyrants administer their government. Of such arts Periander of Corinth is said to have been the great master, and many similar devices may be gathered from the Persians in the administration of their government. There are also the ancient prescriptions for the preservation of a tyranny, in so far as this is possible: the tyrant should lop off those who are too high; he must put to death men of spirit; he must not allow common meals, clubs, education, and the like; he must be on his guard against anything likely to inspire either courage or confidence among his subjects; he must prohibit literary assemblies or other meetings for discussion, and take every means to prevent people from knowing one another (since acquaintance begets mutual confidence). Further, he must compel the inhabitants to appear in public and live at his gates — then he will know what they are doing, and if they are always kept under, they will learn to be humble. In short, he should practise these and the like Persian and barbaric arts, all of which have the same object. A tyrant should also endeavour to know what each of his subjects says or does, and should employ spies, like the ‘female detectives’ at Syracuse, and the eavesdroppers whom Hiero was in the habit of sending to any place of resort or meeting; for the fear of informers prevents people from speaking their minds, and if they do, they are more easily found out. Another art of the tyrant is to sow quarrels among the citizens — friends should be embroiled with friends, the people with the notables, and the rich with one another. He should also impoverish his subjects: he thus provides money for the support of his guards, and the people, having to keep hard at work, are prevented from conspiring. The Pyramids of Egypt afford an example of this policy, as do the offerings of the family of Cypselus, the building of the temple of Olympian Zeus by the Peisistratidae, and the great Polycratean monuments at Samos — all these works were alike intended to occupy the people and keep them poor. Another practice of tyrants is to multiply taxes, after the manner of Dionysius at Syracuse, who contrived that within five years his subjects should bring into the treasury their whole property. The tyrant is also fond of making war, in order that his subjects may have something to do and be always in want of a leader. And whereas the power of a king is preserved by his friends, the characteristic of a tyrant is to distrust his friends — since he knows that all men want to overthrow him, and they above all have the power.

Again, the evil practices of the last and worst forms of democracy are all found in tyrannies. Such are the power given to women in their families, in the hope that they will inform against their husbands, and the licence allowed to slaves in order that they may betray their masters. Slaves and women do not conspire against tyrants, and are of course friendly to tyrannies and also to democracies, since under them they have a good time. The people, too, would fain be a monarch; and so by them, as well as by the tyrant, the flatterer is held in honour. In democracies he is the demagogue, and the tyrant also has his humble companions who flatter him.

Hence tyrants are always fond of bad men, because they love to be flattered, but no man who has the spirit of a freeman in him will demean himself by flattery. Good men love others, but they do not flatter anybody. Moreover, the bad are useful for bad purposes — ‘nail knocks out nail,’ as the proverb says. It is characteristic of a tyrant to dislike everyone who has dignity or independence: he wants to be alone in his glory, but anyone who claims a like dignity, or asserts his independence, encroaches on his prerogative and is hated by him as an enemy to his power. Another mark of a tyrant is that he likes foreigners better than citizens, and lives with them and invites them to his table — since the one are enemies, but the others enter into no rivalry with him.

Such are the notes of the tyrant, and the arts by which he preserves his power; there is no wickedness too great for him. All that we have said may be summed up under three heads, which answer to the three aims of the tyrant. These are: (1) the humiliation of his subjects — he knows that a mean-spirited man will not conspire against anybody; (2) the creation of mistrust among them — for a tyrant is not overthrown until men begin to have confidence in one another. This is the reason why tyrants are at war with the good: they are under the idea that their power is endangered by them, not only because they will not be ruled despotically, but also because they are loyal to one another and to other men, and do not inform against one another or against other men. (3) The tyrant desires that his subjects be incapable of action; for no one attempts what is impossible, and they will not attempt to overthrow a tyranny if they are powerless. Under these three heads the whole policy of a tyrant may be summed up, and to one or other of them all his ideas may be referred: (1) he sows distrust among his subjects; (2) he takes away their power; (3) he humbles them.

This, then, is one of the two methods by which tyrannies are preserved; and there is another which proceeds upon a different principle of action. The nature of this latter method may be gathered from a comparison of the causes which destroy kingdoms: as one mode of destroying kingly power is to make the office of king more tyrannical, so the salvation of a tyranny is to make it more like the rule of a king. But of one thing the tyrant must be careful — he must keep power enough to rule over his subjects, whether they like him or not, since if he once gives this up he gives up his tyranny. Although power must be retained as the foundation, in all else the tyrant should act, or appear to act, in the character of a king. In the first place, he should pretend a care of the public revenues, and not waste money in making presents of a sort at which the common people get excited when they see their miserable earnings taken from them and lavished on courtesans, strangers, and artists. He should give an account of what he receives and of what he spends — a practice which has been adopted by some tyrants — for then he will seem to be the manager of a household rather than a tyrant; nor need he fear that, while he is the lord of the city, he will ever be in want of money. Such a policy is much more advantageous for the tyrant when he goes from home, than to leave behind him a hoard, since the garrison who remain in the city will be less likely to attack his power; and a tyrant, when he is absent from home, has more reason to fear the guardians of his treasure than the citizens, since the one accompany him, but the others remain behind. In the second place, he should appear to collect taxes and to require public services only for state purposes, and that he may form a fund in case of war. He ought to make himself the guardian and treasurer of these, as if they belonged not to him but to the public. He should appear, not harsh, but dignified; when men meet him they should look upon him with reverence, and not with fear. Yet it is hard for him to be respected if he inspires no respect, and so whatever virtues he may neglect, at least he should maintain the character of a statesman, and produce the impression that he is one. Neither he nor any of his associates should ever be guilty of the least offence against modesty towards the young of either sex who are his subjects, and the women of his family should observe a like self-control towards other women. The insolence of women has ruined many tyrannies. In the indulgence of pleasures he should be the opposite of our modern tyrants, who not only begin at dawn and pass whole days in sensuality, but want other men to see them, that they may admire their happy and blessed lot. In these things a tyrant should be especially moderate, or at any rate should not parade his vices to the world. A drunken and drowsy tyrant is soon despised and attacked; not so he who is temperate and wide awake. His conduct should be the very reverse of nearly everything that has been said before about tyrants. He ought to adorn and improve his city, as though he were not a tyrant, but the guardian of the state. He should appear to be particularly earnest in the service of the gods; for if men think that a ruler is religious and has a reverence for the gods, they are less afraid of suffering injustice at his hands, and they are less disposed to conspire against him, since they believe him to have the very gods fighting on his side. At the same time, his religion must not be thought foolish. He should honour men of merit, and make them think that they would not be held in more honour by the citizens if they had a free government. The honour he should distribute himself, but the punishment should be inflicted by officers and courts of law. It is a precaution which is taken by all monarchs not to make one person great; or, if one, then two or more should be raised, that they may look sharply after one another. If after all someone has to be made great, he should not be a man of bold spirit — such dispositions are ever most inclined to strike. And if anyone is to be deprived of his power, let it be diminished gradually, not taken from him all at once. The tyrant should abstain from all outrage, in particular from personal violence and from wanton conduct towards the young. He should be especially careful of his behaviour to men who are lovers of honour: as the lovers of money are offended when their property is touched, so are the lovers of honour and the virtuous when their honour is affected. Hence a tyrant ought either not to use force at all, or he should be thought to employ only fatherly correction, and not to trample upon others; and his acquaintance with youth should be supposed to arise from affection, not from the insolence of power. In general, he should compensate the appearance of dishonour by the increase of honour.

Of those who attempt assassination, they are the most dangerous, and require to be most carefully watched, who do not care to survive if they effect their purpose. Special precaution should therefore be taken about any who think that they or their relatives have been insulted; for when men are led away by passion to assault others, they are regardless of themselves. As Heracleitus says, ‘It is difficult to fight against anger; for a man will buy revenge with life.’

Since states consist of two classes, of poor men and of rich, the tyrant should lead both to imagine that they are preserved and prevented from harming one another by his rule, and whichever of the two is stronger he should attach to his government. Having this advantage, he has no need either to emancipate slaves or to disarm the citizens; either party added to the force he already has will make him stronger than his assailants.

But enough of these details. What the general policy of the tyrant should be is obvious. He ought to show himself to his subjects in the light, not of a tyrant, but of the master of a household and of a king. He should not appropriate what is theirs, but should be their guardian; he should be moderate, not extravagant in his way of life; he should be the companion of the notables, and the hero of the multitude. Then his rule will of necessity be nobler and happier, since he will rule over better men, whose spirits are not crushed — over men to whom he himself is not an object of hatred, and of whom he is not afraid. His power, too, will be more lasting. Let his disposition be virtuous, or at least half virtuous; and if he must be wicked, let him be half wicked only. Yet no forms of government are so short-lived as oligarchy and tyranny. The tyranny which lasted longest was that of Orthagoras and his sons at Sicyon — this continued for a hundred years. The reason was that they treated their subjects with moderation, and to a great extent observed the laws, and in various ways gained the favour of the people by the care they took of them. Cleisthenes in particular was respected for his military ability. If report may be believed, he crowned the judge who decided against him in the games; and, as some say, the sitting statue in the agora of Sicyon is the likeness of this person. A similar story is told of Peisistratus, who is said on one occasion to have allowed himself to be summoned and tried before the Areopagus.

Next in duration to the tyranny of Orthagoras was that of the Cypselidae at Corinth, which lasted seventy-three years and six months: Cypselus reigned thirty years, Periander forty-four, and Psammetichus the son of Gordius three.

Their continuance was due to similar causes. Cypselus was a popular man, who during the whole time of his rule never had a body-guard; and Periander, although he was a tyrant, was a great soldier. Third in duration was the rule of the Peisistratidae at Athens, but it was interrupted: Peisistratus was twice driven out, so that during thirty-three years he reigned only seventeen, and his sons reigned eighteen — altogether thirty-five years. Of other tyrannies, that of Hiero and Gelo at Syracuse was the most lasting. Even this, however, was short — not more than eighteen years in all: Gelo continued tyrant for seven years, and died in the eighth; Hiero reigned for ten years, and Thrasybulus was driven out in the eleventh month. In fact, tyrannies generally have been of quite short duration.
I have now gone through all the causes by which constitutional governments and monarchies are either destroyed or preserved.

In Plato’s Republic, Socrates treats of revolutions, but not well — he mentions no cause of change which peculiarly affects the first or perfect state. He only says that nothing is abiding, but that all things change in a certain cycle, and that the origin of the change is a base of numbers in the ratio of four to three, which when combined with a figure of five gives two harmonies. He means when the number of this figure becomes solid; he conceives that nature will then produce bad men who will not submit to education — in which latter particular he may very likely be not far wrong, since there may well be some men who cannot be educated and made virtuous. But why is such a cause of change peculiar to his ideal state, and not rather common to all states — indeed to everything which comes into being at all? How is the state specially changed by the agency of time, which, as he declares, makes all things change? Things which did not begin together change together: if something has come into being the day before the completion of the cycle, it will change with it. Further, why should the perfect state change into the Spartan? Governments more often take an opposite form than one akin to them. The same remark is applicable to the other changes. He says that the Spartan constitution changes into an oligarchy, this into a democracy, and this again into a tyranny. Yet the contrary happens quite as often: a democracy is even more likely to change into an oligarchy than into a monarchy. Further, he never says whether tyranny is or is not liable to revolutions, and if it is, what the cause of them is, or into what form it changes. The reason is that he could not very well have told. There is no rule: according to him, it should revert to the first and best, and then there would be a complete cycle. But in fact a tyranny often changes into a tyranny, as that at Sicyon changed from the tyranny of Myron into that of Cleisthenes; into oligarchy, as the tyranny of Antileon did at Chalcis; into democracy, as that of Gelo did at Syracuse; into aristocracy, as at Carthage, and as the tyranny of Charilaus at Lacedaemon. Often an oligarchy changes into a tyranny, like most of the ancient oligarchies in Sicily — for example, the oligarchy at Leontini changed into the tyranny of Panaetius, that at Gela into the tyranny of Cleander, that at Rhegium into the tyranny of Anaxilaus; the same thing has happened in many other states. It is absurd to suppose that the state changes into oligarchy merely because the ruling class are lovers and makers of money, as Plato
claims in the period of time which, he says, makes all things change — when things which did not begin together nevertheless change together.

It is also absurd because Plato says the ruling class are lovers and makers of money, and not because the very rich think it unfair that the very poor should have an equal share in the government with themselves. Moreover, in many oligarchies there are laws against making money in trade. But at Carthage, which is a democracy, there is no such prohibition — and yet to this day the Carthaginians have never had a revolution. It is absurd, too, for him to say that an oligarchy is two cities, one of the rich and the other of the poor. Is not this just as much the case in the Spartan constitution, or in any other in which either all do not possess equal property, or in which all are not equally good men? Nobody need be any poorer than he was before, and yet the oligarchy may change all the same into a democracy, if the poor form the majority; and a democracy may change into an oligarchy, if the wealthy class are stronger than the people, the one being energetic and the other indifferent. Once more, although the causes of revolutions are very numerous, he mentions only one — that the citizens become poor through dissipation and debt — as though he thought all, or the majority of them, were originally rich. This is not true. It is true that when any of the leaders lose their property they are ripe for revolution, but when anybody else does, it is no great matter. An oligarchy does not more often pass into a democracy than into any other form of government. Again, if men are deprived of the honours of state, and are wronged and insulted, they make revolutions, and change forms of government, even if they have not wasted their substance — because

they might do what they liked, of which extravagance Plato declares excessive freedom to be the cause. Finally, although there are many forms of oligarchies and democracies, Socrates speaks of their revolutions as though there were only one form of either of them.

chapters.title: Book 6
paragraphs: We have examined the different forms of deliberative, or supreme, authority in states, the various ways of arranging law courts and public offices, and which arrangements suit each kind of government. We have also discussed how states are destroyed or preserved, and the causes that bring about each result.

Democracy, like all other forms of government, exists in several different kinds. It will be useful to assign to each the arrangements that are proper to it and advantageous for it, adding whatever remains to be said about these governments. We must also examine combinations of the arrangements themselves. Such combinations make constitutions overlap, giving aristocracies an oligarchical character and causing constitutional governments to incline towards democracies.

By the combinations still awaiting examination, I mean arrangements such as these: a state may organize its deliberative authority and its election of officials on oligarchical principles, but its courts on aristocratic principles. Alternatively, the courts and deliberative body may be oligarchical while appointments to office are aristocratic. The state's components may also fail to agree in some other way. We have considered which form of democracy suits particular cities, which form of oligarchy suits particular peoples, and which groups are suited to each of the other kinds of government.

We must not merely identify the government best suited to each state. We must also briefly consider how these and other governments can be established. Let us begin with democracy. Doing so will also clarify the opposite form, generally called oligarchy. This inquiry requires us to identify every element and characteristic of democracy, since its different forms arise from combinations of these. There are several varieties, and two causes explain their differences. The first, already mentioned, is variation in population. The common people may consist of farmers, artisans, or labourers. Adding farmers to artisans, or labourers to both, does not simply make a democracy better or worse; it changes its actual character. The second cause remains to be stated. Democracy's various features produce differences according to how they are combined. One democracy has fewer of these features, another more, and another all of them. Knowing them all is useful whether someone wants to establish a new kind of democracy or reform one already in existence. Founders of states try to assemble every element that fits their particular conception of a constitution. As I remarked when discussing how states are destroyed and preserved, this is a mistake. Let us now explain the conditions these states require, their character, and their aims. Freedom is the foundation of a democratic state. People commonly believe that only in such a state can freedom be enjoyed, and they declare it the great purpose of every democracy. One principle of freedom is that everyone should take turns governing and being governed. Democratic justice means numerical equality rather than proportionate equality. Consequently, the majority must be supreme, and whatever it approves must be the final decision and count as just. Every citizen, they say, must have equality. The poor therefore possess more power than the rich in a democracy: there are more of them, and the majority's will is sovereign. This is one feature of freedom that every democrat regards as fundamental to the state. Another is living as one pleases. They call this a free person's privilege, while having to live contrary to one's wishes marks a slave. From this second feature comes the demand that no one should be ruled by anyone, if possible; if that is impossible, people should govern and be governed in turn. It thus converges with the freedom grounded in equality that we identified first.

[An alternative interpretation takes the word for 'rule' in the sense of 'beginning': 'With this as our foundation and starting principle, democracy has the following characteristics.'] Appointments not requiring specialized skill should be made by lot. Offices should require no property qualification, or only a very low one. No one should occupy the same office twice, or at least not often, except in military commands. Every office, or as many as possible, should have a short term. Everyone should participate in judging, or judges chosen from everyone should hear every kind of case, most cases, or at least the greatest and most important: the examination of accounts, constitutional questions, and private contracts. The assembly should have final authority in every matter, or at least in the most important ones; magistrates should have final authority in none, or in very few. A council is the most democratic institution when there is not enough money to pay every citizen. Once citizens are paid, even the council loses its power, because the people draw all business to themselves, as I explained earlier. Another democratic characteristic is payment for public service. When funds permit, everyone receives pay: assembly members, jurors, and magistrates. If there is not enough for everyone, payment goes to courts and regular assemblies, the council, and magistrates, or at least to those magistrates obliged to dine together. Oligarchy is marked by birth, wealth, and education. Democracy seems marked by their opposites: low birth, poverty, and humble occupations. A further characteristic is the absence of permanent magistracies. If any survive from an earlier constitutional change, they should be deprived of power, and their holders selected by lot instead of elected by vote. These features occur in all democracies. But democracy and the demos in their fullest form rest on the accepted democratic conception of justice: every person counts equally. Equality means that the rich should have no greater share in government than the poor, nor govern alone. Instead, everyone should exercise an equal share of rule according to their numbers. This is how people expect to secure equality and freedom in their state.

The next question we must answer is how this equality is to be brought about in practice. Should the property qualification be apportioned so that five hundred wealthy people balance one thousand poor people, and should we give the thousand poor people as much power as the five hundred rich people? Or, keeping this ratio, should we select equal numbers from each group and give them control of elections and courts? Which constitution is more just by democratic standards: this arrangement or one based solely on numbers? Democrats identify justice with the majority's agreement, oligarchs with the agreement of the wealthy. For oligarchs, the amount of property should determine the decision. Both principles contain inequality and injustice. If justice is the will of the few, then one person possessing more wealth than all the other members of his class combined should, by oligarchical reasoning, have sole authority. But that would be tyranny. If justice is the majority's will, on the other hand, the majority will, as I said earlier, unjustly seize the property of the wealthy minority. To

find a principle of equality acceptable to both, we must investigate what each means by justice. Both agree that whatever a majority of citizens decides should count as law. Let us grant that, but with a qualification. Since the state contains two classes, rich and poor, the law should be what both classes, or the greater part of each, approve. If they disagree, the decision should follow the majority understood in terms of the larger property qualification. Suppose there are ten rich people and twenty poor people. Six of the rich favour a proposal and fifteen of the poor oppose it; the remaining four rich people join the poor opponents, and the remaining five poor people join the rich supporters. In that case, add together the property qualifications on each side, and let the side with the greater total prevail. If the totals are equal, the difficulty is no worse than when an assembly or court is evenly divided today and resorts to drawing lots or some similar device. However hard it may be in theory to determine justice and equality, it is far harder in practice to persuade those capable of taking more than their share to restrain themselves. The weak continually ask for justice and equality, while the strong disregard both. As we said in the earlier discussion, the first of the four types of democracy is the best and also the oldest. Here I classify them according to the natural divisions among their inhabitants. An agricultural population provides democracy's best material. It is easy to establish democracy where most people live by farming or raising livestock. Their poverty leaves them little leisure, so they seldom attend the assembly. Because they lack life's necessities, they work continually and do not covet others' property. Indeed, they prefer their work to the responsibilities of government or office, where those positions offer no large financial rewards. Most people desire profit more than honour. This is proved by their patient endurance of ancient tyrannies, as they still endure oligarchies, provided they can work and keep their property. Some quickly become rich, and the others are comfortably enough situated. They also have the power to elect magistrates and demand an account of their conduct, which satisfies whatever ambition they possess. In some democracies they do not even participate directly in every appointment, but act through representatives selected in rotation from the whole population, as at Mantinea. Even there, the many remain satisfied if they retain deliberative authority. This arrangement, too, can be considered democratic, as it was at Mantinea. It is therefore both useful and customary in such a democracy for everyone to elect officeholders, scrutinize their conduct, and serve in the courts. The major offices, however, should be filled by election from people with a property qualification, with higher offices requiring greater qualifications. Alternatively, if no offices require property, those with exceptional ability should be appointed. Citizens are certain to be well governed under this arrangement: the best people will always occupy the offices, since the people are willing to elect them and do not resent [compare IV.13, section 8, and II.12, section 5]

the good. Good men and notable citizens will then be satisfied, because they will not be governed by their inferiors. Those elected will govern justly because others can hold them accountable. Everyone should answer to someone else, and no one should be permitted to act entirely as he pleases. Complete freedom leaves nothing to restrain the evil present in every person. Accountability secures the greatest benefit a state can have: the right people govern, they are prevented from acting wrongly, and the people receive their due. Clearly this is the best kind of democracy, precisely because its people belong to a particular class. Many states had excellent ancient laws designed to make their people farmers. They either limited the amount of land any person could own, or required holdings above that amount to lie beyond a specified distance from the town or acropolis.

In earlier times, many states had a law forbidding anyone to sell the allotment of land originally assigned to him. A similar law attributed to Oxylus required a certain portion of every person's property to remain free from loans secured against it. The Aphytaeans' law would be a useful corrective to the evil we are discussing. Although their population is large and their land limited, they are all farmers. Their property is assessed in the census not as entire estates, but in units small enough to allow even poor people to possess more than the amount required for qualification.

A pastoral population living from its flocks is the next best after a farming population, and resembles it in many respects. [Alternative reading of the preceding passage: 'so that the poor people's qualification may exceed the rich people's'.] Such people are better prepared for war than any others, physically sturdy and accustomed to sleeping outdoors. The populations of other democracies are far inferior because their lives are inferior. Their occupations, whether as artisans, traders, or labourers, leave no room for moral excellence. They can also attend the assembly easily, since they are constantly moving around the city and the agora. Farmers, by contrast, live scattered across the countryside; they do not meet one another or feel the same need to assemble. Where a state's territory reaches far beyond the city, establishing an excellent democracy or constitutional government is easy, since people must settle in the country. Even where there is an urban population, the assembly should not meet when country people cannot attend. We have thus explained the organization of the first and best democracy. The inferior forms plainly depart from it in a regular sequence, with the population excluded at each stage belonging to a lower kind.

The final kind of democracy is the one in which everyone participates on equal terms. Not every state can sustain this form, and it will not last long unless it is properly regulated by laws and established customs. We have already examined fairly fully the general causes that destroy this and other governments. To establish such a democracy and strengthen the people, its leaders habitually admit as many as possible to citizenship. They include not only legitimate children, but illegitimate ones and people with just one citizen parent, whether father or mother. A democracy of this kind welcomes all such additions. Demagogues follow this course. The proper course, however, is to stop adding citizens once the common people outnumber the notables or the middle class, and go no further. [Compare III.5, section 7.] Beyond that point the state becomes disorderly, and notable citizens become agitated and impatient with democracy, as happened in the revolt at Cyrene. A small evil passes unnoticed; once it grows, it becomes conspicuous.

The extreme form of democracy benefits from measures like those Cleisthenes enacted when he wanted to enlarge democratic power at Athens, or those introduced by the founders of popular government at Cyrene. New tribes and brotherhoods should be established. The private religious rites of families should be restricted and transformed into public observances. In short, every available device should be adopted to mingle citizens with one another and break down their old connections.

The policies of tyrants also all seem democratic. Examples include the freedom allowed to slaves, which may be advantageous up to a point; similar freedom for women and children; and permission for everyone to live as he pleases. Such a government will attract many supporters, because most people prefer a disorderly life to a disciplined one.

For a legislator, or anyone seeking to create a democracy, establishing it is neither the sole nor the chief task. Any state, however badly constituted, can survive for one, two, or three days. Preserving it is far more difficult. The legislator should therefore lay secure foundations, following the principles already stated concerning the preservation and destruction of states. He must guard against destructive forces and make written or unwritten laws embodying every means of preservation. He should regard as truly democratic or oligarchical not the measure that maximizes democracy or oligarchy, but the one that enables it to last longest. Today's demagogues frequently arrange confiscations through the courts to gratify the people. Those concerned for the state's welfare should oppose them. They should require confiscated property paid into the treasury to become sacred property rather than public property. Wrongdoers would remain equally afraid, since punishment would be unchanged. But the people would gain nothing and would be less eager to convict defendants. Public prosecutions should also be kept as few as possible, and those bringing unfounded charges should face severe penalties. Such accusations are usually directed against notable citizens, not members of the popular party. Yet all citizens ought to feel equally attached to the state, or at least ought not to regard their governors as enemies.

In the final and worst democracy, citizens are so numerous that assembling them without payment is difficult. Where there is no revenue, paying them burdens the notables severely. The money must come from property taxes, confiscations, and corruption in the courts—practices that have already destroyed many democracies. Where revenue is lacking, therefore, the government should hold few assemblies. Courts should contain many jurors but sit for only a few days. This has two advantages. First, the rich will not fear the cost, even if they receive nothing while poor jurors are paid. Second, cases will be judged better. Wealthy people dislike prolonged absence from their affairs but are willing to spend a few days in court. [Compare V.11, sections 2–3, and section 5.] Where revenue exists, demagogues should not be allowed to distribute every surplus as they habitually do. The poor are continually receiving such payments and are continually in need of still more. Assistance given in this fashion is like water poured into a barrel that leaks. A genuine friend of the people must nevertheless prevent them from becoming excessively poor, because extreme poverty degrades democracy. Measures should also be taken that give them prosperity which will endure, rather than merely momentary relief. Since every class benefits from this, public revenues should be saved up and distributed to the poor in amounts sufficient, if possible, to buy a small farm, or at least to begin trading or farming. If everyone cannot receive this assistance at once, distribute it in rotation by tribes or other divisions. Meanwhile, the rich should pay for poor citizens to attend necessary assemblies and, in return, be excused unnecessary public services. Governing in this spirit, the Carthaginians retain popular affection. Periodically they send some of the people to dependent towns, where they become wealthy. A generous and sensible nobility could also divide the poor among themselves and supply them with the means to work. Tarentum offers another example worth following: by sharing the use of their property with the poor, its people earn their goodwill. They also divide their offices into two groups, choosing half by vote and half by lot. Selection by lot gives the people participation; election by vote improves administration. Dividing the same offices between two sets of magistrates, one elected and the other selected by lot, could produce a similar result.

We have said enough about how democracies should be organized. These arguments also make it easy to see how oligarchies should be constituted. We must work out each oligarchy by reasoning from its opposite, considering its structure in relation to the corresponding form of democracy.

The first and most balanced oligarchy approaches constitutional government. It should have two property qualifications, one high and one low. The lower should admit people to lesser but necessary offices, and the higher to the more important offices. Anyone who attains the required qualification should receive citizenship. Those admitted must be of such a character that the governing body as a whole is stronger than those excluded, and new citizens should always come from the better part of the people. Restricting this principle somewhat produces another oligarchy. Continuing the restriction brings us finally to the most exclusive and tyrannical form, corresponding to extreme democracy. As the worst oligarchy, it demands care proportionate to its badness. Healthy bodies and ships with adequate crews can survive many accidents. Sickly bodies and rotten, poorly crewed ships are destroyed by the slightest mistake. So too the worst governments require the greatest vigilance. Large populations generally preserve democracies, since numbers serve democracy in place of justice based on proportion. Oligarchy's preservation clearly rests on the opposite principle, good order. [Textual note: reading 'of the same office' with Bekker's second edition.] Just as the common people fall into four chief groups—farmers, artisans, retailers, and labourers—military forces have four branches: cavalry, heavy infantry, light troops, and the navy. Where the land suits cavalry, a powerful oligarchy is likely to arise. The inhabitants' safety depends on that force, and only wealthy people can afford horses. The second oligarchical form prevails where heavy infantry is important, because this service is more suitable for the rich than the poor. Light troops and naval forces, however, are wholly democratic. Nowadays their numbers are so great that, when the parties clash, they often defeat the oligarchs. Generals' practice suggests a remedy: they combine an appropriate contingent of light troops with cavalry and heavy infantry. Light arms explain how the poor defeat the rich in civil struggles; they give an advantage against cavalry and heavily armed soldiers. An oligarchy recruiting such troops from the lower classes raises a force against itself. Citizens differ in age, however, so fathers should have their sons trained while young in the quick movements of light troops. Some should then be selected when grown to serve as actual light-armed soldiers. Oligarchy must also grant the people a share in government. As already suggested, it can admit those with the required property; or, following Thebes, those who have avoided lowly occupations for a prescribed number of years; or, following Massalia, men chosen for their merit, whether previously citizens or not. The highest magistracies, properly reserved for the governing body, should carry expensive obligations. The people will then have no wish to occupy them and will not resent their rulers' privileges when they see the heavy price paid for that dignity. On entering office, magistrates should also make splendid sacrifices or erect a public building. The people, who share in the feasts and enjoy seeing their city adorned with votive offerings and buildings, will then have no wish to change the government. The notables, meanwhile, will possess lasting monuments to their generosity. Our modern oligarchs behave quite differently. They desire profit as eagerly as honour, and their oligarchies could aptly be called petty democracies. Let this suffice on the organization of democracies and oligarchies.

We turn next to the proper distribution of offices: how many there should be, what kind they should be, and what duties they should perform. We have already touched on these questions. No state can exist without necessary offices, or be well governed without offices that maintain harmony and order. As we have said, a small state does not need many, whereas a larger state needs more. We must consider carefully which functions can properly be combined and which should remain separate. The market requires a magistrate to oversee contracts and preserve order. Every state necessarily has buyers and sellers supplying one another's needs. This is the most direct means of making a state self-sufficient and fulfilling the purpose for which people unite in a state. A second, similar office supervises and improves public and private buildings, maintains and repairs houses and roads, prevents boundary disputes, and deals with related matters.

This office is usually called that of City-warden. It has several branches, divided among different people in larger towns. One might oversee the walls, another the fountains, and another the harbours. Another equally necessary, similar office manages the same matters outside the walls and in the countryside. Its holders are called Wardens of the country or Inspectors of the woods. Beyond these three comes a fourth office, the tax receivers. They administer the revenue and allocate it among the different departments. They are called Receivers or

Treasurers. Another official records private contracts, court decisions, public accusations, and all preliminary proceedings. This office too is sometimes divided into branches, with one official supervising all the others. Its holders have names such as Recorders, Sacred Recorders, and Presidents.

Next comes an office with duties that are at once among the most necessary and the most difficult. It is responsible for carrying out punishments, collecting fines from those whose names are publicly displayed in the registers, and keeping prisoners in custody. The difficulty arises from the hatred attached to these duties. No one will accept the office unless there is a prospect of considerable profit, and even someone who accepts it is reluctant to carry out the law. Yet the office is indispensable. Judicial decisions serve no purpose unless they take effect. If society cannot exist without such decisions, it cannot exist without their enforcement either. Since this task is so unpopular, it should be divided among several people drawn from different courts, rather than given to one person alone. Similarly, the work of displaying the names of people registered as debtors to the state should be spread among different officials. Some sentences should be carried out by officers whose duties also include other functions. New officials should exact penalties for new offences. In cases that are not new, the authority that imposes the sentence should differ from the authority that collects the penalty. City-wardens, for instance, should collect fines imposed by the wardens of the agora, while other officials should collect the fines imposed by city-wardens. Penalties are more likely to be collected when collecting them attracts less resentment. Those who both pronounce judgment and enforce it incur double hatred. If the same judges always execute the sentences they pronounce, they become enemies of everyone.

In many places, keeping prisoners and enforcing sentences are assigned to different magistracies; Athens provides the example of 'the Eleven'. It is advisable to separate prison custody and devise some means of reducing its unpopularity. The task of keeping prisoners in custody is quite as necessary as the task of carrying out sentences. Yet good men do everything possible to avoid it, while worthless men cannot safely be trusted with it: they need guarding themselves and are unfit to guard others. The duty should therefore not belong to one specially appointed or permanent official. Where young men are organized into a corps or guard, they should undertake it, with different magistrates taking responsibility in rotation.

These are the indispensable offices and must be placed first in our account. Next are others equally necessary but higher in rank, demanding considerable experience and trustworthiness. Among them are the offices entrusted with the protection of the city and with the performance of other military duties. In peace as well as war, their holders must defend walls and gates, muster citizens, and arrange them in formation. Some states have many such offices, others only a few; small states manage with one. Their holders are called generals or commanders. Where a state has cavalry, light infantry, archers, or a navy, each branch sometimes has its own officers, called admirals, cavalry generals, or infantry generals. Below them are naval captains, military captains, and cavalry captains, with further officers under their command. All these fall within the military department. Let this be enough about military command.

Since many, if not all, of these officials deal with public money, another office must examine and audit their work, without undertaking any other duties. Its holders bear various titles: Scrutineers, Auditors,

Accountants, and Controllers. Beyond all these stands an office with supreme authority over them. It is often responsible both for introducing measures and for confirming them; in a democracy it presides over the assembly. The authority that summons the people must necessarily stand at the head of the state. In some places its members are called 'probuli', because they deliberate beforehand; in democracies they are more commonly called 'councillors'. These are the principal political offices.

A further group of officials maintains religion. Priests and guardians oversee the preservation and repair of the gods' temples and attend to other religious matters. Small communities may need only one such office. Larger ones have many in addition to priests, including supervisors of sacrifices, keepers of shrines, and treasurers of sacred revenues. Closely related are officials appointed to perform public sacrifices, except those the law assigns specifically to priests. These officials take their dignity from the city's public hearth. Their titles vary: sometimes archons, sometimes kings, and sometimes prytanes.

These, then, are the necessary offices of a state, and we may summarize their responsibilities in the following way. They concern religion, warfare, public income and expenditure, the market, the city, harbours, and the countryside; the law courts, records of contracts, enforcement of sentences, prison custody, and the auditing and examination of magistrates' accounts. Finally, some preside over the state's public deliberations. Other offices characterize states that are peaceful and prosperous while attentive to good order. These include guardians of women, guardians of laws, guardians of children, and directors of physical training, as well as supervisors of athletic and Dionysiac competitions and similar public spectacles. Some are plainly undemocratic. Guardians of women and children are examples, since poor people have no slaves and must use their wives and children as servants. [Compare IV.15, section 11, and III.14, section 14.] Lastly, the highest elective offices in states take three forms: guardians of the law, probuli, and councillors. Guardians of the law belong to aristocracy, probuli to oligarchy, and a council to democracy. Let this be enough of our discussion of the several different kinds of public office.

chapters.title: Book 7
paragraphs: He who would duly inquire about the best form of a state ought first to determine which is the most eligible life; while this remains uncertain, the best form of the state must also be uncertain. In the natural order of things, those may be expected to lead the best life who are governed in the best manner of which their circumstances admit. We ought, therefore, to ascertain first which is the most generally eligible life, and then whether the same life is or is not best for the state and for individuals.

Assuming that enough has already been said in exoteric discourses concerning the best life, we will now only repeat the statements contained in them. Certainly no one will dispute the propriety of that partition of goods which separates them into three classes — external goods, goods of the body, and goods of the soul — or deny that the happy man must have all three. No one would maintain that he is happy who has not in him a particle of courage, temperance, justice, or prudence, who is afraid of every insect that flutters past him, and will commit any crime, however great, in order to gratify his lust of meat or drink, who will sacrifice his dearest friend for the sake of half a farthing, and is as feeble and false in mind as a child or a madman. These propositions are universally acknowledged as soon as they are uttered, but men

differ about the quantity of goods of fortune and goods of the soul which is desirable, and the relative superiority of this or that good. Some think that a very moderate amount of virtue is enough, but set no limit to their desires of wealth, property, power, reputation, and the like.

To these we reply by an appeal to facts, which easily prove that mankind do not acquire or preserve virtue by the help of external goods, but external goods by the help of virtue; and that happiness, whether consisting in pleasure, virtue, or both, is more often found with those who are most highly cultivated in their mind and character, and have only a moderate share of external goods, than among those who possess external goods to a useless extent but are deficient in higher qualities. This is not only matter of experience but, when reflected upon, will easily appear to be in accordance with reason. External goods have a limit, like any other instrument, and all things useful are of such a nature that where there is too much of them, they must either do harm, or at any rate be of no use, to their possessors. Every good of the soul, by contrast, the greater it is, is also of greater use — if the epithet ‘useful’ as well as ‘noble’ is appropriate to such subjects. No proof is required to show that the best state of one thing in relation to another is proportioned to the degree of excellence by which the natures corresponding to those states are separated from each other. So if the soul is more noble than our possessions or our bodies, both absolutely and in relation to us, it must be admitted that the best state of either has a similar ratio to the other. Again, it is for the sake of the soul that goods external and goods of the body are eligible at all, and all wise men ought to choose them for the sake of the soul, and not the soul for the sake of them.

Let us acknowledge, then, that each one has just so much happiness as he has of virtue and wisdom, and of virtuous and wise action. God is a witness to us of this truth: he is happy and blessed, not by reason of any external good, but in himself and by reason of his own nature. Herein of necessity lies the difference between good fortune and happiness: external goods come of themselves, and chance is the author of them, but no one is just or temperate by or through chance. In the same way, and by a similar train of argument, the happy state may be shown to be that which is morally best and which acts rightly; and rightly it cannot act without doing right actions, and neither individual nor state can do right actions without virtue and wisdom. The courage, justice, and wisdom of a state have the same form and nature as the qualities which give the individual who possesses them the name of just, wise, or temperate.

This much may suffice by way of preface; for I could not avoid touching on these questions, neither could I go through all the arguments affecting them — these must be reserved for another discussion.

Let us assume, then, that the best life, both for individuals and for states, is the life of virtue, having external goods enough for the performance of good actions. If there are any who controvert our assertion, we will in this treatise pass them over, and consider their objections hereafter.

There remains to be discussed the question whether the happiness of the individual is the same as that of the state, or different. Here again there can be no doubt — no one denies that they are the same. Those who hold that the well-being of the individual consists in his wealth also think that riches make the happiness of the whole state; those who value most highly the life of a tyrant deem that city the happiest which rules over the greatest number; while those who approve an individual for his virtue say that the more virtuous a city is, the happier it is. Two points here present themselves for consideration. First, (1) which is the more eligible life — that of a citizen who is a member of a state, or that of an alien who has no political ties? And again, (2) which is the best form of constitution, or the best condition of a state — either on the supposition that political privileges are given to all, or that they are given to a majority only? Since the good of the state, and not of the individual, is the proper subject of political thought and speculation, and we are engaged in a political discussion, while the first of these two points has a secondary interest for us, the latter will be the main subject of our inquiry.

It is evident that the form of government is best in which every man, whoever he is, can act for the best and live happily. But even those who agree in thinking that the life of virtue is the most eligible raise the question whether the life of business and politics is or is not more eligible than one wholly independent of external goods — I mean a contemplative life, which by some is maintained to be the only one worthy of a philosopher. These two lives — the life of the philosopher and the life of the statesman — appear to have been preferred by those who have been most keen in the pursuit of virtue, both in our own and in other ages. Which is the better is a question of no small moment; for the wise man, like the wise state, will necessarily regulate his life according to the best end. Some think that, while a despotic rule over others is the greatest injustice, to exercise a constitutional rule over them, even though not unjust, is a great impediment to a man’s individual well-being. Others take an opposite view: they maintain that the true life of man is the practical and political, and that every virtue admits of being practised quite as much by statesmen and rulers as by private individuals. Others again are of opinion that arbitrary and tyrannical rule alone consists with happiness; indeed, in some states the entire aim of the laws is to give men despotic power over their neighbours. Although in most cities the laws may be said generally to be in a chaotic state, still, if they aim at anything, they aim at the maintenance of power. In Lacedaemon and Crete, the system of education and the greater part of the laws are framed with a view to war. In all nations which are able to gratify their ambition, military power is held in esteem — for example, among the Scythians, Persians, Thracians, and Celts. In some nations there are even laws tending to stimulate the warlike virtues — as at Carthage, where we are told that men obtain the honour of wearing as many armlets as they have served campaigns. There was once a law in Macedonia that he who had not killed an enemy should wear a halter, and among the Scythians no one who had not slain his man was allowed to drink out of the cup which was handed round at a certain feast. Among the Iberians, a warlike nation, the number of enemies whom a man has slain is indicated by the number of spits fixed in the earth round his tomb; and there are numerous other

practices among other nations of a like kind, some of them established by law and others by custom. Yet to a reflecting mind it must appear very strange that the statesman should be always considering how he can dominate and tyrannize over others, whether they will or not. How can that which is not even lawful be the business of the statesman or the legislator? Unlawful it certainly is to rule without regard to justice, since there may be might where there is no right. The other arts and sciences offer no parallel: a physician is not expected to persuade or coerce his patients, nor a pilot the passengers in his ship. Yet many appear to think that a despotic government is a true political form, and what men affirm to be unjust and inexpedient in their own case they are not ashamed of practising towards others. They demand justice for themselves, but where other men are concerned, they care nothing about it. Such behaviour is irrational — unless the one party is born to command and the other born to serve, in which case men have a right to command, not indeed all their fellows, but only those who are intended to be subjects. Just as we ought not to hunt mankind, whether for food or sacrifice, but only the animals which are intended for food or sacrifice — that is, such wild animals as are eatable. Surely there may be a city happy in isolation, which we will assume to be well-governed (for it is quite possible that a city thus isolated might be well-administered and have good laws); but such a city would not be constituted with any view to war or the conquest of enemies — all that sort of thing must be excluded. Hence we see very plainly that warlike pursuits, although generally to be deemed honourable, are not the supreme end of all things, but only means. The good lawgiver should inquire how states, races of men, and communities may participate in a good life, and in the happiness which is attainable by them. His enactments will not always be the same; and where there are neighbours, he will have to deal with them according to their characters, and to see what duties are to be performed towards each. The end at which the best form of government should aim may be properly made a matter of future consideration.

Let us now address those who, while they agree that the life of virtue is the most eligible, differ about the manner of practising it. Some renounce political power, and think that the life of the freeman is different from the life of the statesman, and the best of all; but others think the life of the statesman best. The argument of the latter is that he who does nothing cannot do well, and that virtuous activity is identical with happiness. To both we say: ‘You are partly right and partly wrong.’ The first class are right in affirming that the life of the freeman is better than the life of the despot — there is nothing grand or noble in having the use of a slave, in so far as he is a slave, or in issuing commands about necessary things. But it is an error to suppose that every sort of rule is despotic, like that of a master over slaves. There is as great a difference between the rule over freemen and the rule over slaves as there is between slavery by nature and freedom by nature, about which I have said enough at the commencement of this treatise. It is equally a mistake to place inactivity above action, since happiness is activity, and the actions of the just and wise are the realization of much that is noble.

But perhaps someone, accepting these premises, may still maintain that supreme power is the best of all things, since the possessors of it are able to perform the greatest number of noble actions. If so, the man who is able to rule, instead of giving up anything to his neighbour, ought rather to take away his power; and the father should make no account of his son, nor the son of his father, nor friend of friend — they should not bestow a thought on one another in comparison with this higher object, since the best is the most eligible, and ‘doing well’ is the best. There might be some truth in such a view if we assumed that robbers and plunderers attain the chief good. But this can never be, and so we infer the view to be false. The actions of a ruler cannot really be honourable unless he is as much superior to other men as a husband is to a wife, or a father to his children, or a master to his slaves. Therefore he who violates the law can never recover, by any success however great, what he has already lost in departing from virtue. Equals share alike in the honourable and the just, as is just and equal. But that the unequal should be given to equals, and the unlike to those who are like, is contrary to nature, and nothing which is contrary to nature is good. If, therefore, there is anyone superior in virtue and in the power of performing the best actions, him we ought to follow and obey — but he must have the capacity for action as well as virtue.

If we are right in our view, and happiness is assumed to be virtuous activity, the active life will be the best, both for the city collectively and for individuals. Not that a life of action must necessarily have relations to others, as some persons think, nor are those ideas only to be regarded as practical which are pursued for the sake of practical results — but much more the thoughts and contemplations which are independent and complete in themselves; since virtuous activity, and therefore action, is an end, and even in the case of external actions the directing mind is most truly said to act. Neither, again, is it necessary that states which are cut off from others, and choose to live alone, should be inactive; there may be activity also in the parts, and there are many ways in which the members of a state act upon one another. The same is equally true of every individual. If this were otherwise, God and the universe — who have no external actions over and above their own energies — would be far enough from perfection. Hence it is evident that the same life is best for each individual, and for states, and for mankind collectively.

Thus far by way of introduction. In what has preceded, I have discussed other forms of government; in what remains, the first point to be considered is what should be the conditions of the ideal or perfect state. The perfect state cannot exist without a due supply of the means of life, and so we must presuppose many purely imaginary conditions — but nothing impossible. There will be a certain number of citizens, a country in which to place them, and the like. As the weaver, the shipbuilder, or any other artisan must have the material proper for his work — and in proportion as this is better prepared, so will the result of his art be nobler — so the statesman or legislator must also have the materials suited to him.

First among the materials required by the statesman is population. He will consider what should be the number and character of the citizens, and then what should be the size and character of the country. Most persons think that a state, in order to be happy, ought to be large; but even if they are right, they have no idea of what a large and what a small state is. They judge of the size of the city by the number of inhabitants; whereas they ought to regard, not their number, but their power. A city, too, like an individual, has a work to do, and that city which is best adapted to the fulfilment of its work is to be deemed greatest — in the same sense in which Hippocrates might be called greater, not as a man, but as a physician, than someone else who was taller. Even if we reckon greatness by numbers, we ought not to include everybody, since there must always be in cities a multitude of slaves, sojourners, and foreigners. We should include only those who are members of the state, and who form an essential part of it. The number of the latter is a proof of the greatness of a city; but a city which produces numerous artisans and comparatively few soldiers cannot be great, since a great city is not to be confounded with a populous one. Moreover, experience shows that a very populous city can rarely, if ever, be well governed: all cities which have a reputation for good government have a limit of population. We may argue on grounds of reason, and the same result will follow. Law is order, and good law is good order; but a very great multitude cannot be orderly — to introduce order into the unlimited is the work of a divine power, of such a power as holds together the universe. Beauty is realized in number and magnitude, and the state which combines magnitude with good order must necessarily be the most beautiful. To the size of states there is a limit, as there is to other things — plants, animals, implements; for none of these retain their natural power when they are too large or too small, but they either wholly lose their nature, or are spoiled. A ship which is only a span long, for example, will not be a ship at all, nor a ship a quarter of a mile long; but there may be a ship of a certain size, either too large or too small, which will still be a ship, but bad for sailing. In the same way, a state, when composed of too few, is not as a state ought to be, self-sufficing; when composed of too many, though self-sufficing in all mere necessaries, it is a nation and not a state, being almost incapable of constitutional government. Who can be the general of such a vast multitude, or who the herald, unless he have the voice of a Stentor?

A state, then, only begins to exist when it has attained a population sufficient for a good life in the political community; it may indeed somewhat exceed this number. But, as I was saying, there must be a limit. What the limit should be will be easily ascertained by experience. Both governors and governed have duties to perform: the special functions of a governor are to command and to judge. If the citizens of a state are to judge and to distribute offices according to merit, then they must know each other’s characters; where they do not possess this knowledge, both the election to offices and the decision of lawsuits will go wrong. When the population is very large, they are manifestly settled at haphazard, which clearly ought not to be. Besides, in an over-populous state, foreigners and metics will readily acquire the rights of citizens — for who will find them out? Clearly, then, the best limit of the population of a state is the largest number which suffices for the purposes of life and can be taken in at a single view. Enough concerning the size of a city.

Much the same principle will apply to the territory of the state. Everyone would agree in praising the state which is most entirely self-sufficing — and that must be the state which is all-producing, since to have all things and to want nothing is sufficiency. In size and extent it should be such as may enable the inhabitants to live temperately and liberally in the enjoyment of leisure. Whether we are right or wrong in laying down this limit we will inquire more precisely hereafter, when we have occasion to consider what is the right use of property and wealth — a matter much disputed, since men are inclined to rush into one of two extremes, some into meanness, others into luxury.

It is not difficult to determine the general character of the territory required. There are, however, some points on which military authorities should be heard. They tell us that it should be difficult of access to the enemy, and well situated in regard both to sea and land. This, then, is one principle: it should be a convenient centre for the protection of the whole country. The other is that it should be suitable for receiving the fruits of the soil, and also for the bringing in of timber and any other products.

Whether a communication with the sea is beneficial to a well-ordered state or not is a question that has often been asked. It is argued that the introduction of strangers brought up under other laws, and the increase of population, will be adverse to good order — since a maritime people will always have a crowd of merchants coming and going — and that intercourse by sea is inimical to good government. Apart from these considerations, however, it would undoubtedly be better, both with a view to safety and to the provision of necessaries, that the city and territory should be connected with the sea. The defenders of a country, if they are to maintain themselves against an enemy, should be easily relieved both by land and by sea; and even if they are not able to attack by sea and land at once, they will have less difficulty in doing mischief to their assailants on one element, if they themselves can use both. Moreover, it is necessary that they should import from abroad what is not found in their own country, and that they should export what they have in excess. A city ought to be a market — not, indeed, for others, but for herself.

Those who make themselves a market for the world only do so for the sake of revenue; and if a state ought not to desire profit of this kind, it ought not to have such an emporium. Nowadays we often see in countries and cities dockyards and harbours very conveniently placed outside the city, but not too far off; and they are kept in dependence by walls and similar fortifications. Cities thus situated manifestly reap the benefit of intercourse with their ports, and any harm which is likely to accrue may be easily guarded against by the laws, which will pronounce and determine who may hold communication with one another, and who may not.

There can be no doubt that the possession of a moderate naval force is advantageous to a city. The citizens require such a force for their own needs, and they should also be formidable to their neighbours in certain cases, or, if necessary, able to assist them by sea as well as by land.

The proper number or magnitude of this naval force is relative to the character of the state. If her function is to take a leading part in politics, her naval power should be commensurate with the scale of her enterprises. The population of the state need not be much increased, since there is no necessity that the sailors should be citizens. The marines, who have the control and command, will be freemen, and belong also to the infantry; and wherever there is a dense population of Perioeci and husbandmen, there will always be sailors more than enough. We see instances of this at the present day. The city of Heraclea, for example, although small in comparison with many others, can man a considerable fleet. Such are our conclusions respecting the territory of the state, its harbour, its towns, its relations to the sea, and its maritime power.

Having spoken of the number of the citizens, we will proceed to speak of what should be their character. This is a subject which can be easily understood by anyone who casts his eye on the more celebrated states of Hellas, and generally on the distribution of races in the habitable world.
