Those who live in a cold climate and in northern Europe are full of spirit, but wanting in intelligence and skill; and so they keep their freedom, but have no political organization, and are incapable of ruling over others. Whereas the natives of Asia are intelligent and inventive, but they are wanting in spirit, and so they are always in a state of subjection and slavery. The Hellenic race, situated between them, is likewise intermediate in character, being high-spirited and also intelligent. Hence it continues free, and is the best governed of any nation, and, if it could be formed into one state, would be able to rule the world. There are also similar differences in the different tribes of Hellas: some of them are of a one-sided nature, and are intelligent or courageous only, while in others there is a happy combination of both qualities. Clearly, those whom the legislator will most easily lead to virtue may be expected to be both intelligent and courageous. Some, like Plato, say that the guardians should be friendly towards those whom they know, fierce towards those whom they do not know. Now, passion is the quality of the soul which begets friendship and inspires affection — notably, the spirit within us is more stirred against our friends and acquaintances than against those who are unknown to us, when we think we are despised by them. For which reason Archilochus, complaining of his friends, very naturally addresses his soul in these words:

‘For wert thou not plagued on account of friends?’ The power of command and the love of freedom are in all men based upon this quality, since passion is commanding and invincible. Nor is it right to say that the guardians should be fierce towards those whom they do not know, for we ought not to be out of temper with anyone; and a lofty spirit is not

fierce by nature, but only when excited against evil-doers. This, as I was saying before, is a feeling which men show most strongly towards their friends if they think they have received a wrong at their hands — as indeed is reasonable; for, besides the actual injury, they seem to be deprived of a benefit by those who owe them one. Hence the saying:

‘Cruel is the strife of brethren’; and again, ‘They who love in excess also hate in excess.’ Thus we have nearly determined the number and character of the citizens of our state, and also the size and nature of their territory. I say ‘nearly,’ since we ought not to require the same minuteness in theory as in fact.

As in other natural compounds the conditions of a composite whole are not necessarily organic parts of it, so in a state, or in any other combination forming a unity, not everything is a part which is a necessary condition. The members of an association have necessarily some one thing the same and common to all, in which they share equally or unequally — for example, food, or land, or anything else. But where there are two things, one a means and the other an end, they have nothing in common except that the one receives what the other produces. Such, for example, is the relation in which workmen and tools stand to their work; the house and the builder have nothing in common, but the art of the builder is for the sake of the house. So states require property — but property, even though living beings are included in it, is no part of a state. A state is not a community of living beings only, but a community of equals, aiming at the best life possible. Now, whereas happiness is the highest good, being a realization and perfect practice of virtue (which some attain, while others have little or none of it), the various qualities of men are clearly the reason why there are various kinds of states and many forms of government — different men seek after happiness in different ways and by different means, and so make for themselves different modes of life and forms of government. We must see also how many things are indispensable to the existence of a state, since what we call the parts of a state will be found among them. Let us, then, enumerate the functions of a state, and we shall easily elicit what we want.

First, there must be food. Secondly, arts, since life requires many instruments. Thirdly, there must be arms, since the members of a community have need of them in order to maintain authority both against disobedient subjects and against external assailants. Fourthly, there must be a certain amount of revenue, both for internal needs and for the purposes of war. Fifthly — or rather first — there must be a care of religion, which is commonly called worship. Sixthly, and most necessary of all, there must be a power of deciding what is for the public interest, and what is just in men’s dealings with one another.

These are the things which every state may be said to need. A state is not a mere aggregate of persons, but a union of them sufficing for the purposes of life; and if any of these things is wanting, it is simply impossible that the community can be self-sufficing. A state, then,

should be framed with a view to the fulfilment of these functions. There must be husbandmen to procure food, artisans, a warlike and a wealthy class, priests, and judges to decide what is just and expedient. Having determined these points, we have in the next place to consider whether all ought to share in every sort of occupation. Shall every man be at once husbandman, artisan, councillor, judge — or shall we suppose the several occupations just mentioned assigned to different persons? Or, thirdly, shall some employments be assigned to individuals, and others common to all? The question, however, does not occur in every state. As we were saying, all may be shared by all, or not all by all, but only some by some; and hence arise the differences of states. In democracies all share in all; in oligarchies, the opposite practice prevails. Now, since we are here speaking of the best form of government, and that under which the state will be most happy (and happiness, as has already been said, cannot exist without virtue), it clearly follows that in the state which is best governed, the citizens who are absolutely — and not merely relatively — just men must not lead the life of mechanics or tradesmen, since such a life is ignoble and inimical to virtue. Neither must they be husbandmen, since leisure is necessary both for the development of virtue and the performance of political duties.

Again, there is in a state a class of warriors, and another of councillors, who advise about the expedient and determine matters of law; and these seem in an especial manner to be parts of a state. Should these two classes be distinguished, or are both functions to be assigned to the same persons? Here again there is no difficulty in seeing that both functions will in one way belong to the same persons, and in another to different persons. To different persons in so far as their employments are suited to different ages of life — the one requires wisdom, the other strength. But on the other hand, since it is impossible that those who are able to use or to resist force should be willing to remain always in subjection, from this point of view the persons are the same; for those who carry arms can always determine the fate of the constitution. It remains, therefore, that both functions of government should be entrusted to the same persons — not, however, at the same time, but in the order prescribed by nature, who has given to young men strength and to older men wisdom. Such a distribution of duties will be expedient and also just, since it is in accordance with desert. Besides, the ruling class should be the owners of property, since they are citizens, and the citizens of a state should be in good circumstances. Mechanics, or any other class whose art excludes the art of virtue, have no share in the state. This follows from our first principle, since happiness cannot exist without virtue, and a city is not to be termed happy in regard to a portion of the citizens, but in regard to them all. Clearly property should be in their hands, since the husbandmen will of necessity be slaves, barbarians, or Perioeci. Of the classes enumerated, there remain only the priests, and the manner in which their office is to be regulated is obvious. No husbandman or mechanic should be appointed to it, since the gods should receive honour from the citizens only. Now, since the body of the citizens is divided into two classes — the warriors and the councillors — and it is beseeming that the worship of the gods should be duly performed, and also that a

rest should be provided in their service for those who from age have given up active life — to the old men of these two classes should be assigned the duties of the priesthood. We have shown what the necessary conditions are, and what the parts of a state are. Husbandmen, craftsmen, and labourers of all kinds are necessary to the existence of states; but the parts of the state are the warriors and councillors. And these are distinguished severally from one another, the distinction being in some cases permanent, in others not.

It is no new or recent discovery of political philosophers that the state ought to be divided into classes, and that the warriors should be separated from the husbandmen. The system has continued in Egypt and in Crete to this day, and was established, as tradition says, by a law of Sesostris in

Egypt, and of Minos in Crete. The institution of common tables also appears to be of ancient date, being in Crete as old as the reign of Minos, and in Italy far older. The Italian historians say that there was a certain Italus, king of Oenotria, from whom the Oenotrians were called Italians, and who gave the name of Italy to the promontory of Europe lying between the Scylletic and Lametic Gulfs, which are distant from one another only half a day’s journey. They say that this Italus converted the Oenotrians from shepherds into husbandmen, and besides other laws which he gave them, was the founder of their common meals; even in our day some who are derived from him retain this institution and certain other laws of his.
On the side of Italy towards Tyrrhenia dwelt the Opici, who are now, as of old, called Ausones; and on the side towards Iapygia and the Ionian Gulf, in the district called Syrtis, the

Chones, who are likewise of Oenotrian race. From this part of the world originally came the institution of common tables; the separation into castes, which was much older, came from Egypt, since the reign of Sesostris is of far greater antiquity than that of Minos. It is true that these and many other things have been invented several times over in the course of ages — or rather times without number; for necessity may be supposed to have taught men the inventions which were absolutely required, and once these were provided, it was natural that other things which would adorn and enrich life should grow up by degrees. We may infer that in political institutions the same rule holds. Egypt witnesses to the antiquity of all things, since the Egyptians appear to be of all people the most ancient, and they have laws and a regular constitution existing from time immemorial. We should therefore make the best use of what has been already discovered, and try to supply defects.

I have already remarked that the land ought to belong to those who possess arms and have a share in the government, and that the husbandmen ought to be a class distinct from them; and I have determined what the extent and nature of the territory should be. Let me proceed to discuss the distribution of the land, and the character of the agricultural class. I do not think that property ought to be common, as some

maintain, but only that by friendly consent there should be a common use of it, and that no citizen should be in want of subsistence. As to common meals, there is general agreement that a well-ordered city should have them, and we will hereafter explain our own reasons for taking this view. They ought, however, to be open to all the citizens. Yet it is not easy for the poor to contribute the requisite sum out of their private means, and to provide also for their household. The expense of religious worship should likewise be a public charge.

The land must therefore be divided into two parts, one public and the other private, and each part should be subdivided. Half of the public land should be appropriated to the service of the gods, the other half used to defray the cost of the common meals. Of the private land, half should be near the border, the other near the city, so that each citizen, having two lots, may have land in both places. There is justice and fairness in such a division, and it tends to inspire unanimity among the people in their border wars. Where there is no such arrangement, some of them are too ready to come to blows with their neighbours, while others are so cautious that they quite lose the sense of honour. Hence there is a law in some places which forbids those who dwell near the border to take part in public deliberations about wars with neighbours, on the ground that their interests will pervert their judgment. For the reasons already mentioned, then, the land should be divided in the manner described.

The very best thing of all would be that the husbandmen should be slaves, not all of the same race, and not spirited — since if they have no spirit they will be better suited for their work, and there will be no danger of their making a revolution. The next best thing would be that they should be Perioeci of foreign race, and of a like inferior nature; some of them should be the slaves of individuals, and employed on the private estates of men of property, while the remainder should be the property of the state and employed on the common land. I will hereafter explain what the proper treatment of slaves is, and why it is expedient that liberty should always be held out to them as the reward of their services.

We have already said that the city should be open to the land and to the sea, and to the whole country as far as possible. As to the place itself, our wish would be to find a situation for it fortunate in four things. The first is health — this is a necessity. Cities which lie towards the east, and are blown upon by winds coming from the east, are the healthiest; next in healthfulness are those sheltered from the north wind, since they have a milder winter. The site of the city should likewise be convenient both for political administration and for war. With a view to war, it should afford easy egress to the citizens, and at the same time be inaccessible and difficult of capture to enemies. There should be a natural abundance of springs and fountains in the town; or, if there is a deficiency of them, great reservoirs may be established for the collection of rain-water, such as will not fail when the inhabitants are cut

off from the country by war. Special care should be taken of the health of the inhabitants, which will depend chiefly on the healthiness of the locality and of the quarter to which they are exposed, and secondly, on the use of pure water — this latter point is by no means a secondary consideration. The elements which we use most and oftenest for the support of the body contribute most to health, and among these are water and air. Hence, in all wise states, if there is a want of pure water and the supply is not all equally good, the drinking water ought to be separated from that which is used for other purposes.

As to strongholds, what is suitable to different forms of government varies. An acropolis is suited to an oligarchy or a monarchy, but a plain to a democracy; neither is suited to an aristocracy, but rather a number of strong places. The arrangement of private houses is considered to be more agreeable, and generally more convenient, if the streets are regularly laid out after the modern fashion which Hippodamus introduced. But for security in war, the antiquated mode of building, which made it difficult for strangers to get out of a town and for assailants to find their way in, is preferable. A city should therefore adopt both plans of building: it is possible to arrange the houses irregularly, as husbandmen plant their vines in what are called ‘clumps.’ The whole town should not be laid out in straight lines, but only certain quarters and regions; thus security and beauty will be combined.

As to walls, those who say that cities making any pretension to military virtue should not have them are quite out of date in their notions; and they may see the cities which prided themselves on this fancy confuted by facts. True, there is little courage shown in seeking for safety behind a rampart when an enemy is similar in character and not much superior in number; but the superiority of the besiegers may be — and often is — beyond the power of men to resist, and too much for the valour of a few. If they are to be saved and to escape defeat and outrage, the strongest wall will be the best defence of the warrior, more especially now that catapults and siege engines have been brought to such perfection. To have no walls would be as foolish as to choose a site for a town in an exposed country, and to level the heights — or as if an individual were to leave his house unwalled, lest the inmates should become cowards. Nor must we forget that those who have their cities surrounded by walls may either take advantage of them or not, but cities which are unwalled have no choice.

If our conclusions are just, not only should cities have walls, but care should be taken to make them ornamental as well as useful for warlike purposes, and adapted to resist modern inventions. As the assailants of a city do all they can to gain an advantage, so the defenders should make use of any means of defence which have been already discovered, and should devise and invent others; for when men are well prepared, no enemy even thinks of attacking them.

Since the walls are to be divided by guardhouses and towers built at suitable intervals, and the body of citizens must be distributed at common tables, the idea will naturally occur that we should establish some of the common tables in the guardhouses. The arrangement might be as follows. The principal common tables of the magistrates will occupy a suitable place, and there also will be the buildings appropriated to religious worship — except in the case of those rites which the law or the Pythian oracle has restricted to a special locality. The site should be a spot seen far and wide, which gives due elevation to virtue and towers over the neighbourhood. Near this spot should be established an agora, such as that which the Thessalians call the ‘freemen’s agora.’ From this all trade should be excluded, and no mechanic, husbandman, or any such person allowed to enter, unless he be summoned by the magistrates. It would be a charming use of the place if the gymnastic exercises of the elder men were performed there. In this noble practice different ages should be separated, and some of the magistrates should stay with the boys, while the grown-up men remain with the magistrates in the freeman’s agora — since the presence of the magistrates is the best mode of inspiring true modesty and ingenuous fear. There should also be a traders’ agora, distinct and apart from the other, in a situation convenient for the reception of goods both by sea and land.

But in speaking of the magistrates we must not forget another section of the citizens, namely the priests, for whom public tables should likewise be provided in their proper place near the temples. The magistrates who deal with contracts, indictments, summonses, and the like, and those who have the care of the agora and of the city respectively, ought to be established near the agora and in some public place of meeting; the neighbourhood of the traders’ agora will be a suitable spot. The upper agora we devote to

the life of leisure, the other is intended for the necessities of trade. The same order should prevail in the country: the magistrates there — called by some ‘Inspectors of Forests,’ and by others ‘Wardens of the Country’ — must have guardhouses and common tables while they are on duty; temples should also be scattered throughout the country, dedicated some to gods, and some to heroes.

But it would be a waste of time for us to linger over details like these. The difficulty is not in imagining them, but in carrying them out. We may talk about them as much as we like, but the execution of them will depend upon fortune. Let us, then, say no more about these matters for the present.

Returning to the constitution itself, let us seek to determine out of what, and what sort of, elements the state which is to be happy and well-governed should be composed. There are two things in which all well-being consists. One is the choice of a right end and aim of action; the other, the discovery of the actions which are means towards it — since the means and the end may agree or disagree. Sometimes the right end is set before men, but in practice they fail to attain it; in other cases they are successful in all the means, but they propose to themselves a bad end; and sometimes they fail in both. Take, for example, the art of medicine. Physicians do not always understand the nature of health, and the means they use may not effect the desired end. In all arts and sciences, both the end and the means should be equally within our control.

The happiness and well-being which all men manifestly desire, some have the power of attaining; but to others, from some accident or defect of nature, the attainment of them is not granted. A good life requires a supply of external goods — in a less degree when men are in a good state, in a greater degree when they are in a lower state. Others again, who possess the conditions of happiness, go utterly wrong from the first in the pursuit of it. Since our object is to discover the best form of government — that, namely, under which a city will be best governed — and since the city is best governed which has the greatest opportunity of obtaining happiness, it is evident that we must clearly ascertain the nature of happiness.

We have said in the Ethics, if the arguments there adduced are of any value, that happiness is the realization and perfect exercise of virtue, and this not conditional, but absolute. I used the term ‘conditional’ to express that which is indispensable, and ‘absolute’ to express that which is good in itself. Take the case of just actions: just punishments and chastisements do indeed spring from a good principle, but they are good only because we cannot do without them — it would be better that neither individuals nor states should need anything of the sort. Actions which aim at honour and advantage, however, are absolutely the best. The conditional action is only the choice of a lesser evil, whereas these are the foundation and creation of good. A good man may make the best even of poverty, disease, and the other ills of life; but he can only attain happiness under the opposite conditions. As we have already said in the Ethics, the good man is he to whom, because he is virtuous, the absolute good is his good. It is also plain that his use of other goods must be virtuous and, in the absolute sense, good. This makes men fancy that external goods are the cause of happiness — yet we might as well say that a brilliant performance on the lyre was to be attributed to the instrument and not to the skill of the performer.

It follows, then, from what has been said, that some things the legislator must find ready to his hand in a state, while others he must provide. We can therefore only say: may our state be constituted in such a manner as to be blessed with the goods of which fortune disposes (since we acknowledge her power); whereas virtue and goodness in the state are not a matter of chance but the result of knowledge and purpose. A city can be virtuous only when the citizens who have a share in the government are virtuous, and in our state all the citizens share in the government. Let us, then, inquire how a man becomes virtuous. Even if we could suppose all the citizens to be virtuous, and not each of them, yet the latter would be better, since in the virtue of each, the virtue of all is involved.

There are three things which make men good and virtuous: nature, habit, and reason. In the first place, every one must be born a man and not some other animal; in the second place, he must have a certain character, both of body and soul. But some qualities there is no use in having at birth, since they are altered by habit, and there are some gifts of nature which may be turned by habit to good or bad. Most animals lead a life of nature, although in lesser particulars some are influenced by habit as well. Man has reason, in addition, and man only. Hence nature, habit, and reason must be in harmony with one another (for they do not always agree); men do many things against habit and nature, if reason persuades them that they ought. We have already determined what natures are likely to be most easily moulded by the hands of the legislator. All else is the work of education: we learn some things by habit, and some by instruction.

Since every political society is composed of rulers and subjects, let us consider whether the relations of one to the other should interchange or be permanent. The education of the citizens will necessarily vary with the answer given to this question. If some men excelled others in the same degree in which gods and heroes are supposed to excel mankind in general — having in the first place a great advantage even in their bodies, and secondly in their minds, so that the superiority of the governors over their subjects was patent and undisputed — it would clearly be better that once for all the one class should rule and the others serve.

But since this is unattainable, and kings have no marked superiority over their subjects, such as Scylax affirms to be found among the Indians, it is obviously necessary on many grounds that all the citizens alike should take their turn at governing and being governed. Equality consists in the same treatment of similar persons, and no government can stand which is not founded upon justice. If the government is unjust, every one in the country unites with the governed in the desire to have a revolution, and it is an impossibility that the members of the government can be so numerous as to be stronger than all their enemies put together. Yet that governors should excel their subjects is undeniable. How all this is to be effected, and in what way they will respectively share in the government, the legislator has to consider. The subject has been already mentioned. Nature herself has given the principle of choice when she made a difference between old and young (though they are really the same in kind), of whom she fitted the one to govern and the others to be governed. No one takes offence at being governed when he is young, nor does he think himself better than his governors — especially if he will enjoy the same privilege when he reaches the required age.

We conclude that from one point of view governors and governed are identical, and from another different. Their education must therefore be the same and also different. He who would learn to command well must, as men say, first of all learn to obey. As I observed in the first part of this treatise, there is one rule which is for the sake of the rulers and another rule which is for the sake of the ruled — the former is despotic, the latter a free government. Some commands differ not in the thing commanded, but in the intention with which they are imposed. Hence many apparently menial offices are an honour to the free youth by whom they are performed; for actions do not differ as honourable or dishonourable in themselves so much as in the end and intention of them. Since we say that the virtue of the citizen and ruler is the same as that of the good man,

and that the same person must first be a subject and then a ruler, the legislator has to see that they become good men, by what means this may be accomplished, and what is the end of the perfect life. Now, the soul of man is divided into two parts: one of which has reason in itself, and the other, not having reason in itself, is able to obey reason. We call a man good because he has the virtues of these two parts. In which of them the end is more likely to be found is no matter of doubt to those who adopt our division: for in the world both of nature and of art, the inferior always exists for the sake of the better or superior, and the better or superior is that which has reason. Reason, too, in our ordinary way of speaking, is divided into two parts, since there is a practical and a speculative reason; and there must be a corresponding division of actions. The actions of the naturally better principle are to be preferred by those who have it in their power to attain to both or to all — that is always to every one the most eligible which is the highest attainable by him. The whole of life is further divided into two parts: business and leisure, war and peace; and all actions into those which are necessary and useful, and those which are honourable. The preference given to one or the other class of actions must necessarily be like the preference given to one or other part of the soul and its actions over the other. There must be war for the sake of peace, business for the sake of leisure, things useful and necessary for the sake of things honourable. All these points the statesman should keep in view when he frames his laws. He should consider the parts of the soul and their functions, and above all the better and the end; he should also remember the diversities of human lives and actions. Men must engage in business and go to war, but leisure and peace are better; they must do what is necessary and useful, but what is honourable is better. In such principles, children and persons of every age which requires education should be trained. Whereas even the Hellenes of the present day, who are reputed to be best governed, and the legislators who gave them their constitutions, do not appear to have framed their governments with regard to the best end, or to have given them laws and education with a view to all the virtues; but in a vulgar spirit have fallen back on those which promised to be more useful and profitable. Many modern writers have taken a similar view: they commend the Lacedaemonian constitution, and praise the legislator for making conquest and war his sole aim — a doctrine which may be refuted by argument and has long ago been refuted by facts. Most men desire empire in the hope of accumulating the goods of fortune; and on this ground Thibron and all those who have written about the Lacedaemonian constitution have praised their legislator, since the Lacedaemonians, by a training in hardships, gained great power. But surely they are not a happy people now that their empire has passed away, nor was their legislator right. How ridiculous is the result if, while they continue in the observances of his laws, and no one interferes with them, they have lost the better part of life. These writers further err about the sort of government which the legislator should approve. The government of freemen is noble, and implies more virtue than despotic government. Neither is a city to be deemed happy, nor a legislator to be praised, because he trains his citizens to conquer and obtain dominion over their neighbours, since there is great evil in this. On a similar principle, any citizen who could would obviously try to obtain the power in his own state — the crime which the Lacedaemonians accused king Pausanias of attempting, although he had so great honour already. No such principle, and no law having this object, is either statesmanlike, useful, or right. The same things are best both for individuals and for states, and these are the things which the legislator ought to implant in the minds of his citizens. Neither should men study war with a view to the enslavement of those who do not deserve to be enslaved; first of all they should provide against their own enslavement; in the second place obtain empire for the good of the governed, and not for the sake of exercising a general despotism; and in the third place, they should seek to be masters only over those who deserve to be slaves. Facts, as well as arguments, prove that the legislator should direct all his military and other measures to the provision of leisure and the establishment of peace. Most of these military states are safe only while they are at war, but fall when they have acquired their empire — like unused iron, they lose their edge in time of peace. For this the legislator is to blame, having never taught them how to lead the life of peace.

Since the end of individuals and of states is the same, the end of the best man and of the best state must also be the same. It is therefore evident that there ought to exist in both of them the virtues of leisure; for peace, as has been often repeated, is the end of war, and leisure of toil. Leisure and cultivation may be promoted not only by those virtues which are practised in leisure, but also by some of those which are useful to business — since many necessaries of life have to be supplied before we can have leisure. A city must therefore be temperate and brave, and able to endure: for truly, as the proverb says, ‘There is no leisure for slaves,’ and those who cannot face danger like men are the slaves of any invader. Courage and endurance are required for business, intellectual virtue for leisure, temperance and justice for both — more especially in times of peace and leisure, since war compels men to be just and temperate, whereas the enjoyment of good fortune and the leisure which comes with peace tends to make them insolent. Those, then, who seem to be the best off, and to be in possession of every good, have special need of justice and temperance — for example, those (if such there be, as the poets say) who dwell in the Islands of the Blest. They above all will need philosophy, temperance, and justice, and all the more the more leisure they have, living in the midst of abundance. There is no difficulty in seeing why the state that would be happy and good ought to have these virtues. If it is disgraceful in men not to be able to use the goods of life, it is peculiarly disgraceful not to be able to use them in time of peace — to show excellent qualities in action and war, and when they have peace and leisure, to be no better than slaves.

We should not, therefore, practise virtue after the manner of the Lacedaemonians. They, while agreeing with other men in their conception of the highest goods, differ from the rest of mankind in thinking that these goods are to be obtained by the practice of a single virtue. Since these goods, and the enjoyment of them, are clearly greater than the enjoyment derived from the virtues of which they are the end, we must now consider how, and by what means, they are to be attained.

We have already determined that nature, habit, and reason are required, and we have also defined what should be the character of the citizens. But we still have to consider whether the training of early life is to be that of reason or of habit, since these two must accord, and when in accord they will then form the best of harmonies. Reason may make mistakes and fail in attaining the highest ideal of life, and there may be a like evil influence of habit. Thus much is clear in the first place: as in all other things, generation starts from a beginning, and the ends of some beginnings are related to another end. In men, reason and mind are the end towards which nature strives, so that the generation and moral discipline of the citizens ought to be ordered with a view to them. In the second place, as the soul and body are two, we see also that there are two parts of the soul — the rational and the irrational — and two corresponding states: reason and appetite. As the body is prior in order of generation to the soul, so the irrational is prior to the rational.

The proof is that anger, will, and desire are implanted in children from their very birth, but reason and understanding are developed as they grow older. Hence the care of the body ought to precede that of the soul, and the training of the appetitive part should follow — none the less, our care of it must be for the sake of the reason, and our care of the body for the sake of the soul.

Since the legislator should begin by considering how the frames of the children whom he is rearing may be as good as possible, his first care will be about marriage — at what age should his citizens marry, and who are fit to marry? In legislating on this subject, he ought to consider the persons and their relative ages, that there may be no disproportion in them, and that they may not differ in their bodily powers (as will be the case if the man is still able to beget children while the woman is unable to bear them, or the woman able to bear while the man is unable to beget); from these causes arise quarrels and differences between married persons. Secondly, he must consider the time at which the children will succeed to their parents. There ought not to be too great an interval of age, since then the parents will be too old to derive any pleasure from their affection, or to be of any use to them. Nor ought they to be too nearly of an age — to youthful marriages there are many objections: the children will be wanting in respect to their parents, who will seem to be their contemporaries, and disputes will arise in the management of the household. Thirdly, and this is the point from which we digressed, the legislator must mould to his will the frames of newly-born children. Almost all these objects may be secured by attention to one point. Since the time of generation is commonly limited within the age of seventy years in the case of a man, and of fifty in the case of a woman, the commencement of the union should conform to these periods. The union of male and female when too young is bad for the procreation of children. In all other animals the offspring of the young are small and ill-developed, and generally of the female sex; the same is true of man, as is proved by the fact that in those cities in which men and women are accustomed to marry young, the people are small and weak. In childbirth, also, younger women suffer more, and more of them die. Some persons say this was the meaning of the response once given to the Troezenians — ‘Shear not the young field’ — the oracle really meant that many died because they married too young; it had nothing to do with the ingathering of the harvest. It also conduces to temperance not to marry too soon: women who marry early are apt to be wanton, and in men too the bodily frame is stunted if they marry while they are growing (since there is a time when the growth of the body ceases). Women should marry when they are about eighteen years of age, and men at thirty-seven; then they are in the prime of life, and the decline in the powers of both will coincide. Further, the children, if their birth takes place at the time which may reasonably be expected, will succeed in their prime, when the fathers are already in the decline of life, and have nearly reached their term of three-score years and ten.

Thus much of the age proper for marriage. The season of the year should also be considered. According to our present custom, people generally limit marriage to the season of winter, and they are right. The precepts of physicians and natural philosophers about generation should also be studied by the
parents themselves. The physicians give good advice about the right age of the body, and the natural philosophers about the winds — of which they prefer the north to the south.

What constitution in the parent is most advantageous to the offspring is a subject which we will hereafter consider, when we speak of the education of children; we will only make a few general remarks at present. The temperament of an athlete is not suited to the life of a citizen, or to health, or to the procreation of children, any more than the valetudinarian or exhausted constitution; but one which is in a mean between them. A man’s constitution should be inured to labour, but not to labour which is excessive, or of one sort only, such as is practised by athletes; he should be capable of all the actions of a freeman. These remarks apply equally to both parents. Women who are with child should be careful of themselves; they should take exercise and have a nourishing diet. The first of these prescriptions the legislator will easily carry into effect by requiring that they shall take a walk daily to some temple, where they can worship the gods who preside over birth. Their minds, however, unlike their bodies, they ought to keep unexercised — since the offspring derive their natures from their mothers as plants do from the earth.

As to the exposure and rearing of children, let there be a law that no deformed child shall live; but where there are too many (since in our state population has a limit), when couples have children in excess, and the state of feeling is averse to the exposure of offspring, let abortion be procured before sense and life have begun. What may or may not be lawfully done in these cases depends on the question of life and sensation.

Now, having determined at what ages men and women are to begin their union, let us also determine how long they shall continue to beget and bear offspring for the state. Men who are too old, like men who are too young, produce children who are defective in body and mind; the children of very old men are weakly. The limit, then, should be the age which is the prime of their intelligence; and this, in most persons, according to the notion of some poets who measure life by periods of seven years, is about fifty. At four or five years later, they should cease from having families; and from that time forward only cohabit with one another for the sake of health, or for some similar reason.

As to adultery, let it be held disgraceful for any man or woman to be unfaithful when they are married, and called husband and wife. If during the time of bearing children anything of the sort occur, let the guilty person be punished with a loss of privileges in proportion to the offence.

After the children have been born, the manner of rearing them may be supposed to have a great effect on their bodily strength. It would appear, from the example of animals and of those nations who desire to create the military habit, that the food which has most milk in it is best suited to human beings — but the less wine the better, if they would escape disease.

Also, all the motions to which children can be subjected at their early age are very useful. But in order to preserve their tender limbs from distortion, some nations have had recourse to mechanical appliances which straighten their bodies. To accustom children to the cold from their earliest years is also an excellent practice, which greatly conduces to health, and hardens them for military service. Hence many barbarians have a custom of plunging their children at birth into a cold stream; others, like the Celts, clothe them in a light wrapper only. Human nature should be early habituated to endure all which by habit it can be made to endure — but the process must be gradual. Children, from their natural warmth, may be easily trained to bear cold. Such care should attend them in the first stage of life.

The next period lasts to the age of five. During this, no demand should be made upon the child for study or labour, lest its growth be impeded; and there should be sufficient motion to prevent the limbs from being inactive. This can be secured, among other ways, by amusement; but the amusement should not be vulgar, tiring, or riotous. The Directors of Education, as they are termed, should be careful what tales or stories the children hear, since the sports of children are designed to prepare the way for the business of later life, and should be for the most part imitations of the occupations which they will hereafter pursue in earnest. Those are wrong who, like Plato in the Laws, attempt to check the loud crying and screaming of children, since these contribute towards their growth, and, in a manner, exercise their bodies. Straining the voice has an effect similar to that produced by the retention of the breath in violent exertions. Besides other duties, the Directors of Education should have an eye to their bringing up, and should take care that they are left as little as possible with slaves. Until they are seven years old they must live at home; and so, even at this early age, all that is mean and low should be banished from their sight and hearing. Indeed, there is nothing which the legislator should be more careful to

drive away than indecency of speech, since the light utterance of shameful words is akin to shameful actions. The young especially should never be allowed to repeat or hear anything of the sort. A freeman who is found saying or doing what is forbidden, if he be too young as yet to have the privilege of a place at the public table, should be disgraced and beaten, and an elder person degraded as his slavish conduct deserves. Since we do not allow improper language, clearly we should also banish pictures or tales which are indecent. Let the rulers take care that there be no image or picture representing unseemly actions, except in the temples of those gods at whose festivals the law permits even ribaldry, and whom the law also permits to be worshipped by persons of mature age on behalf of themselves, their children, and their wives. But the legislator should not allow youth to be hearers of satirical iambic verses or spectators of comedy until they are of an age to sit at the public tables and to drink strong wine; by that time education will have armed them against the evil influences of such representations.

We have made these remarks in a cursory manner — they are enough for the present occasion; but hereafter we will return to the subject and after a fuller discussion determine whether such liberty should or should not be granted, and in what way granted, if at all. Theodorus, the tragic actor, was quite right in saying that he would not allow any other actor, not even if he were quite second-rate, to enter before himself, since the spectators grew fond of the voices which they first heard. The same principle of association applies universally to things as well as persons — we always like best whatever comes first. Hence youth should be kept strangers to all that is bad, and especially to things which suggest vice or hate. When the five years have passed away, during the two following years they must look on at the pursuits which they are hereafter to learn. There are two periods of life into which education has to be divided: from seven to the age of puberty, and onwards to the age of twenty-one. The poets who divide ages by sevens are not always right; we should rather adhere to the divisions actually made by nature, since the deficiencies of nature are what art and education seek to fill up.

Let us, then, first inquire if any regulations are to be laid down about children; secondly, whether the care of them should be the concern of the state or of private individuals (which latter is in our own day the common custom); and in the third place, what these regulations should be.

chapters.title: Book 8
paragraphs: No one will dispute that a legislator's first concern should be the education of the young, or that neglecting education damages states. Citizens must be formed to fit the government under which they live. Every constitution has a distinctive character that first brings it into existence and then keeps it in being. A democratic character produces democracy, and an oligarchical character produces oligarchy. In every case, the better the character, the better the government.

Exercising any ability or art requires prior training and the formation of habits; clearly, the practice of virtue does too. Since the entire city pursues one end, everyone should plainly receive the same education, provided publicly rather than privately. At present, each person looks after his own children independently and arranges whatever separate instruction he considers best. But training in matters of common concern should be shared by all. Nor should we think that a citizen belongs to himself alone. All citizens belong to the state; each is a part of it, and caring for a part cannot be separated from caring for the whole. On this point the Lacedaemonians deserve praise: they devote the greatest attention to their children and make education a public responsibility.

We cannot deny that education should be governed by law and undertaken by the state. What this public education should be like, however, and how the young should be educated, remain open questions. [Compare sections 11–16, and Nicomachean Ethics X.9, section 13.] People disagree profoundly about what should be taught, whether the aim is virtue or the best life. Nor is it clear whether education should concern itself more with intellectual or moral virtue. Present practice leaves us perplexed. No one knows which principle should guide us: should training pursue practical usefulness, virtue, or higher knowledge? Each of these aims has its advocates. There is no agreement about the means either. People begin with different conceptions of virtue and naturally disagree about how to practise it. Children must certainly learn useful things that are necessary, but they need not learn everything useful. Occupations divide into those worthy of free people and those that are not. Young children should acquire only the kinds of useful knowledge that do not debase them. Any occupation, art, or science that makes a free person's body, soul, or mind less capable of practising virtue is debasing. Hence we call trades that deform the body vulgar, and the same applies to paid employment, which engrosses and degrades the mind. Some liberal arts are suitable for a free person to learn, but only to a certain extent. Pursuing them too closely in the effort to attain perfection produces the same harmful effects. The purpose for which someone acts also makes a considerable difference. Learning or doing something for oneself, for one's friends, or for the sake of excellence does not appear servile. Doing exactly the same thing for other people may be regarded as menial and fit for a slave. [Compare III.4, section 13.] As I have already remarked, the established subjects of instruction are partly liberal and partly illiberal. There are four customary branches of education: reading and writing, physical training, music, and, sometimes, drawing. Reading, writing, and drawing are considered useful in various aspects of life, while physical training is thought to cultivate courage. Music presents a difficulty. Today most people practise it for pleasure. It was originally included in education, however, because nature herself, as we have often said, requires us to use leisure well as well as to work well. I must repeat that leisure is the first principle of all activity. Both work and leisure are necessary, but leisure is better than work. We must therefore ask in earnest what activities we ought to pursue during the time we have at leisure. Plainly, we should not simply amuse ourselves, since that would make amusement life's purpose. Such a conclusion is inconceivable. Yet amusement is particularly necessary during serious work: someone working hard needs relaxation, and amusement supplies it, whereas work always involves effort and exertion. We should therefore introduce amusements at suitable times, using them as remedies. The feeling they create relaxes the soul, and their pleasure brings rest. Leisure itself supplies pleasure, happiness, and the enjoyment of life. These belong to those at leisure, not to those occupied with work. A busy person is pursuing an end he has not yet reached, whereas happiness is itself an end, which everyone associates with pleasure rather than pain. People understand this pleasure differently, according to their individual habits. The best person's pleasure is best and comes from the noblest sources. Clearly, then, some kinds of learning and education should be pursued so that we can enjoy leisure, and valued for their own sake. Knowledge useful for business, by contrast, is necessary and serves other ends. Our forefathers therefore included music in education neither because it was necessary nor because it was useful. It is not necessary, and it is not useful in the way reading and writing are useful for earning money, managing a household, acquiring knowledge, or participating in politics. Nor does it serve drawing's purpose of helping us judge artists' work more accurately, or physical training's purpose of providing health and strength. Music provides neither of these advantages. Its remaining purpose is intellectual enjoyment during leisure. This apparently explains its introduction into education: it was thought to be one way a free person should spend leisure. As Homer says—

'How fine it is to invite people to a delightful feast!' Later he describes others inviting 'the singer who would bring pleasure to them all'. [An alternative interpretation, perhaps intended by Aristotle though not the passage's original meaning, is 'to invite Thalia to the feast'. Odyssey XVII, 385.]

Elsewhere Odysseus says that there is no better way to live than when 'people's hearts are joyful, and the guests seated in order in the hall listen to the singer's voice'. Clearly, then, parents should give their sons a kind of education pursued for its nobility and its fitness for free people, rather than for necessity or usefulness. Whether there is just one such subject or several, what these subjects are, and how to teach them must be decided later. For now, we can say that the ancients support our position. Their view is evident from music's place among the accepted, traditional branches of education. Children should also clearly learn certain useful skills, such as reading and writing, not merely for their practical value but because these open the way to many other kinds of knowledge. Drawing can be taught with a similar purpose. Its aim should not be to prevent mistakes in one's purchases, or to protect against deception when buying and selling goods, but to develop judgment of beauty in the human form. Constantly pursuing utility is unworthy of free and noble souls. In education, moreover, habits plainly must precede reasoning, and the body must be trained before the mind. Boys should therefore be entrusted to the trainer, who develops the proper bodily condition, and to the wrestling-master, who teaches them the exercises.

Among states that now seem most attentive to children's upbringing, some seek to produce the physique of an athlete. In doing so, however, they damage children's bodily form and restrict their growth. [Odyssey IX, 7; compare Plato, Republic VII, 535 and following.]

The Lacedaemonians avoid this particular mistake, but make their children brutal through exhausting exercises that they believe will produce courage. In truth, as we have repeatedly said, education must not pursue this or any other single aim exclusively. Even supposing their chosen aim to be correct, they fail to reach it. Among both barbarians and animals, courage accompanies a gentle, lion-like disposition rather than the greatest ferocity. Many peoples are perfectly willing to kill and eat human beings, including the

Achaeans and Heniochi who live around the Black Sea. Other tribes farther inland are equally bad or worse. All live by plundering, yet lack courage. It is well known that the Lacedaemonians surpassed others while diligently maintaining their arduous drill, but now suffer defeat both in warfare and in athletic contests. Their former superiority came not from the particular method of training their young, but from training them at a time when others did not. We should conclude that nobility, rather than brutality, deserves first place. No wolf or other wild creature will confront a truly noble danger; that belongs to the courageous man. Parents who devote their children to gymnastics while neglecting the education they need actually debase them. They make them useful to the state in only one capacity, and our argument shows that even in that capacity they fall below others. We should judge the Lacedaemonians by their present condition, not their past. Their educational system now has competitors, whereas formerly it did not.

We agree that physical exercises belong in education, and that children's exercises should be gentle. Strict regimens and painful exertion must be avoided so that bodily growth is not damaged. Olympic victors provide striking evidence of the harm caused by excessive training in childhood. No more than two or three have won prizes both as boys and as adults, because early training and strenuous exercises wore out their constitutions. After boyhood, three years should be given to other studies; the period after that can be devoted to demanding exercise and a strict regimen. People should not work their minds and bodies strenuously at the same time. The two kinds of effort interfere with each other: bodily exertion hinders mental work, and mental exertion hinders the body.

We have already raised some questions about music. Let us return to them and pursue them further, using our remarks as an introduction to this or any other inquiry into the subject. It is difficult to determine what music is or why anyone should study it. Is it for amusement and relaxation, like sleep or drinking? These are pleasant rather than good in themselves, and, as Euripides says, they 'put an end to care'. People therefore place them alongside music and use all three—sleep, drinking, and music—with some adding dance. Or should we say that music contributes to virtue because it shapes our minds and trains us to enjoy the right pleasures, just as our bodies acquire their character through

physical training? [Compare Plato, Republic VII, 537 B; Euripides, Bacchae, 380.] Or does it serve the enjoyment of leisure and the cultivation of the mind, a third possibility? Plainly, education for the young cannot aim at amusement, since learning is painful rather than pleasant. Nor is intellectual enjoyment appropriate to boys of that age. It is the final end, and what is still incomplete cannot attain completeness or the end. Perhaps, however, boys learn music so they can enjoy amusement as adults. If that is the purpose, why must they learn to perform themselves? Why not follow the Persian and Median kings, who gain pleasure and instruction from listening to others? Surely musicians who have devoted their lives to the art as their profession perform better than those who practise merely as part of their education. If personal study is necessary, the same reasoning would require them to learn cookery, which is absurd. Even if we grant that music shapes character, the objection remains. Why learn to perform ourselves? Why not acquire sound judgment and the right pleasures by listening to others, as the Lacedaemonians do? They claim to judge good and bad melodies correctly without studying music. Again, suppose music promotes cheerfulness and cultivated intellectual enjoyment. The same objection persists: why learn it ourselves instead of enjoying others' performances? Our conception of the gods illustrates the point. In the poets, Zeus neither sings nor plays the lyre himself. Indeed, we call professional performers vulgar; a free man would not sing or play unless drunk or joking. Let us leave these matters for the moment.

The first question is whether music belongs in education at all. Of the three distinct purposes mentioned in our discussion, which should we assign to it: education, amusement, or intellectual enjoyment? It can be placed under all three and seems to partake of each. Amusement provides relaxation, and relaxation must be pleasant, since it remedies the pain produced by work. Everyone also acknowledges that intellectual enjoyment includes pleasure as well as nobility, for happiness consists of both. Everyone agrees, too, that music, with or without singing, is among the most pleasurable things. As Musaeus says,

'For mortals, song is the sweetest thing of all.' We therefore rightly bring music into gatherings and celebrations, because it gladdens people's hearts. This alone would give us grounds for training the young in it. Harmless pleasures accord with life's complete purpose and also offer relaxation. People seldom reach that ultimate end, but often pause along the way to rest and amuse themselves. They do so not only for some further good, but also for pleasure itself. It may therefore be good for them sometimes to find refreshment in music.

People sometimes make amusement their final aim. The true end probably includes pleasure, though not pleasure of an ordinary or inferior kind. They confuse the inferior pleasure with the higher one, and while pursuing the latter encounter the former, because every pleasure resembles the end of action. The final end is not chosen for the sake of some future good. Likewise, the pleasures just described do not look towards a future benefit, but back towards what has already happened: they relieve previous exertion and pain. This may explain why people look for happiness in ordinary pleasures.

Music is pursued not only to relieve past exertion, but also as recreation. Who can say that, alongside this use, it has no higher purpose? Its pleasure is natural and therefore suits every age and character; everyone feels and shares in it. But beyond this common pleasure, may music not also influence character and the soul? It must do so if it affects our dispositions. The songs of Olympus and many other composers demonstrate that it does. They unquestionably inspire enthusiasm, and enthusiasm is a feeling belonging to the soul's ethical part. Moreover, hearing imitations moves our feelings in sympathy even without melody or rhythm. Music gives pleasure, while virtue consists in taking pleasure, loving, and hating in the right way. Clearly, then, we should chiefly cultivate the ability to judge correctly and to delight in good dispositions and noble actions. Rhythm and melody imitate anger, gentleness, courage, temperance, and virtues and vices generally, with a force scarcely less than the feelings themselves. We know this from our own experience: when we listen to music of this kind, our souls themselves undergo a change. Feeling in this way about an imitation is close to feeling the same way about reality. For example, if someone enjoys looking at a statue solely for its beauty, he must also enjoy seeing

the original. Other senses, such as taste and touch, offer nothing resembling moral qualities. Sight offers a little, since visible forms have some moral character and everyone responds to them to that extent. Yet shapes and colours are signs of moral dispositions rather than imitations of them. These signs appear only when emotion affects the body. Their connection with morals is slight; nevertheless, insofar as it exists, young people should look at the works of Polygnotus or another painter or sculptor who expresses moral character, rather than those of Pauson. Mere melodies, by contrast, already imitate character. Musical modes differ fundamentally, and each affects its listeners differently. Some, such as the so-called Mixolydian, make people solemn and sad. Relaxed harmonies weaken the mind. Others produce a measured, steady disposition, which seems to be the distinctive effect of the Dorian. The Phrygian arouses enthusiasm. Philosophical writers on this branch of education have examined the subject well, supporting their reasoning with observed facts. Rhythms follow the same principles. Some express rest, others movement; among those expressing movement, some are more vulgar, others nobler. We have said enough to establish that music can form character and therefore belongs in the education of the young. It suits their age, because young people avoid anything that is not made pleasant if they can, and music is naturally sweet. [Compare Poetics 2, section 2, and 6, section 15; Plato, Republic III, 398–399.] There seems to be something within us that has a natural affinity with musical harmonies and rhythms. This leads some philosophers to call the soul a harmony, while others say it possesses harmony.

We must now settle the question already raised: should children themselves learn to sing and play? Actually practising the art clearly makes a considerable difference to character. Judging other people's performance well is difficult, perhaps impossible, for someone who has never performed. Besides, children need something to occupy them. Archytas' rattle was an excellent invention: people give it to children to keep them amused and stop them breaking things in the house, since a young child cannot remain still. A rattle is a toy suited to an infant's mind; musical education is a rattle or toy for older children. We conclude that children should learn music in a way that makes them performers as well as judges.

It is easy to answer the question of what is or is not appropriate to different ages. We can also readily answer those who object that studying music is vulgar. First, those who will judge performances must themselves have experience of performing. They should begin practising while young, though when older they can be excused from actual performance. Through the knowledge acquired in youth, they should have learned to recognize what is good and to take pleasure in it. Second, music's allegedly degrading influence is a question of degree. We shall have no difficulty settling it once we consider how far free people being trained for political virtue should pursue this art, what kinds of melodies and rhythms they should be allowed to use, and which instruments should be employed in teaching them to play. The instrument itself, as well as the manner of teaching, makes a difference. [Compare sections 5–8 and, above, section 7.] Our answer to the objection depends on these distinctions, since certain ways of teaching and learning music may indeed have a degrading effect. Clearly, musical study must neither interfere with the work of mature life nor degrade the body or make it unfit for civic or military duties, whether for the early practice of those duties or for their later study.

Students will reach the right level if they stop before acquiring the techniques used in professional competitions. They should not pursue the astonishing displays of execution now fashionable in those contests, which have spread from competitions into education. Let young people continue their studies until they can enjoy noble melodies and rhythms, rather than merely the ordinary pleasures in music that appeal to every slave and child, and even to some animals.

These principles also tell us which instruments to use. The flute, and other instruments demanding great technical skill, such as the harp, should be excluded from education. We should admit only instruments that develop intelligent understanding of music or other educational subjects. Besides, the flute does not have a beneficial moral influence; it is excessively exciting. Its appropriate use is in performances meant to relieve the passions rather than instruct. A further objection is that playing it prevents use of the voice, reducing its educational value. [Compare section 3.] The ancients were therefore right to forbid the flute to young people and free men, although they had previously allowed it. As wealth brought them more leisure, their ideas of excellence grew loftier. Elated by their successes before and after the Persian War, they pursued every branch of knowledge with more enthusiasm than judgment, and introduced the flute into education. A Choragus at Lacedaemon directed the Chorus with a flute. At Athens the instrument became so popular that most free men could play it. The tablet dedicated by Thrasippus when he supplied the Chorus for Ecphantides illustrates its popularity. Later experience taught people to distinguish what genuinely contributes to virtue from what does not. They rejected the flute and several other old instruments: the Lydian harp, the many-stringed lyre, the 'heptagon', 'triangle', 'sambuca', and similar instruments, intended merely to entertain listeners and requiring exceptional manual skill. The ancient story of Athene inventing the flute and then throwing it away also has meaning. The explanation that the goddess disliked it because it distorted her face was not a bad one. But there is a better reason for saying she rejected it: learning to play the flute contributes nothing to the mind, whereas we associate Athene with knowledge and art.

We therefore reject instruments designed for professionals, as well as the professional manner of teaching music. By 'professional' I mean the training adopted for competitions. Here a performer practises the art not to improve himself, but to give pleasure to his listeners, and pleasure of a vulgar kind at that. This is why the performance of such [compare Plato, Republic III, 399 D]

music is the work of a paid performer, rather than a free person. The performers are debased by it because the goal they pursue is low. The spectator's vulgarity lowers the character of the music and consequently of the musicians. They direct their attention towards him: he makes them what they are, and even moulds their bodies through the movements he expects them to display. We must also consider the question of rhythms and harmonies. Should we use every kind in education, or distinguish between them? If we make a distinction, should we adopt the one used by people engaged in education, or should we choose another? We can see that melody and rhythm together produce music. We therefore need to know the influence each has on education, and whether to prefer excellence in melody or excellence in rhythm. Many contemporary musicians have discussed these questions very well, as have philosophers with considerable practical experience of musical education. To them we refer anyone seeking a more exact study of the subject. Here we shall discuss it only from the legislator's standpoint, with attention to its general principles.

We accept certain philosophers' division of melodies into ethical melodies, melodies of action, and melodies that stir passion or enthusiasm. Each, they say, has a corresponding mode or harmony. But we also maintain that music should be studied for several benefits, not just one. It serves, first, education; second, purgation—we leave that word unexplained for now, but shall discuss it more precisely when we examine poetry; and third, intellectual enjoyment, relaxation, and recovery after exertion. We must therefore use every harmony, though not all in the same way. Education should favour ethical melodies, while melodies of action and passion may be enjoyed by listening to others perform them. Feelings such as pity, fear, and enthusiasm are exceptionally strong in some souls and influence everyone to some degree. Some people fall into religious frenzy; we see sacred melodies release them from it, bringing healing and purgation to their souls. Those subject to pity or fear, and emotional temperaments generally, experience something similar. Other people likewise experience these feelings in their own degree, each being moved by something that has a particular influence on him. Everyone is in some sense purged by the experience, and their souls are left lighter and filled with pleasure. Melodies of purgation likewise give people harmless pleasure. These are the harmonies and melodies in which theatre musicians should be invited to compete. But there are two kinds of spectators: free, educated people, and a vulgar crowd of artisans, labourers, and similar people. Competitions and performances should provide relaxation for the second group too. Their music will correspond to their minds. Just as their minds depart from the natural condition, so exaggerated and corrupted harmonies represent a comparable departure. People enjoy what is natural to them, so professional musicians may perform this inferior music for an inferior audience. For education, however, as I have already said, we should employ ethical modes and melodies, such as the Dorian, together with any others approved by philosophers who possess musical training. Socrates in the

Republic wrongly keeps the Phrygian alongside the Dorian as the only modes. His rejection of the flute makes this all the more mistaken, since the Phrygian is among modes what the flute is among instruments: both excite and stir the emotions.

Poetry confirms this. The flute most appropriately expresses Bacchic frenzy and similar feelings, which suit the Phrygian harmony better than any other. The dithyramb, for example, is acknowledged to be Phrygian. Musical experts offer many proofs, including the story that Philoxenus tried to compose his Tales as a Dorian dithyramb, found it impossible, and reverted to the more suitable Phrygian. Everyone agrees that Dorian music is the most solemn and manly. We hold that one should avoid extremes and follow the mean. Since the Dorian stands between the other harmonies, the Phrygian and Lydian, it plainly follows that the young should be taught Dorian music.

We must keep two principles in view: what is possible and what is fitting. Everyone should aim at these, but both depend on age. Older people, whose powers have declined, cannot readily sing demanding melodies. Nature herself seems to indicate that their songs should be more relaxed. Musicians are therefore right to criticize Socrates for excluding relaxed harmonies from education on the ground that they intoxicate. He does not mean intoxication in the usual sense, since wine tends to excite people, but rather that these harmonies lack vigour. Looking ahead to the time when they begin to age, people should therefore practise gentler harmonies and melodies alongside the others. If any harmony suits very young children and combines order with educational value, we should clearly use it. The Lydian seems above all to have this quality. Education should thus rest on three principles: the mean, the possible, and the fitting.
